- _ VERY WINDY WEATHER.—A gala day. INFANTRY, BUT NOT FOOT.—Children in arms. MELTING CEA/UM—The frost begins to give. CURRENT LITERATURE.—" Books in the running brooks. SAYING or SOLlCiToßs.—Noyember is at best a petti- fogger. When is a father most like a serpent? When he casts •f his kin (his skin). Cos. FOR CASVISTS.—Can a man be said to indulge in the lie circumstantial when he lies at full length? RAISING THE WlND.—Bore is evidently quite a literary wind. He is a Norther (an author), don't you see. CABAIAN's COUPLET. If she be not "fare" for me, What care I whose fare she be? Meet. rou MALLOCE.—What is the difference between eternity and life? One is " the great peut-a re," the other 56a very small potato." WARFARE ON LAND AND WATER.—Pitched battles are mostly fought by land forces, but, in general, without any pitch. In action on board ship there is usually both pitch und tar. ARABIAN 7".ZIGHT Tuonentes.—" The only person who, to My mind," observed an eminent British Associate, "ever seemed to have a real power of concentration, was the gigantic Genie who returned into the little earthenware ceseel from which he had been released by the Fisherman." 'But this was only in fiction, after all. , RECREATIONS IN SCIENCE.—Youth, home for the boll- can procure bladders of india-rubber, which are sold in the streets, inflate them with hydrogen, coat them over oatside with luminous paint, and let up the balloons thus made after dark. Shortly afterwards letters from scientific ob- servers will appear in the newspapers, describing meteors which they have seen floating about in the sky. LINES TO IrY LADY LOVE. By a Medical Student. Fair though thine outward form and face, 'Tis all integument, that owes 17n5tab1e tissues' transient grace; • The cellular and adipose. Behind them I discern and prize A beauty deeper than the skin It's equal there is none at Guy's. The splendid skeleton within ALL THE YEAR ROUND. —(Weather Mnemonics, war ranted always to apply.) January, bltek and beastly; February, wind north-eastiv ; March, neuralgic, nipping, nasty; April, pluviose and hlasty ; May, wet, prematurely torrin ; June, dull, glacial, Arctic, horrid; July, delugy and dismal; August, drowned in floods abysmal; September, biting, blustrous, boggy; October, frosty, frowsy, foggy; November, sort of short sham summer ; December, cold as June, bat glummer. The STEAM-LALTNCH IN VENICE.—(Sic transit gloria nundi.) 'AndsOme 'Arriet : "Ow my! If it 'yn't that bloomin' old Temple Bar, as they did wey with onto' Fleet- street!" Mr. Belleville (referring to Guide-book) : "Now, it 'yn't! Its the fymons Bridge o' Sighs, as Byron went and stood on; 'im as wrote 'Our Boys,' yer know !" 'And- some 'Arriet : "Well, I never! It 'yn't much of a Size, any'ow ! " Mr. Belleville : " 'Ear ! 'ear ! Fustryte ! " DISTINGUISHID AMAZE/YRS.—THE POET—poetic Hus- band: "Hear this Sonnet of Mine, Emily. It has cost me much Labour; and though say it who shouldn't, it's not unworthy of Shilespere or Milton." Prosaic Wife: "Cer- tainly, my Love. But I wish you wouldn't write Sonnets on our best cream-laid Note-Paper ! I must get you some Foolscap !" Recrritoctrv.—Northern Gamekeeper: "Will ye gie me Some Oil to my Guns this Morning, Cook ? " Cook: "If ye watt Oil free me, Keeper,' ye'll need to mind. MA Name's no Cook—ma Name's Misthress Micphairson !" Gamekeeper (with a sniff): " Weel, gin ye're no to be Cook,' I'm nae to be ' Keeper'! be as gude as gie me • Maisther Forr-biss' ! !" BISHOP MARLBY.—Bishop Marley had a good deal of the humour of Swift. Once when the footman was out of the way, be ordered his coachman to fetch some water from the well. To this the coachman objected, that his business was to drive, not to run errands. "Well, then," said Mar- ley, "bring out the coach and four, set the pitcher inside, and drive to the well."—a service which was several times repeated, to the great amusement of the villagers. AMONG THE PHILISTINES —Grigsby : Do you know the Joneses ?" Mrs. Brown: "No we—er—don't care to know Business People, as a rule, although my Husband's in B asi- nese ; but then Ha's in the Coffee Business—and they're all Gentlemen in the Coffee Business, you know!" Grigsby (who always suite himself to his Company): "Really, now! Why, that's more than can be said of the Army, the Navy, the Church, the Bar, or even the House of Lords. I don't • Wonder at your being rather Exclusive ! " When Burns's " Auld Farmer" addressed his New Year's morning salutation to his "sold mare Maggie " " A guid new year I wish thee, Maggie • Rae, there's a ripp to thy auld boggle." he does not seem to have been in the least aware that he was observing a custom that had.come down to him from heathen ancestors in their celebration of yule. Dr. Jamieson, in his Scotch dictionary, tells U 3 that it was a custom to keep the last handful of corn gathered from the previous harvest, and on the morning of Christmas Day to divide it amongst the horses and cows of the farm as a sort of henget of coming plenty at the next harvest. It is impossible to doubt that this is a custom dating back to the ancient ob- servances of Yule-tide, transferred to New Year's Day, with much else of an analogous character, at the "godly and thorough reformation" in Scotland. 'The well-spread table ' also, which used to be, and perhaps still is, in many parts set opposite the hOuse-door to let in the New Yeir 'With snit- able hospitality, is in all probability connected with the older custom of letting in Yule in a similar manner. This connection of New Year's rejoicings with the Chris- tian feast of Christmas, and through it with the pre-Chris- tian Yule and Saturnalia, explains the constancy with which popular observances have stuck to the Ist of January, even when the New Year has been formally and legally reckoned to begin at a different time. Down to 1751 the legal New Year's Day in England was March the 25th, though Scot- land was before the southern kingdom in abaudoning this ecclesiastical mode of reckoning. But to popular feeling the New Year, even in England, began on January the Ist; and so far as it was customary to observe the opening of the New Year at all it was this latter day, and not March 25th, that was celebrated. But then, as now, much more was made of the New Year's festival in Scotland than in England, and the reason is obvious. The Scotch people were animated by a much more thorough determination than were their southern neighbours to throw off every yes. • tige of Romish ceremonial, and they looked upon the Christ- Inas feast as an intolerable remnant of the old leaven. Hence the ancient festivities were suppressed, not merely by autho- rity, but by the almost unanimous resolve of the people. Still, the old Adam is strong in his propensity to junketing .and carousing. The ancient fathers of the Church were compelled to make a compromise with him by christening the heathen festivals, and devoting them to ecclesiastical memories. The Puritan democracy of Scotland did not take that course ; but, by a happy thought, transferred to the let of January a considerable number of the merry customs formerly belonging to Christmas Day. A very remarkable instance of the transfer of Christmas or Yule observances to New Year's Day is given by Dr. Jamie- son. It used to be the custom on Christmas morning to skim the surface of the household well at the earliest mo- ment after midnight. Special blessings were supposed to attend the member of the house who succeeded first in getting, as the phrase was, the "skim or ream'ci'fe m (cream) of the well. It was ales) customary te take aha n the f store of corn, and to gather kail at the same time. Part, at any rate, of these observances was transfereed to New Year's Day. In describing the customs of New Year'e Eve, Nicoll has the following lines : Ye-all struck —twa neighbour hizzies raise, An' liltin', gaed a sad gate. The flower o' the well to our house gad, An' the bonniest lad get." That this superstition had a heathen origin, and one of very remote antiquity, there can be no doubt. In a well-known passage of the 2Eneid, quoted also by Dr. Jamieson, Nneas is described as drawing water from the topmost surface of a fon-dein while he fills the air with loud invocations of the gods —Good Words. ARCHBISHOP Tieeorreoer.—A good story is told of Tillot- son's encounter with Sir John Trevor, the Tory trimmer, Master of the Rolls, and at one time Speaker of the House o! Commons. Trevor met the archbishop one day in a pub- lic thoroughfare near the House of Lords. He hated Tillot- son for being a Low Churchman, so he had the ill-breeding to mutter audibly as he passed, "I hate a knave in lawn sleeves." Fortunately,Tillotson had his wits about him, and instead of being startled into helplessness by this extra- ordinary assault, he replied to it with delightful effect. Stopping in his walk, the primate arrested the lawyer by a sign, and then, after a minute's pause, during which he coolly surveyed his enemy with evident amusement, he oh- -erred, with deliberate enunciation, and in a tone of play- ulness rather than irritation, "And I hate a knave in any eelreS." e EPPS'S CoCOA.—GRATEFIIL AND COITFORTING. —" By a thorough knowledge of the natural laws whlcrhefguolvaeprnp the lt lon o oper- ations of digestion and nutrition, and by aca the fine properties of well•selected cocoa, Mr. Epps has prov:ded Our breakfast tables with a delicately-flavoured beverage which may save us many heavy doctors' bills. The shooting party which has just been staying with Lord Windsor, at Etewell Grange, brought down 2,400 head, every one of given way. A.liberal supply was sent to every wtehniacnbt,svacosmplimentary hampers were despatched to many 'neighbours, and BOnle eight or ten hospitals, some of them many miles away, received very large hampers. There is a smack of feudal open-handedness of old about this distribu. tion. A good story of a foolish tenant comes from Brussels. A householder applied to the town authorities to have his roof repaired. The request was treated as a joke, but the in- quiaitiveness of one of the officials led to a very curious dis- covery. It appeared that some years ago the houses in a certain street were inhabited by very questionable charac. I tens, and it was decided to pull the whole street down and I rebuild it. All the houses were demolished except one, and I this one, it was found, the foolish tenant had occupied far ' ten years without paying any rent. If he had kept quiet I for twenty years longer, he could have claimed the house I as his own. EFFECT OF FROZEN FOOD lIPON Asruar.s. —The effect of frozen grass and other herbage is sometimes disastrous to the health of the animals fed upon it. Usually my cows I spend the forenoon in the stalls ruminating and digesting ' the morning's feed, and are not turned out until noon, when they have the range of a pasture. But one day they were turned out earlier, and while the frost was thick upon the grass in places where it was shaded by a hill from the early morning sun. The cows fed upon this frozen grass, and oni being brought in, in the afternoon, one was found with the udder very hard and hot and inflamed. From 7 quarts of , milk at a meal she fell off at once to less than 2 quarts, and half the udder had no milk. After a whole week's care the udder is not well. Here is a week's product of a good ' cow lost by one little neglect and thoughtless departure ' from a regular system of management. But a Curious effect occurred in churning the cream three or four days after this frozen grass was eaten. The whole churning of 251 b. of batter was of an unusually light colour and defective in flavour ; and, more than that, it required several days to completely recover the quality and appearance of the butter. —Xis York Times. THE MATTER or PURE MILK.—A letter from the Ameri- can Consul-Geaeral at Frankfort relates how the difficulty of getting pare milk is dealt with in that city. A police rinspection had already been established, the lactometer being I also in common family use. Oat of 309 analysds made in 1880 in 1,,1 innheim 245 showed impurity, and 650 reich- marks were collected in a single month as fines, at the rate of 1 mark for each 1 per cent. of water added. Bat as a , means of coping with not only this difficulty, but with un- " evenness of quality, injury frcm carrying. dirt and disease , in the anhnals, the Franckfurtur Milchkind Anstalt was established four years ago, largely by the medical profes- sion. It is managed by a commission of three physicians, one veterinary surgeon, and one chemist. The cows kept are of two kinds, only, carefully selected; they are kept con- stantly in stalls, fed with care and perfect uniformity on dry food, with every attention given to ventilation and cleanli- ness. To insure uniformity of quality and dilate the power for harm of a single animal which might possibly become unhealthy, the milk of every ten different animals is poured I in together. The milk for delivery is put into quart bottles, I stopped with wax, and sealed with the Anstalt seal. So I strictly is the cleanliness required that the empty bottles are washed twice a week in a weak solution of soda, and the corka (which are only used a short time) are boiled in a soda solution after each use. Spring waggons, with apertures for ventilation, are used for delivery. In hot weather they are covered with cocoa mats, and no waggon must take out more than can be delivered in three and a half hours. The chemist tests one bottle daily. The Anita-it milk retails for 50 pfennings (about 61) per quart, and it is claimed to I have actually diminished the number of nurses employed in Frankfort, and to have produced eurprisingly good results otherwise. These are so noticeable, that a benevolent move- ment has been started to provide the Anetalt milk at half price for all infants supported. by artificial nourishment dar- ing the first year of their existence. AMERICAN COMPETITION.—A fresh view of the causes of the successful competition of American agricultural pro- ducts in the European markets is put forward by Mr. Henry Semler, to German resident in California. Mr. Semler has worked for ten years on American farms in the Eastern and Western Stites, as well aeon the Pacific cost, and has writ- ten a book for the encouragement of his countrymen, in which he contends that the greet advantage enjoyed by the Amer'can agriculturist is not a natural one against which it would be hopeless to contend, but that it lies in his superior methods and habits. The natural fertility of the soil and the low price of land are in great part neutralised by the cost of transportation to Europe. The particular points in which the farmers of the United States excel their German competitors are these. They use machinery, improved tools,light whicles, and. all sorts of labour-saving and time- saving appliances. Then, again, the dress of the labourers, , the hours of work, and. the domestic arrangements generally are arranged with a view to the most profitable application of labour. Farther advantages arise out of the prevalence of the habit of temperance and a wide application of the principle of the organisation of labour. Thus there are farms devoted specially to wheat, .to dairy products, to peaches, to strawberries, and there are farmers who apply themselves to little else but the rearing of turkeys. On all these and other questions of management the writer gives copious details, and declares that he sees no reason why Ger- man farmers should not adopt American ways at home, since they so readily accustom themselves to them when they go Westward. The author offers some remarka which do not support the popular notion that the successful competition of the Chinese labourer in the United States is his frugality. Mr. Semler has worked side by side with Chinese labourers on Californian farms, and he assures us that although they live in narrow quarters their food and clothing are just as abundant and costly as that of Americans and Europeans in the same position. They are able to do more work because they are better organised than their competitors. It thus appears, according to the testimony of this experienced writer, that not only have European farmers much to learn or, the question of organisation from those of America, but also that both may with advantage take a leaf out of the book of John Chinaman, to whom steam engines and elec. tricity are as yet practically unknown. . TakvspoaTitza FRESII l'vfEay.—The Vienna method of sending fresh mutton and beef to the London and. Paris markets appears to have met with considerable success. 9.trached to the slaughterhouses is a cooling-room with well fitted double doors, and as much as possible protected against external influences of temperature. At one end of the cooling-room is a large blowing engine, Which Sucks the air from the roof of the room, and then forces it through a tribe behind the ice-holder at the opposite end of the room. I This is a large ice case, to be filled from without, in which the air to be cooled. comes directly in contact with the ice. I Before the flesh has quite stiffened, it is treated. with chemi- cally pure borax. This is applied to the meat, in the form , of fine gunpowder, by means of a bellows similar to that I used in France for sulphurisation of vioe stocks. It is poured through a funnel into the bellows, the filling hole is stopped, and the substance is then blown out through the dust-producing apparatus introduced at the point. The quantity of borax used is so small that it is presently dis- , solved by the moisture on the surface of the meat. It is, I therefore, not perceptible by the eye, especially as, also, it 1 does not in the least alter the aspect of the meat. After I complete cooling, the meat is bound in linen sacks, and is I ready for being sent off. The cooling-house is situated I close to the railway, and it is of the highest importance that the cooled meat be put directly into the ice.svaggons. The principle of the cooling in these is, similarly, air-tight closure, steady motion of the inner air, and the forcing of this through an ice-chest. The air is. drawn through a funnel in the roof of the waggon, passes through a tube into an air bag, and from this through slits into the ice chest, filled with ice, which it leaves on the other side. -

THE LAND QUESTION. xiv. In Saxon times every freeholder had the full liberty of sporting over his land, provided he ab- stained from the King's forests, but after the Norman Conquest a new doctrine was asserted, and the right of taking all beasts of chase or venery wherever they might be found, and without regard to the ownership of the soil, was claimed by the Sovereign for him- self, or for" such only as he should duly authorise. The early Norman kings were so passionately de- voted to the pleasures of the chase that they depopu- lated whole districts without the consent of the owners or giving any compensation for the damage done, and in order to preserve the game the killing of any animal was punishable in the same manner as the killing of a man. In the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle of the year 1037 we read of William the Conqueror —" He made large forests for the deer, and enacted laws therewith, so that whoever killed a hart or a hind should be blinded. As he forbade killing the deer, so also the boars ; and he loved the tall stags as if he were their father. He also appointed concern- ing hares that they should go free. The rich com- plained and the poor murmured, but he was so sturdy that he reeked nought of them. They must will all I that the King willed, if they would live or would I keep their lands, or would hold their possessions, or 1 be maintained in their rights." Does not this descrip- tion represent the same spirit which exists to-day 1 among the game preserving landlords and the posi- tion of their yearly tenants ? In the reign of King John winged game was included among the Sove- reign's prerogatives, but the seventies of the Forest' Laws were so insupportable that the barons appliedl pressure to the Monarch, and by the Charts de Forests (9 Henry III.) A.D. 1225, confirmed by Edward I. I MI 1299, large districts were disafforested and freed from the Forest Laws, and the Royal Forests were stripped of their most oppressive privileges and regu- lations. The great landlords, however, having estab- lished their own rights as against the Crown did not extend similar rights to their tenants. They obtained grants from the Crown of chase and free warren in their manors, and exercised against their tenants the same rigour against which they had themselves rebelled. Sir William Waclestone (who was created Justice of the Court of Common Pleas in 1770), re- ferring to the Forest Laws, says, " From this root 1 has sprung a bastard slip, known by the name of the Game Laws, now arrived to. a wantoning in its highest vigour, both founded on the same unreason- able notion of permanent property in wild creatures, and both productive of the same tyranny, to the com- mons [i.e., the people], but with this difference, that the Forest Laws established a mighty hunter through- out the land, the Game Laws have raised a little Nim- rod in every manor." The same eminent authority further says, "It is indisputable that the wild deni- zens of the field, marsh, and forest, known to lawyers under the name Feres natures, are the common pro- perty of men, be their degree what it may.". So the Game Laws continued with slight variations until 1831, at wleiph time no person was permittedto I kill game unless qualified either by the possession of freehold or leasehold property of the annual value of £lOO, or by holding the status of esquire. Land- owners by virtue of this qualification, and irrespec- tive of agreement, practically exercised the exclusive right of sporting over their lands let to farming tenants. Lords of manors still claimed the right to game on the laids of the copyhold tenants of their i manors, and the sale of game was wholly illegal, and was punished by severe penalties. The unreformed 'Parliament of 1831 (elected so far as the counties were concerned by freeholders, as tenant farmers had then no votes) consisted largely of the nominees of the aristocracy by means of pocket and rotten boroughs, and yet it was compelled by the popular agitation for reform to deal with the Game Laws. They were amended in a sweeping manner, and privilege abolished. The lion. G. C. Brodrick shows that at the present time sporting rights, as understood in England are essentially the creation of statute, and could not exist for a day without legal protection, The semi- wild but semi-domestic animals known as " game " have been well described as "privileged vermin," and would soon become extinct in many parts of the country but for the maintenance of the Game Laws. Even the Game Laws do not countenance, but only recognise, the peculiar custom which is so mischie- vous to good husbandry. The separation of sporting rights from the occupation of land is in itself an anomaly, at variance .with the presumption of Com- mon Law, no less than with that provision in the \ Cism in the tenant, and made the right of sporting rune Act of 1831, which expressly vested the game with the land, unless it should be reserved by deed or agresment. Under this last clause most English 1 landlords took care to keep the game in their own I hands, and prohibited their tenants from keeping it 1 down, while many let the right thus reserved to strangers, who had no motive for exercising it with, any regard for the interests of farmers or the peusblhicis.l The Game Laws are injurious alike to the farmer, theFiargsr,caualtutoraltiliaeboFuarrenar,earn;dtpoeggaenanee damages public.arnag crops. Then there is the immense damage done by ground game, hares and rabbits, for notwithstanding the Ground Game Act of 1880, on the estates where the tenants are subject to six months' notice to quit (and would get it too if they presumed to exercisetheir legal rights) the Act is practically inoperative, as the farmers dare not protect themselves by the destruction of these pests. The gamekeeper of a noble lord in Cheshire clearly illustrated this when he said," Act of Parlia- ment be blowed; anyetenant as meddles wie rappits on this estate will have to go, and sharp too." Here is a specimen of the present position of farmers :—A recent letter in the Liverivol Courier (a Conservative paper by the way) contains the following :—" I will take the two largest landlords within six miles of Liverpool on the Game Question alOne, in face of the Ground Game Act, and ask, 'Will the people of Liver- pool credit it. that these landlords withheld from their tenants this much-needed redress I° So it is, the tenant suffers all the ravages of this game. I can point to farms where they kill 600 head of game over a radius of a few acres in a day, and these farmers must have the game running through the best of their ripening corn, trampling, feeding on it, and otherwise destroying it. A farmer here will tell you that he can't produce per acre within twenty or thirty bushels that the man without game can. Look at the loss to the community. The system of the game- keeper is to produce pheasants under his own fowls by hundreds in the season, and then to carry them to different parts of his beat, laying them beside corn fields, where it will cost him little feed- ing. Now, the farmer has these barn-door fowls trespassing on him, besides as many ducks (wild) that are bred for I - know not what purpose. I lift my voice against this system, and I moreover ad.- vise the farmers to co-operate and see what can be done to lessen this wilful waste." The actual damage done to the crops, however, is only a part of the loss which the farmer has to fear in consequence of the preservation of game, because he has to bear his share of the expense of the prose- cution of poachers and to maintain them and their families while they are in prison, and, to crown all, by the last efforts of the game preservers in Parlia- ment, the rural police have been converted into game- keepers, and thus the expense of preserving game in all its branches is chiefly thrown upon the farmer. It is said sometimes, "Oh, but the farmers are com- pensated for the loss they sustain to their crops!" Are they? Let anyone make proper inquiries in a game preserving district, and he will find it is not so in, at the least, nineteen cases out of twenty. Now, if the game-preserving landlords were con- tent with a moderate quantity of this game which the farmers have to keep, the evil would not be so great as it is, but the recent rage for what is called

" battue shooting," which has been well described as "a mixture of barbarity and snobbery," has led to over preservation, and to the landlord's deriving a considerable income from the results of these mas- sacres, and positively profiting by what has in many cases almost ruined their tenants. To keep free from the charge of making rash assertions, we will take the statement of a Tory Peer, Lord Malmesbury, who in the House of Lords, in, 1862, said "The sum realised every year by the sale of pheasants and partridges alone is £62,500, paid to somebody every year in England—to whom? To the licensed deal- ers? Yes; but where do the licensed dealers get ' their stock? They can't make it. It does not fall from heaven into their shops. Then how does it come there? Do the breeders and owners of game make them a present of it ? No; they also sell it. The great unlicensed dealers in game sell to the little licensed dealers. Will no honourable member, in the Lower House, at any rate, if no noble Lord can be found to do it, more a clause that there shall be a register of game-selling landlords published yearly in every county, to be posted by the side of the list of persons who take out certificates, on village church doors, and that all such registered landlords shall take out licenses for the sale of game? Why are we to have two rules? We boast of England, I that all of us are equal before the law—that here, at any rate, what is sauce for the goose is sauce for the gander. In heaven's name, let us stop this talk, or put the Knights of the Garter and the Thistle on the same level with their humbler brethren, the licensed poulterer." This is not amiss for a Peer Secondly. How do the Game Laws affect the agri- cultural labourer? Small farmers and cottagers with cultivated patches of land have always been suspected of poaching by snaring the hares and rab- bits devouring their vegetables, and it has been the settled policy of landlords to discourage small hold- ings in game-preserving districts, and they have paid exorbitant prices for such small holdings coming into the market, in order to have the occupants under their thumbs, or to pull the houses down and cause the tenants to leave the neighbourhood, which has caused small freeholders and tenants (a most valu- able class) to be seriously diminished in number. The agricultural labourer does not consider it I morally wrong if he has the opportunity of doing a little poaching. As Mr. Joseph Arch told the Parlia- mentary Committee in 1873—" If I were working for an employer and anyone robbed him of the value of a sixpence, I would immediately report it; but if he took a hare, I would not say a word about it." We will take a different sort of witness to Mr. Joseph Arch—viz., the Marquis of Ailesbury. What Bevil° of the labourer? "He comes home to his cottage, , and there is hardly enough to make a dinner for his Iwife and children; over the next hedge are a lot of halt-tamed pheasants, and the temptation is too much for the hungry man, and he commits an offence which those wicked laws constitute a crime, lor which he is to be sent to prison. How can any just man attempt to defend such laws ?" The Bishop of Manchester has given much similar testimony from his experience as a country clergyman; and the fact is that there are annually many thousands of convic- tions for offences under the Game Laws; but though the game preservers, sitting as unpaid magistrates, are very severe on these offences, they seldom scruple themselves to employ well-known quasi-professional poachers as gamekeepers, and wilfully ignore the means by which pheasant- eggs are often procured for , sitting. • Thirdly, the effect of the Game Laws on the coun- try at large is that they diminish the area of land under cultivation, reduce the quantity of food pro- duced, lessen the capital employed on the land, and seriously limit the demand for labour. The conse- quences are that the price of food is to that extent increased, capital has to find outlets elsewhere, often in foreign countries, and the most enterprising la- bourers either migrate to large towns or leave Eng- land altogether, and all this for the sake of the sport of a privileged class, whether aristocracy or plu- tocracy, or both, matters not. Tens of thousands of acres in this country, chiefly in Scotland, well adapted for the pasturage of sheep, and in some cases ordinary farming, have been depopulated of the inhabitants by the wealthy landlords and devoted to "game." It is all very well to ask, " Cannot a man do what he likes with his own ?" but, in the words of Mr. John Stuart Mill, "with regard to land, in everything which he does with it, and in everything which he ilbstains from doing, he is morally bound, and should whenever the case admits be legally compelled, to make his interest and pleasure consistent with the public good." The well worn parrot cry of "confis- cation" may be raised by "privilege when its unjust monopolies are threatened,' but the time will come, and before long, too, when we shall have a Parliament which will endorse the opinion of Lord Chancellor Hatherley, who said," I do not believe that the great I grievances arising from the Game Laws can be re- lieved by any palliations, and therefore they must be entirely got rid of." In conclusion, the Game Laws musl oe abolished, for the following reasons amongst many others : They increase the wealth of a few rich men at the txpense of the rest of the community. They cause great loss to the farmers, and agricul- ture is thereby discou aged, and the demand for labour decreased. • They diminish the quantity of food which the country should produce, and thereby increase the I cost of that which is produced. They find lucrative employment for professional poachers. They demoralise the labourer. They are an obstacle to the letting of land in small I holdings and on secure-leases. When the electors of both town and country (re- inforced by the at present unenfranchised millions in the counties) realise the importance of the ques- tion and insist upon Parliamentary candidates pledg- ing themselves to remedy the present evils the Game Laws will soon be numbered among the things of the past, like their predecessors, the obnoxious Forest Laws.

The Duke of Westminster contradicts the report that he signed the memorial for the remission of the sentence of the bribers. Damage estimated at between £3,000 and £lO,OOO has been caused by fire at a woollen mill at Bingley, occupied by Messrs. J. H. Ackroyd & Co. and Mr. G. Ackroyd, jun. Last year there were 41 election petitions. In 16 cases the elections were declared void, and in nine valid. The rest were not tried. The costs were £7,459 16s. 3d., of which £3,795 19s. 10d. was taxed off. , It is stated that Lord Delawarr proposes early in the session to introduce a Bill in the House of Lords to make it 1 compulsory upon railway companies to employ a continuous brake on all passenger trains. At the Cannock Police Court on Monday, Joseph Holden, a miner, was remanded on a charge of murdering his infant daughter, aged eight weeks, whom he is alleged to have strangled with his hands in a drunken fit. ' REMISSION OF RENT.—The half-yearly rent audit of the tenants on Mr. Leopold Rothschild's estates was held at the King's Head Hotel, Aylesbury, when a remission of 15 per cent on the half year was allowed to the tenantry. The Standard says it is intended that Mr. Herbert Glad- stone, whose services during the last two months have been highly appreciated by the Chief Secretary, shall return to Ireland. It appears from the official returns just issued that the number of volunteers in the country is 203,000, the largest number since the force was formed, and an increase of about 1,600 over last year. The efficients number 200,161, being an increase of 3,223. Mr. Gladstone in reply to a letter on the practice of Mor- mon misionaries, who visit Great Britain for the purpose of decoying young persons to a life of immorality in Utah, says he fears it is not a matter in which he can interfere. He presumes that the young persons go voluntarily. Sir William Harcourt, replying to the memorials praying for the remission of the sentences passed upon the impri- soned bribers, says he is unable to find in the memorials such reasons as would justify him in advieing the Crown to interfere with the sentences pronounced by the judges ap- pointed to administer the law. Three children have lost their lives by burning at Chatham. Their mother went out for a short time, and during her absence a piece of lighted coal flew out of the firegrate and set fire to the children. It is stated that the precaution had been taken of placing a guard in front of the fire. In the Scotch Court of Session on Saturday the widow and children of a miner who was fatally injured while working in one of the shale pits belonging to Young's Paraffin Light Company, recovered the full compensation allowed by the Employers' Liability Act—an amount equiva- lent to three years' earnings. The Cunard steamer Catalonia, outward bound from Queenstown to New York, and the Dundee clipper ship Helenslea, which was only launched last year, came into collision on Sunday evening on Roches Point, and the latter sank, carrying down with her nine of her crew. The captain of the Heleuslea and 15 of his crew were saved by the C ,talonia. A daring robbery is reported to have been committed at Cassiobury, Watford, the seat of the Earl of Essex. The Bishop of St. Albans and his daughter, Miss Claughton, were the guests of Lord Essex, and the apartment allotted to Miss Claughton was entered by means of a ladder placed against the window. The theives secured jewellery belong- ing to Miss Claughton valued at between £2OO and £3OO. ‘A very destructive fire occurred on Sunday at Rochdale. A large warehouse, the property of the Lancishire and Yorkshire Railway Company, situated near to their passenger station, and stored with grain, wool, and cotton, took fire early in the morning. The greater portion of the contents of the warehouse was destroyed or damaged and a good deal of in- jury was done to the building. The damage is estimated at £30,000 to £lOO,OOO. , Tux BRIBERY PRISONERS: RELEASE OF MACKIE.— Mackie, one of the Deal men undergoing imprisonment at Canterbury for briberyrthe man who has saved 50 lives— was released on Monday by order of the Home Secretary upon a certificate of the prison surgeon to the effect that further confinement would endanger his life. Mackie has been ill for tide past two days. and became much worse after the answer to the memorial for the release of the prisoners was made known to him. He was so weak that he had to , be carried to the railway station. 1 A terrible disaster as a result of panic was well nigh 1 occurring at Bradford on Monday night. As it was the con- sequence were serious. While a performance was proceed- ing at Keith's Circus, a cry of " Fire!" was heard at the rear of the gallery. Immediately a rush was made from all parts of the building. The manager came forward and an- nounced that nothing had occurred to cause alarm, but panic had seized the audience, and in the rush out several ladies were trampled underfoot, and two had to be ccnveyed to the infirmary suffering from broken legs. The perform- ance subsequently proceeded. Tim SALVATION ARMY.—Mrs. General Booth, of the Sal- vation Army, in a recent speech, described the army as an essentially Holy Ghost people, and claimed that they formed the only body which had effectually reached the masses, and showed how it had from humble beginnings grown to an extensive organisation, which for the purposes of its work spent £12,000 annually on the hire of buildings. They entirely employed 445 officers, held 4,300 services weekly, had 12000 soldiers ready to speak at any time, accommodated 178,000 persons in their buildings, and talked to 3,000,000 in the streets and highways weekly. They had spent , £21,000 odd on property and furnishing officers' quarters, and they bad in addition expended £45,000, subscribed principally in copper coin. Ross then fled. Another case of homicide is reported from Preston. Two men got to words in a beer-house—in this case, too, at closing time,—and when they got into the street one struck ' the other in the face, knocking him down. TRADE NOTES. In response to an appeal from the operatives, the cotton spinners of Ashton, Stalybridge, and Dukinfield have agreed to calculate wages in future by "indicated length," instead of by " weight" as heretofore. The iron masters of- the North of England propose to give to the blast furnacemen an increase of 10 per cent for the first six months, and an additional 2i when the price of pig iron reaches 42e. The question is to stand over for a week. The extensive lead mines in Weardale, leased by Mr: Beaumont, M.P., from the Ecclesiastical Commissioners, will be closed on Saturday, owing to a dispute about rents. Some hundreds of families are dependent on the work of these mines. An important meeting of the Federated Union of Miners for the Midland Counties was held in Wolverhampton on Wednesday. It was attended by representatives from North and South Staffordshire,. Cannock Chase, Worcestershire, and Shtopshire. A review Was made of the year's preeeBa- ings in connection with the settlement of wages disputa lamong colliers in the Midlands. The retrospect resulted in a unanimous resolution strongly urging each district to fol- low the recent example of the Cannock Chase men, and form boards of conciliation and arbitration, to avoid the disastrous , consequences of strikes and lock-outs.

• George Barnes was a machinist by trade, and a whistler by profession. The statement is probably given in an in- verse order; his profession was certainly the most promi- nent of the two qualifications; for whatever rank he might claim as a machinist, no one ever questioned his abilities as a whistler. Whistling is very well at a proper time and place, and witha s. farther qualification as to quantity. It does much to relieve the tedium cf shop manipulation, and is a common pastime with machinists; but the hero of this story was possessed of a mania for this shrill music, and hour after hour, if not day after day, he plied his notes, with pleasure and comfort to himself, no doubt, but often to the great an- noyance of those around him. George, because of a want of musical taste on the part of his employers, had whistled himself out of a situation; and as his pecuniary affairs rendered it imperative that his machine-fitting should go on with the whistling, he applied promptly for a new job at the large works near to where he had been previously employed. The foreman being in need of hands, and favourably int- presied with George, at once gave him a job to commence on the following morning. He was there promptly at the time with his tools and overalls, ready to begin. The fore- man not having arrived, George sauntered around the shop examirfing the tools and began several times in an uncon- scious way to whistle; but finding that it attracted the at- tention of the other workmen, who had never heard such an adept, he checked himself, feeling that he was taking an unwarranted privilege in a strange shop. The foreman arriving, George was given his job for the day. The works, among other tools, employed several large punching ma- chines; one of the dies having failed, George was given the bed-piece to prepare. The die was a solid block, about twelve inches square, requiring a cylindrical hole four inches in diameter to be made through the centre. It was forged from a tough, fibrous iron, about four inches deep, with a steel facing half an inch thick on the face side. George first drilled a starting hole through the piece, and then proceeded to "chuck" it on an old but powerful lathe, used for drilling purposes. While mounting the work, his attention was so much taken up in the search for bolts and blocks, that the whistling was for the time neglected; be- sides, there had continually to be questions asked as to where tools were kept, and other things, and while George could do almost anything else and whistle at the same time, talking, of course, stopped his music. When he finally had all arranged, his work chucked, a large flat drill prepared, and the belts adjusted, he began drilling, and there was nothing to prevent the music from commencing at the same time. Now, if there is any- thing more than another that provokes whistling in a machine shop, it is drilling, especially a large, deep hole, and the man who does not whistle when engaged at such work can be set down as "without music in his soul." There is a kind of stupor of the mind induced by its being.l for the time released from care of the work, and a person will whistle almost unconsciously, as a kind of relief to the Spell.bound.—B-o-n.n-d. FOREIGN INTELLIGENCE.

By the explosion of the West Point steamer in York River, Virginia, twenty dock labourers were killed and several others badly hurt. It appears that 29 persons lost their lives through the Panicl.which occurred in the church of the Holy Cross at Warsaw, on Sunday, 30 being seriously and upwards of 100 Slightly injured. A St Petersburg telegram, received through Vienna, states that on Sunday the whole of the naval port of Crons- tadt was on fire, and that the loss was enormous, one quarter of the town having been destroyed. The origin of the fire IS attributed to, Nihilists. During the celebration of High Mass on Christmas Day in the Holy Cross Church, Warsaw' a man who was seized in the act of picking pockets created a panic by calling out "Fire," and during the confusion which followed several Were crushed to death and many more were seriously injured. The report on Sunday night was that 30 persons had died of their injuries. In the Guiteau case medical evidence was given on Friday and Saturday, the whole of which contradicted the theory of insanity set for the prisoner. The superintendent of an asylum in Ohio was of opinion that the prisoner by his extravagant conduct in the court was exaggerating his Peculiarities, which were "egotism, sharpness, smartness, vulgarity, and ingratitude." Another plot to kill the Czar is reported from St. Peters- burg. The conspirators, it is stated, were all arrested a few days ago at an assembly of revolutionists in the outskirts of the town. From information of which the police are now in possession it is authoritatively stated that nothing could have saved the life of the Emperor had he passed along the Street where the plot was to have been carried out when he Was expected there on his way from the Palace to the Michael Riding School. The Emperor of Austria, in order to give a permanent ex- pression to his sympathy for the sad fate of those lost by the burning of the Ring Theatre, has resolved to erect on the Site of the theatre, at his own cost, a building, in connection With which will be an appropriate memorial chapel. With regard to the actual number of people who were lost on the fatal evening, the latest records issued by the police show that altogether 447 persons perished, of whom 153 have been recognised. The Prone}, innrnal napnted to be the organ of M. Gambetta, publishes a telegram from London to toe effect that Sir C. Dilke will shortly have a meeting with M. Gambetta and M. Rouvier, not, as certain French papers have announced, to continue the Commercial Treaty nego- tiations. The English Cabinet, the correspondent states, has received satisfactory assurances from M. Gambetta' and the signature of the Treaty is henceforth a mere form subject to the discussion of a few details, which will be easily and Promptly settled. The Judge who presides at the trial of Guiteau has made a statement to an 'interviewing " reporter. He admits that the criminal has had his own way too much, but believes ithat the end of the trial will vindicate the course which has been adopted. On entering the court on Tuesday Guiteau informed everybody that he had had a "good time" on Christmas Day—" lots of fruit, flowers, and lady visitors." Pr. Macdonald, superintendent of a great hospital for the !tisane at New York, gave conclusive evidence on the Insanity plea. He related his conversations with the pri- jlener in gaol, and threw fresh light on the scheme, as Ingenious as it was odious and cowardly, which Guiteau had arranged in order to avoid the due punishment of his Crime. Austria, the "mighty neighbour" of Roumania, has dSigned to express satisfaction with the somewhat humble aPology which was tendered on Tuesday. In a despatch, Which was obviously written to order, the Roumanian Mm- ter protests protests with great earnestness that his Government ;°,ad not the slightest intention of wounding the suscepti- Vities of the Government of Austria, and begs that his f I°Ysl and sincere " declarations may be received with .vour. An official Vienna newspaper graciously intimates cnat the "regrettable incident" is now at an end, and ex- Presses the hope that the relations between the two countries 1,1,1aj in the future be firmer and more intimate than ever. IS hope may be realised, but it is more probable that flustria will discover some day that Roumanian statesmen "aye good memories for insults which they desire to avenge.

THE STATISTICS OF _CHURCH AND
-CHAPEL ATTENDANCE.

Mr. C. S. Miall, who published eight years ago in the N'onconformist returns of religious accommodation, is making aa effort to deal with the recently published statis- tics of attendance in places of worship in our large towns.

He says:— So far as they go, the present returns substantially con- firm those of 1873. Then it fell to my lot to procure, arrange, and defend a huge Ma.. 99 of statistics. Now I pro- pose to assume the less responsible and more agreeable position of an outside critic. The interest in the statistics of 1831 arises from the fact that they refer to attendance at public worship as well as accommodation; that they appear from time to time in local newspapers, which have to a large extent employed their own enumerators; that, so far as I know, their general accuracy has not been challenged; and that nothing of the kind has been done since 1851. With a view to give a bird's-eye view of the general result, I have compiled the following summary table, omitting half-a-dozen smaller places, and adding together morning and evening attendances, so as not to encroach too much upon your space, and including in the total the afternoon attendance. In nearly every town, it should be remarked, the evening attendance is larger than the morning, probably to the extent of 20 per cent, on the average. With regardl to the last column, I should explain that the percentages are calculated on the assumption that one-fourth of the wor- shippers at the two services combined attended only one service. Some people may think a deduction of one-third would be nearer the mark, but it is better to err on the right side.

ATTENDANCES AT PLACES OF WORSHIP: SUMMARY TABLE. , Proportion per cent. of Total at- attendants Population. Sittings. tendances. to popit'n. Liverpool Sheffield Bristol - 109,452 40 Hull 153,000 73,760 63.133 31 Leicester Wolverhampton 73,738 30 000 20 214 213 Stockport Bath 51,790 33.957 33,885 52 Northampton 51,226 20,512 21,924 32 Ipswich Warrington Stockton 40,000 --- 14,681 27-5 Gloucester Rotherham 30,115 13,966 11,215 31-9 Hastings, &c 31,250 - - 21,958 52-7 Baresley Runcorn -- - 678,160 36-16 .

It will be observed that the returns for Newcastle and Gateshead, which were the first published, and set the fashion to other towns, are not included in the above. They were statistics of morning attendances only ; together 28.795, or 13-8 per cent, in proportion to the combined popu- lation (214,649). The aggregate comparison in the above is more favourable than might have been expected from recent fragmentary returns. It thus appears that at the two services on one Sunday in these 17 places, with a popula- tion somewhat short of two millions, there was an attend- ance of about 36-16 per cent, of the population. Taking the two services instead of one, Liverpool shows 19-9 per cent, instead of 11-9 per cent. The variations in the last column are extraordinary, and it would seem that the inhalitants of Northampton, whose reputation, owing to exceptional reasons, is under a cloud, are better church- goers than those of Liverpool, Sheffield, Wolverhampton. Hull, Sm. As to the last-named town, the religious census was taken on a Sunday when it was blowing a gale all day, which possibly made a difference of from 10 to 20 per cent. in the attendance. There are many other points suggested by the above table which I cannot at present ask permission to refer to. But it is to be remembered that on a given Sunday in these several towns, which may be regarded as representative, 62-4 per cent, of the population were absent from public worship, and Bishop Byle has publicly declared that if a census were taken "of every town and every city and of every rural town or:parish, the result would not be much more satisfactory than at Liverpool." This, if true, is a very graN,e fact. If I proceed to analyse the above table I know that I am verging on "a burning question." But it is better for all parties the truth should be known. For the sake of your space I will take only the first six boroughs on the list.
A).TILYSIS OF ATTENDLNCES. Church of Noncon- Roman _ _ . _ .
—.....-- _......,_ England. form ist. Catholic. Total. Liverpool 51,551 67,775 , 23,930 146,256 Sheffield Bristol Hull Leicester Wolverhampton 12,289 12,157 1,768 26,214

Totals With regard to the other boroughs, I may add that the Church of England has a majority of attendances over Non- conformists in the following:—Bath (8,843), Ipswich (1,813), Gloucester (33); in the others, Dissenters greatly preponderate. The above table shows that the Established Church had 36-9 per cent, of the entire attendances in the six towns referred to; and the Nonconformists of all sections 55.6 per cent. The meaning of this is that the Church of England. in a numerical sense, is no longer the "national Church," though it greatly surpasses in numbers every other religious bpc,lv in the land. Ido not ask further space to comment on tnissuggestive cart; out I shown ue glail to add two brief quotations from the recent charge of the Bishop of Rochester. "Are we quite at sufficient pains," he asked, "to measure the living forces of Nonconformity ?" Further on, he adds ;—" But this I am sure of, that if we could have a little more of that despised Puritanism (some- times so savagely reproached at those who can only wish they better deserved it)—Puritanism without its flaws and defects—there might be more substance in our sermons, more backbone in our manhood, more honesty in our markets,

div.head: ABRAM COLLIERY EXPLOSION.
div.p: THE ABRAM COLLIERY EXPLOSION.

Mr. Barker, deputy county coroner, resumed his "inquiry on Wednesday into the deaths of 45 of the persons killed by the explosion at the Arley Pit of the Abram Coal Company last week. Mr. Hall, inspector of mines, and Messrs. Heyes and Johnson, proprietors, were amongst those present. Evi- dence in identification of the bodies recovered since the previous sitting of the jury was given. Several of the wit- nesses recognised their relatives by means of their clothing. The deputy coroner said that completed the evidence of identity except as to one body which had not been identi- fied, and which was buried the previous day. A photograph of the body had been taken, so that possibly it might here- after be identified. Should this be so the evidence as to that one and also the one still missing, supposing it were found in the meantime, might be given at the next sitting, when they would enter upon the real and substantial work of the inquiry. Scientific evidence would then be placed before them, and everything possible would be done ot elucidate the cause of the disaster. The proprietors, he felt sure, were most anxious to have as complete an investiga- tion as possible. He was assured that this colliery was as well managed as any in the district, and perhaps as any in the country, and the jury would have the best assistance in arriving at a decision as to the accident. With reference to the adjournment, time would have to be aiven for 'a careful examination of the workings, and the Home Office would have to make their arrangements ia connection with the in- quiry. He was informed that a month or six weeks would be sufficient, and by then several of the injured would pro- bably be well enough to attend and to state what they knew ,of the explosion. After a short consultation, it was decided to adjourn the inquest until Tuesday, February 7. A jury- man stated that the relatives of the deceased had had much difficulty in connection with the registrar, and asked if the coroner could not now give his certificates. Mr. Barker said the giving of certificates rested with the registrar, who could not fill in the particulars required until the conclu- sion of the inquest.—Mr. Ackerley, who appeared for the proprietors of the colliery, stated that under the Friendly Societies Act claims only were to be paid on the production of the certificate of death, which could not be given until the jury had come to a verdict. In such inquiries as that this was felt to be a great hardship, and he thought the Act required amending.—Mr. Campbell, general secretary of the Lancashire and Cheshire Miners' Relief Society, said they had adopted the practice in this and other simiiar accidents of paying the claims at once, although they knew that by so doing they violated the law and exposed themselves to prosecutions.—The deputy coroner said he thought the breach of the law was, under the circumstances very ex- cusable. No jury would convict for ,such an offence.—Mr. Campbell said he did not believe there would be any prose- cutions if officers of friendly societies would adopt the course taken in connection with his fund.—The proceedings the' terminated.

div.head: SHOCKING ACCIDENT AT A MUSIC
div.p: SHOCKING ACCIDENT AT A MUSIC
HALL.

A frightful accident occurred at the Oxford Theatre of Varieties, New-road, Brighton, on Tuesday night. A China- man, named Ling Look, who is described as "The Lord of Fire, Cannon, and Sword," had almost closed his perfor- mance his final feat being to balance a cannon on a sword which he holds in his mouth. In this position the cannon, which is a yard long, with a 3in. bore, is fired, of course only hay- ing a small charge. He requested the audience in the gallery to be seated prior to getting his gun into position, and the Chinaman further explained his request. The Chinaman then placed the point of his sword in a hole in the cannon, and passed it down his throat, so that the sannon rested across his face Otis wife, who takes part in the entertainment, then applied a red hot iron to the touch-hole. The report followed. Just at that moment a ladls, named Smyth, who was sitting on the front row of the left side of the gallery, unfortunately projected his head, and was struck with a large pellet of paper which had been in some inexplicable manner placed in the cannon. The pellet was abaut the size of a small orange. This completely scattered the poor lad's brains in all directions. The scene in the hall was most horrible. The blood bespattered a number of people sitting around the lad, and a scene of confusion followed. Shouts were heard to proceed from the gallery and some cries of "Fire," and a rush was made to the doors, fully half the audience leaving. At one time it looked as if a panic would occur with serious results. The chairman, with either great presence of mind or perhaps not knowing the extent of the disaster, announced the next artiste, and this to some degree restored something approaching order. Before any appearance could be made, however, an intimation as to the nature of the occurrence was conveyed to the chairman, and he promptly closed the performance. Medical aid was at once procured, but it was of no avail, the poor lad having been instantaneously killed. The scene in the hall, as des- cribed by those present, was of the most horrible character. Blood ran over the side of the gallery, and the scene was ghastly in the extreme. Screams followed the shot, which it was at first thought were the result of timidity, but on the elod h.ed of the lad being seen panic for a time held its sway. In the rush out of the hall several were bruised, but not seriously, The poor lad's remains were taken to the mortuary at the Town Hall, where they await an inquest. Ling Look has been apprehended, and will be brought before the magistrates. It was stated that he was carefully explicit in asking his audience to keep their heals low, and out of the line of fire. The pellet is stated to have been a compact ball of paper almost as hard as wood. Ling Look, on being apprehended, he not being able to speak English, wrote that he did not cause the death of the lad, meaning, no doubt, that he did not do it wilfully. It is not thought that Ling Look knew of the pellet being in the cannon.

div.head: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The usual fortnightly meeting of this Board was held at the Whiston Workhouse, on Thursday, Mr. S. Marsh presid- ing. There were also present the Revs. T. Chambers and John Barnacle, Messrs. Tyrer, Fidler, Hall, Penkelh, Fisher, Gerrard, Sadler, Leatherbarrow, Tusoi, Birch, Dobell, Ken- wrigh t, Ranson, Syder, W. Birchall, Swift, Buckley, Eatock, and Meadows; with Mr. S. H. Hartley, clerk.

div.head: BOARD'S FINANCIAL DIFFICULTIES.
div.p: THE BOARD'S FINANCIAL DIFFICULTIES.

At the last meeting the clerk was directed to write to the overseers of Whines, stating that unless they paid, on or be- fore:the 28th instant, the sum of £l,OOO of the £6,000, arrears of rates, then due, proceedings would be taken against them. The CLERK now read the following letter, signed by John Taylor and Thomas Sadler, the Widnes overseers:—" We duly received your letter on the 16th instant requesting payment of £l,OOO on or before the 28th instant. We very much regret that we are still without funds to meet your demand, and we can only attribute our present position to the fact that little or no attention was paid by our collector to the repeated requests made by u 3 months ago that he would push on with his collecting. We wrote him on the 11th August, Bth October, 4th November, and again on the sth December, calling his attention to the slowness of his collections, and instructing him to summon everyone who refused to pay. In addition to this we have at our various meetings cautioned him of the difficulty into which we were drifting, and begged Of him to push on as fast as he could, and to all this he has promised over and over again that the rate would be got in without any delay. We have been similarly placed with regard to the School Board precept, but that has all been paid with the exception of about £2OO. It is a difficult matter, we have no doubt, to collect the sum required in a few days, but had Mr. Rigby devoted the whole of his time to his duties, which he has not, we are of opinion that the majority of our out- standings would have been collected long ago. It is very annoying to us to be placed in our present situation, and that from no fault of our own. We have no control over Mr. Rigby as he is appointed by your board of guardians, and our desire and anxiety to meet your demands are entirely frustrated by the inatten- tion of our collector to our requests." The Clerk then read a letter from Mr. Rigby, which was as follows :—" In reply to your letter to the Widnes overseers notifying them of your intention of proceeding against them, I would ask you, if possible, to postpone the matter for a short time. Our rate outstanding will not realise the amount required, and it will take some time to get a new rate out."—Mr. Itaxs,R4 : Does that first letter say the collector has not devoted the whole of his time to the collection of the rates?—The CHAIRMAN : The overseers' letter says so. The collector, in his letter, asks that the matter might be allowed to remain over a few days.—Mr. SADLER said they would see from the letter of the overseers that the latter had had several meet- ings. They called a meeting for the 17th November, but Mr. Rigby sent word that be could not attend. A meeting, however, was held on the 22nd, and they went through the accounts then appearing in the book. There appeared to be due something like £3,000, of which they estimated only about £1,500 would be recoverable, owing to failures and other disappointments in Widnes. They urged Mr. Rigby at the time to get in the old rate as early as possible and he promised to do so. They called another meeting for the 22nd December, but Mr. Rigby could not attend, and the over- seers have not been able to see him since. They had done all as they could to impress upon Mr. Rigby the advisable- ness of getting in the rate at once. lie had called at the bank and found that nearly £4OO had been paid in since the previous Thursday. The overseers had been in the same predicament with the School Board; they received a letter from that body just before the letter from the Guardians thrteening them for the school rate. They had, however, got in the rate with the exception of about £2OO. They in- structed the collector to give poor-rate defaulters notice that unless they paid their rates within a certain time he had in- structions to proceed against them. Of course he was the Guardians' servant, and he thought they should help the overseers in the matter.—The CHAIRMAN remarked that the Guardians had no power or control over Mr. Rigby at all, but the overseers had. Certainly the Board had the power of appointing him, but he was not an officer of the Board. The Guardians could not take any proceedings against him. —After some unimportant conversation, Mr. Rigby was called into the room' and in answer to the chairman, said he met the overseers last month. He might say that he had collected, more money in Widnes this year than had ever had been collected by any previous collector in the same length of time and the overseers knew, and Mr. Sadler should know, that ft was impossible for him to take legal proceedings against de- faulters before October for various reasons which he did not wish to state. He afterwards took proceedings aginst over 30 persons, and there was only about £3OO out at the present time. Mr. Rigby then enumerated the difficulties he had had to contend with in the collection of the rates. The assessment of the Midland Railway had been_ reduced to a merely nominal sum, and there were nearly. 1,000 houses empty at Widnes. The rate had never been collected in twelve months before this year, in fact it was not eleven months since the rate was laid. He had not yet been re- lieved of the out-lying districts (Bold, Crouton, and Ditton), and he had been very busy making a new rate for the town- ship of Bold.—Mr. SADLER understood that Mr. Rigby had been relieved of Bold, Crouton, and Ditton, and that Mr. Houghton was responsible for the collection of those townships. The CLERK said that was not so. Mr. Houghton's appointment had not yet been confirmed by the Local Government Board.—Mr. FIDLER (to Mr. Rigby): You can't raise this money unless you have a new rate P—Mr. RIGBY : I have only £2OO or £3OO out of the present rate.—The CHAIRMAN asked if in case Mr. Rigby summoned the defaulters whether they would be able to pay ?—Mr. RIGBY said he could not say. The property in Widnes had very much changed hands of late, and he had not been able to find owners for some of it.—Mr. TYRER: Why did you not take legal proceedings against defaulters before October?—Mr. RIGBY : Well, because the overseers had not paid.—ln answer to Mr. Sadler, Mr. RIGBY said that he issued about 30 summonses against those who had not paid their rates, in accordance with the instruc- tions he received from the overseers.—Mr. FIDLER pointed Out that the letter contained sweeping charges against Mr. Rigby of his inattention to his duties, and it was only fair that he should have an opportunity of replying to them.— Mr. RIGBY : You see I cannot be in all she townships at ithe same time. Time overseers think I should be in Widnes altogether, and I can't—Mr. LEATHERBARROW ; What arrears were there when you took office P—Mr. RIGI3Y : About £3,000. There had not been a rate laid for 12 months.—ln answer to Mr. Hall, Mr. RIGBY said he should be able tc get in the arrears of the old rate by the beginning of next month.—Mr. HALL; And in the meantime you will get the new rate out 7—Mr. Runny: I am busy with it nefw.—The CLERK said he should like to snow whether the overseers had fixed upon the amount in the pound of the new rate. If the present overseers found that their predecessors had laid a rate of is. 6d. in the pound they would be reluctant to increase it for fear of getting a bad name. The next rate ought to be double the present one, or they would always be in the same difficulty.—Mr. RIGBY said that was so.—Mr. FIDLER said he supposed the over- seers could procure assistance for Mr. Rigby to help him with the making of the new rate or collecting the arrears.— The CLERK replied that they could if they saw the neces- sity of it.—The CHAIM\ SIN : What amount of rate would you levy P—Mr. RIGBY : I should say not less than 3s.—Mr. TYRER suggested that the Clerk should meet the Widnes overseers and assistant overseer, and go through the accounts and see if he could recommend any course to get them out of the present difficulty.—The suggestion was agreed to.—Mr. TYRER proposed that the resolution passed at the last meeting threatening the overseers of Widnes with legal proceedings should be suspended for a fortnight.—This was seconded and agreed to.

div.head: DESERTED WIVES AND CHILDREN.
div.p: DESERTED WIVES AND CHILDREN.

The CLERK read a return of the number of women and children who had been deserted by their husbands and fathers in the Workhouse. There were 14 WOMeR and 47 children, total 61; of which 38 were from the Widnes dis- trict, three from Sutton, eight from Windle, and twelve from Eccleston.—The return was referred to the General Purposes Committee.

A CLERGYMAN CHARGED \VITA FIRING MS CHURCII. The Rev. George Sanger, vicar of Carlton-in-Cleveland, was on Tuesday lodged in gaol at Stokesley on a charge of wil- fully and maliciously setting fire to his own church on the 19th October last. He was apprehended in London, and during the afternoon was brought before the magistrates and remanded until January sth. It appears that up to the present 27 colliery explosions have been recorded this year, 13 of which were label, with a loss of 97 lives. In addition, two deaths occurred from suffocation, making a total of 99. In the last 30 years only two years show so small a loss of life, the average aanual less being about 200. Of the 43 warnings issued, 23 were justified by subsequent events, and two accidents occurred before a warning was issued. DEATH OF LORD JUSTICE LUSH. The death is announced of Lord Justice Lush, which event took place on Tuesday morning. The deceased judge was born at Shaftesbury on October 25, 1807, and has thus only recently completed his seventy-fourth year. He was educated at his native place, and was called to the bar in 1840. He practised with much success, and in 1857 became (4.c., and in November, 1865, was appointed one of the judges of the Queea's Bench, and received the honour of knighthood. He was the author of "Notes on the New Will Act" and the. "Act for Abolishing Arrest for Debt," published in 1835; "Practice of the Superior Courts," issued in 1846, and other minor works. In August, 1878, he was appointed a member of the Royal Commission to inquire into the provisions of the Draft Code relating to indictable offence, and in 1880, on the death of Lord Justice Thesiger, became Lord Justice of Appeal.
