div.head: CHRISTMAS PROCEEDINGS AT Sr.
div.p: CHRISTMAS PROCEEDINGS AT Sr.
HELENS.

Christmas Day passed away quietly at St. Helens Ordinarily, Christmas-tide in our town is not marked by any ostentatious manifestations of pleasure, and Christmas Day this time falling on Sunday, it was very quiet indeed. Unlike coins towns there was, with one or two exceptions, an utter absence of public tea parties and public meetings where an interchange of the compliments of the season could be freely exercised. The churches were decorated a little, and services suitable to the season of the year were conducted in some of the places of worship in the town. The weather in this part of the country as in many other places was any- thing but seasonable, and beyond some minor displays there were few public indications of the festive season of the year. On Friday and Saturday tradesmen's shops were profusely decorate(Twith their various classes of articles for sale, to which we alluded in our issue of last week, and the purchases of the good things of the season were very heavy so that what might be the state of things outside, there were in the mijority of the homes of the inhabitants plenty of Christ- mas cheer, and enjoyable family parties. The works were stopped on Monday, and on account of Christmas Day falling on Sunday, a good many of the people secured an extra holiday. The shops as announced were shut up on Monday and Tuesday in accordance with the resolution of the Shop Assistants' Association. A pleasant feature this Christmas, and one which was very noticeable, was the absence of general distress in the town, making a striking contrast to the previous two or three Christmas Days, when it was unfortunately found necessary to help the poor of the town by the establishment of soup kitchens on account of the great distress on every hand. We be- lieve there were better Christmas dinners, and a wider observance of the traditional "roast beef and plasm pudding" festivity than last year. While many stayed in their homes enjoying the comforts of the season in the family gathering there was quite an exodus for the time being of a large number of people to various parts of the country, some to join in the family reunion and see their friends, others to participate in the amusements to be found in some of our large towns. At the railway station there was the usual bustle. On Friday a large number were booked for long journeys. About 700 were booked to various parts on Friday, and on Saturday 3,407 passengers were booked, of which 800 were booked to Liverpool, the theatre and pan- tomime attractions accounting for the large number of visitors to the city. On Sunday there was very little traffic, the travellers by that time having reached their destinations. On Monday the weather was very mild,.if not dull and dis- piriting, and the appearance of the town was that of a holi- day. The stre.s were traversed by pedestrians who had been lured into the streets by the mildness of the weather. If the roads had been anything like fit for the comfortable exercise of pedestrianism, a walk into the country would not have been out of keeping with the character of the day, even if there had been a slight incong,ruity, when we take into account the season of the year. There were on Monday 2,400 passengers booked to various parts by rail. Friday was very foggy, but this was not the case with Saturday, Sunday, and Monday, which was of great advantage to the Railway Company, thus enabling the company to conduct their traffic with facility and without the slightest accident of any description. The trains ran almost as regularly as on ordinary occasions. From what can be gathered at the railway station there was a marked improvement in the conduct of the people, there being very little drunkenness and misbehaviour on the railway station. A few staggering inebriates could be seen, but they were exceptionally few in number. The tramway traffic was very heavy on Monday. It is calculated that 3,000 persons went by tramcar Prescot way. Many of these would go forward to Liverpool. The cars ran as usual with the ex- ception of there being two extra cars at night. On Christ- mas Day the seats were somewhat better than latterly on Sundays, but there was nothing striking for us to record. Probably there would be 1,700 or 1,800 passen- gers. On Saturday the traffic was about as usual. The postal officials had extra wcrk imposed upon ' them by the interchange of Christmas greet- ings among friends. The average number for Christmas Day is about 5,000, but this year there 10,400 The extra number mny be set down to the large number .of Christmas cards. On the previous day there were forwarded from the St. Helens office quite as many to other towns. Saturday was a very heavy day, and the men were occupied for the last delivery two hours over the usual time. On Christmas morning a large number of boys were employed to assist in carrying the large bulky parcels, and on that day the delivery lasted two hours over the usual time. The exceed ingly heavy work on Saturday necessitated the addition of two clerks, and on that day, as well as on the preceding day, special bags were despatched to Warrington and Crewe to relieve tke office of the excessive correspondence. The notices requesting the early posting of the letters seemed to be taken notice of by the public, and the despatch of the business is creditable to the postal officials. Our readers are reminded to post their New 1-ear's cards early in order to ensure punctuality. It is not, however, expected that the number of missives will be equal to those despatched at Christmas.

div.head: ST. HELENS SCHOOL ATTENDANCE COMMITTEE.
div.p: THE ST. HELENS SCHOOL ATTEN- DANCE COMMITTEE.
The monthly meeting of this Committee was held on Wednesday, Mr. Wilcock presiding. There were also present :—Alderman Cook; Councillors Bishop, Twyford, T. Cook, and T. Fisher.

Mr. CRACK (deputy town clerk) said that on Saturday last, at the invitation of the governors, he attended the annual dinner and prize distribution to the scholars of the Liverpool Certified Industrial School. Mr. Whitley, 31. F., was present, distributed the prizes, and made a very in- structive address to the boys. He (Mr. Craik) was pleased to learn that one of the boys named Emmanuel Spash, com- mitted to that school at the instance of the Committee, had been successful in gaining a prize for general proficiency. The boys enjoyed their dinner immensely and seemed to be very comfortable. Disappointment was expressed because the Committee had not acceded to the request to be present. Mr. EDMUND BAMFORD reported-l'--Since the date of your last meeting the names of 883 absent and irregular scholars have been reported by the teachers in my district. Fifty- two notices have been served upon the parents of 93 of the most irregular of the above scholars to appear bekre your sub-committee on the Bth instant,'when their eases were en- quired into; and no reasonable excuse being made, the parents were warned of the consequence of a further violation of the law. Two boys were recommended to be sent to industrial schools. During the month 31 cases have been taken before the magistrates with the following results: —2l were fined the usual penalty of sixpence and costs; three cases dismisp.d, three attendance orders granted, and four boys committed to industrial schools' namely, William Herron, and Henry and -G2orge McCawley to the Boys' Refuge; and Richard Geoghan to the Liverpool School Board Industrial School, Hightown. I have signed 187 children's school books containing the usual evidence of age. I beg to ask for leave of absence during the present Christ- mas holidays at the schools. I Mr. THOMAS DUTTON reported :—ln the past month 780 absent and irregular scholars have been reported by the teachers of the schools in my district. Fifty-four notices have been served on parents representing 100 of the most irregular of such scholars who appeared before your Investi- gation Committee, on the Bth inst., wjaen 10 of them not being able te give a reasonable excuse for their children's absence or irregularity were ordered to be summoned; and in the six cases investigated at your last monthly meeting, proceedings have also been taken in accordance with your directions then given, making together 16 summonses taken out during the month with the following result; 13 fined in the usual penalty of ss. including costs, two attendance , orders granted, and one order to commit the boy to the Truant School at Hightown, but which order has not yet been executed owing to there being no vacancy in that ' department of the School to which he was ordered to be sent. The two cases referred to in my last report as being then adjourned were further adjourned by the magistrates on the 28th ult, to the 9th proximo. I beg to ask for leave of absence during the holidays at the schools. It was decided to take proceedings against the boys re- ferred to in the former report, with the object of sending them to the industrial school. The officers were granted their holidays.
Major Bond's resignation of the office of Chief Constable of Birmingham was on Tuesday accepted by the Watch Committee, who agreed to pay him half a year's salary (£350).

A young nun who had been compelled to enter a convent at Gratz, nearly lost her life on Wednesday in attempting to escape by jumpinz from the nunnery into a mill stream. She was taken from the water in an unconscious state, and removed to the polica station. The police subse- quently refused to surrender her to the superior of the convent. . _ _

An adjourned inquest was held eh Thurslty in London on the body of a young woman named Eanu t Cummins, recently employed as barmaid at the Criterion Restaurant. The girl had given up her situation in order to live with a certain Lieutenant Henry Ponsonby, who is on the retired list of the Royal Navy. She appears to have been tempted by the promise of a considerable allowance, and went delib- erately to her ruin in spite of the strongest remonstrances from her family. In a short time Ponsonby left her in an exceedingly cruel and heartless manner, and she thereupon committed suicide. Ponsonby was called as a witness on Thursday. The Jury, after hearing his evidence, found that the unhappy victim had committed suicide whilst in a state of mental excitement produced by the miserable and un- fortunate condition in which he had left her. The Coroner added some stinging observations of his own to the Jury's deliverance, and the crowd which had waited for the verdict made an attempt to seize Lieutenant Ponsonby as he drove away under police protection. div.head: ST. HELENS SMOKE NITTSANCE.
div.p: THE ST. HELENS SMOKE NITTSANCE.
• MEETING OF COUNCILLORS AND MANUFACTURERS.

A special meeting of the St. Helens Town Council was held on Wednesday morning, to confer with manufacturers and consumers of fuel, as to the best means, with least in- convenience to them, of carrying out the provisions of the Public Health Act, 1875, and other Acts relating to the . emission of smoke from chimneys. There were present the Mayor (Mr. R. Pilkington), who presided, Aldermen Gamble, Cook, Mcßryde, Harrison, Johnson, Councillors J. C. Gamble, Twyford, Jamison, Belsher, Bishop, Brook, Mc- Kechnie, T. Cook, Fisher, W. W. Pilkington, Walker, Massey, Captain Bramwell, Messrs. W. Pilkington, T. Pil- kington, Major Windus, Captain McTear, A. Sinclair (Bownes and Robinson), Binney (London and Manchester Plate Glass Company), W. Gamble, Hill (Union Plate Glass Company), Joseph Wallace, L. Mooney, S. Urmson Leith, Bell (Messrs. Glover's), Rigg, Bibby, Cannington kynas- ton, Chadwick, Lyon, T. Pilkington, Captain Windus, W. Blinkhorn, jun., Wigg, W. D. Marshall, Samuel Harrison, Rayner, Birarn, Duffy, B. Gardner, W. Gardner, H. J. Rawlinson.

The MAYOR: Before I begin the business of to-day, AA it is the first time we have met since Christmas Day, I hope you will allow me to wish you all the compliments of the season. (Hear, hear.) It is necessary for me to state why this meeting has been called. For some little time certain reports have been before the Health Committee, and in con- sequence of those reports the attention of the Health Com- mittee has been drawn to the question of the smoke nuisance. The first 0 those, reports was on the Ist of October, and there have been reports since. The committee found that there was an undue emission of black smoke in the borough, and they found it necessary to take steps.l They instructed the surveyor, after the October meeting, to make periodical reports, which he had done. In conse- quence of this action on the part of the Health Committee, and the attention of the, Corporation having been called to the fact of suclt undue emission, they found it necessary to take steps to reduce the nuisance as much as practicable and as much as they ought to do. In consequence of that, this meeting is called to-day. These reports I will ask the Town Clerk to read directly. Of course, we have certain powers, and those powers we are obliged to put in force. We do not wish to use any undue severity or anything of that kind, but we wish the manufacturers to co-operate with us as quickly as possible. I feel that there is no doubt in the minds of the manufacturers that they ought to use all haste and all their energies, to adopt such measures as are ,J practicable, and reduce the smoke as much as they can. I Colonel Gamble will have some remarks to make, as he was the mover of the resolution through which this meeting has been called.

I The DEPUTY Tows CLERK then read the reports of the medical officer and surveyss on the emission of black smoke in the borough, the clauses of the Acts in force, and the resolution •of the committee that notice be given to the manufacturers that the provisions of the Public Health Act would be more strictly enforced after the let of March. The resolution of the Council upon this recommendation of the committee that the matter be adjourned two months, and that the Town Clerk be instructed to endeavour to bring about a meeting of the Council and the manufacturers, was read.

The MAYOR said: You have now the whole matter before you. You know what the proceedings of the Health Com- mittee and the Council have been, and what powers we have; and we shall be very glad to have any suggestion from any manufacturer as to how this matter can be satis- factorily dealt with. Aid. GAMBLE: The idea of this conference did not arise with me, as the recommendation appears in the report of the Medical Officer for October. When the report of the Health Committee came before this Council that the provisions of the Smoke Act should be put in force on the Ist March next, and that notice should be given to the manufacturers to that effect, I thought the result of such a proceeding would I be that some manufacturer would be found wanting in com- pliance with the Act. Proceedings would then be taken against him, and he might take the ordinary course of band- ing the summons over to his solicitor, with instructions to defend him to the best of his ability. I thought that would not be a result satisfactory to the Council or of advantage to the community. We know that the Public Health Act provides for our enforcing the discontinuance of the nuisance as far as practicable, but there are many possible means of escape for those who are unable or unwilling to comply with the Act. There are the proper means of escape for those who are unable, and there are the improper means of escape for those who are unwilling to do their best, and make the nuisance as inconvenient as possible to their neighbours. I ' then thought there were a good many instances in which the manufacturers of St. Helens were rather different from other towns in which these Acts have been in force, but still I was satisfied that something could be done by most of the manufacturers to abate the nuisance that exists at ; present. I am afraid that a good many oI us—no doubt most-of us—are less careful about smoke than we ought to be. There is an amount of smoke unavoidable, and pro- bably some think that a little more or less added to it will not be of much consequence; but I believe very much may be done to diminish the amount of smoke. If it can be done without any serious cost to them I should be very glad. I am very glad this has been taken up, and the Council, I hope, will endeavour to have it carried through without anY injury to the manufacturers, and yet with benefit to the neighbourhood. In our old Commissioners' Act there were special provisions that the Szneke Act should not apply to the borough. I believe it was not attempted to introduce these clauses in the Improvement Act of the Corporation, because it was thought that public opinion would not stand it when the Act for the Incorporation of the Borough was passed. I hoped that such a conference as this imuldenable the manufacturers to consult and confer with the Corpora- tion so as to provide for the carrying out of the clauses in reference to black smoke as far as we can. We have been talking very much at random. The advocates of no smoke have said that half cur fuel goes into the atmosphere in the form of smoke, and that it would cost us nothing to consume it all; whereas the manufacturers, many of them, say that a small quantity of fuel is sent out of the chimney, and that its worthls a very small item indeed. I think there is a middle course between these extremes. One man says that it would cost us nokhing to consume the smoke, and others say that it is caused by not having half the boiler power. All these things want bringing to an intermediate point so that we can do away with any excessive amount of smoke. lam sure the Corporation do not want to interfere with the manufacturers of the town. The manufacturers,when theycome M the same mind, no doubt will do all they can; but it is not human to expect one manufacturer to go to the expense of improving his chimneys whilst others are doing nothing to- wards it. I think the whole matter ought to be carried out in the way the Noxious Vapours Act has been carried out— on the principle of whatever anybody could do to avoid a nuisance to his neighbour he ought to be obliged to do it. I mean without serious inconvenience. It will cost something how mach we do. It will cost us in the first place positive expense with all kinds of apparatus, and extra wages for more efficient stokers and surveyors. I hope that will not be anything that should frighten us in not doing what is wanted.
The MAYOR: We shall be glad to hear any other manu- facturer.

Alderman GAMBLE: I have rather spoken as a member of the Council, and as Dr. Jamison rather claims credit, as originator of the movement he will tell us something. Dr. JAMISON said Colonel Gamble had spoken as a mem- ber of the Council, and if all the manufacturers re-echoed all Colonel Gamble had said everything would sail smoothly and nicely. There was no doubt that the black smoke which hung over St. Helens was extremely bad and injurious, and he hoped by the end of next year the evil would be reduced. A portion of it could be easily diminished, and a small portion, however so little, 'com- ing from all the chimneys, made matters serious and rendered the town, to a large extent, a town not fit to be lived in. Those who could manage it got out of the town as soon as possible. A town ought .to be a place where people could live comfortably and rationally, but they could not possibly do so when the air was charged with smoke, gas, and noxious vapours. One naturally felt that something might be done to diminish it. Nothing had yet been done, but he hoped the matter would be entered into in a generous spirit so that something could be effected without undue compul- sion. He knew of towns where processes were carried on nearly as they were in St. Helens, and he was convinced from the working there that something might be done. He did not know what standard they would adopt in St. Helens, but other towns had standards. There were many ways in _

which the nuisance might be diminished. He was not a manager of works, 20 that it would be yery rude of him to intrude his opinions on the company. He could only say , that it could he done. He had gone over nearly all the mann- ' factorimand he was sure there was enough spirit and loyalty in St. Helens to make the town much be tter than it was. He hoped whatever was said would be said freely and with- out restraint. He might add that the real question at issue at present, was not as to how the nuisance should be dimin- ished but, as they were the administrators of the Public Health Act, when it should be carried out. The great thing was to give ample time so that when the Act was put in force, it should not come harshly, that there might be no hardship, no nnfairness or injustice in the matter. After a pause Alderman GAMBLE said: The managers do not seem to speak. Dr. Jamison says nothing has been done here.

Dr. Itanscis : Well, I wont say that nothing has been done. Alderman GAMBLE: That is exactly what you did iay. Dr. JAMISON: I was speaking comparatively, as to what might hava been done. _ , Alderman GAMBLE: I see the danger we hate to incur in. exaggerating what is possible, what is done, and what can be done. Dr. Jamison knows that Sutton Plate Glass Works have done a great deal in this way. I know they spent a good deal of money, some years ago, in putting up smoking apparatus. At our works at Hardshaw Brook we tried to pug up apparatus to consume all the smoke. We actually fire chimneys at these works, four of which, for three or four years, would have complied with the requirements of the strictest Smoke Act in the kingdom. But we had to alter them; they don't pay and would not work. One or two are absolutely' smoke consuming; the others are not. I would, as a manager, remitid those who think that we are doing very badly that there are works, the largest works in the town—the new Plate and Crown Glass Works, where they produce no smoke whatever, although they burn twelve or fifteen hundred tons of coal a week—without a palticle of smoke; and the Lower Plate G'ass Works the same. It • must not be considered that a cbitnaey which lass one fur-

nace going Into in, has to produce smoke for the same length of time as a chimney with twenty furnaces going into it; or that Works consuming 20 or 30 tons of coal should produce as much smoke as a works consuming 1,500 tons. I hope the Council will remember that these things have to be con. sidered. The Melees ! The manufacturers are here, and know just as much as any town councillor. We have told them everything that has been done, and what the Corporation think. We have laid the whole thing before them, and taken them thoroughly into our confidence, in order, supposing that in three mouth if the Act is put in forte according to Councillor Jamison's motion, that they may not be taken unawares. Many of the manufacturers, perhaps, are persons deeply engaged in business and do not read the papers, or do not pay much attention to them, and they might have been taken by sur- prise by the Act being put in force. Now you know as muck as we know. We trust that each manufacturer will do his best to control the nuisance as far as practicable. We have told you everything, but have heard nothing from any manufacturer who is not a councillor.

Mr. W. PILKINGTON: I should like to know about the smoke of dwelling-house chimneys. I think they are just as great, if not greater, culprits than the chimneys of the large works, looking at the amount of coal which is burned in both houses and works.

Alderman G A 11f-B-L ; -latink that is a subject we ought not to venture upon at present. It is too difficult. I don't know how we are to reduce the smoke of dwelling-houses. I made an observation on Sunday last; the valley between Cowley Hill and Knowsley was filled with the smoke caused by the people who were cooking their dinners at Liverpool. You could see that from Liverpool there was a streak of smoke, and the country around was clear. I looked at it, and was satisfied it came from there, because I have seen it on formec occasions when no work was going on, on Sunday, travelling 12 or 13 miles. lam afraid there is as much black smoke mAde in the dwelling-houses of St. Helens as there is in the works; and it is all delivered at 30 or 40 feet from the ground, thus causing greater nuisance than the smoke fro= the works do. _

Mr. W. PILICINGTON did not want to lay it all on the manufacturers, but be found that there was a great deal of eaal consumed in houses. In Staffordshire very nearly half the coal raised was burnt In house consumpti(n. Mr. W. W. PILICINGTON said that the manufacturers seemed to think that because they were not elected to sit in that room they had no right to speak. If that, was the case their coming was going to be a farce. What they wanted now was the manufacturers to speak, because as soonas ever that meeting was over there would be such a lot of talking. They wanted the manufacturers to say what they had to say, and let the public know. Alderman Coos: It has occurred to some of us that per- haps they would like to have a meeting amongst themselves before they express their particular views to the Council. Such a thing might be arranged even while we are here by utilising ona of the ante rooms.

Aldeiman GAMBLE: Perhaps some gentlemen have a diffi- culty in speaking their minis fully before the reporters, and as this is really intended as a conference there ought to be no difficulty of that kind. If the presence of the reporters is any deterrent to our discussing this matter freely and fully we ought to exclude them. The MAYOR: Of course it is quite clear that all out deliberations of the Council have been concluded from time to time without the manufacturers; and now, perhaps, for the first time the manufacturers are called, upon to express their views with the reporters present, they may not like to enter very fully into detail. If the object of the meeting is to get the smoke down to the least possible amount, and if that object will be furthered and promoted by freedom of discussion which will not go on while the reporters are here; I should be very glad if it is the wish of the conference that they be asked to withdraw. lam ready to receive a resolu- tion_to that effect.

Alderman HARRISON: I cordially endorse what Major Pilkington has just said with reference to the manufacturers speaking out, but I don't see what they have to fear in speaking before the. reporters. I should be very glad if they could freely speak here publicly and before the reporters. The MAYOR: I think it Is pretty clear that a great many of them have certain arrangements inside their works they would not care for everybody in the world to know'about. If any of the Council were to go to any particular manatee.. tater in St. Helens, he would get a far greater amount of informatton in talking with him than he would if he were I told publicly. He would tell and show him a great many things that he would not care for a great number of people to know.

Alderman GAMBLE : As the origination of this conference has been laid on my shoulders I should beery sorry if it failed; and I would point out to the es-mayor that if a question arose in this meeting upon which one gentleman j might say that it was perfectly impossible to consume smoke ' quickly, whereas Mr. Harrison might get up and say it was entirely a mistake, we should go on very awkw.rdly an/ perhaps would not like to see it in the papers afterwards. It is not a question of public right or public business exactly, but of our own.

Dr. Jamiscer ; I bog to propose that the reporters retire. Alderman JOHNSON said the question was an important one, and one in which the public was interested. It was clear from what had been said that something could be done" what they had to complain of in St. Helens was the • chimneys which were very low. The Maxon said unless the reporters retired the Council would get no more information; and by the repoeters with. drawing nobody would be losers. The motion was put to the meeting when 17 voted for it, and 3 against it, the three being Mr. Leith, Mr. W. Pilking- ton, and Mr. Massey. After the reporters bad retired a desultory consultation took place between the manufacturers and the town Council, and subsequently th 3 manufacturers had a conference amongst themselves when they decided to accede to any reasonable requirements of the Council. The meeting was adjourned for a fortnight when something more definite will be decided upon.

A GIRL DROWNED AT ST. HELENS.—A distressing case of drowning occurred on Christmas eve in the canal, near to the double locks, which is owned by the London and North-Western Railway Company, the victim being a girl named Mary Ann Lawton, 11 years of age. The girl lived with her parents on the bank of the canal, with which she was familiar. On Saturday night a neighbour named Knowles and his wife called at the house of deceased's parents, and remained there for a short time in conversatior, They then left the house and walked along the canal side to go to St. Helens, where they intended to make some pur- chases. They had not proceeded far when deceased came running after them and asked them to make a purchase for her mother. A thick fog existed at the time, and Knowles and his wife carried a lamp with them. They consented to do the required work, and bade her be careful how she returned. The deceased replied that he could :see well enough, and returned. The Knowles's continued their journey, but nothing was seen or heard of deceased for a long time. The parents became alarmed, and search was made for her. At about three o'clock on Sunday afternoon her body was found in the canal not more than 50 yards from her parents' house. The jury returned a verdict of "Found drowned," the deceased having come by her death through ths dense fog, _

MUSICAL ENTERTAINXEST AT ST. HELENS. Ucder the auspices of the St. Helena Wesleyan Improvement Associa- tion, a musical entertainment was given in the Waterlo... street School-room, on Wednesday evening, being the close of the first half of the session. The Rev. W. G. Pascoe, president of the association, presided over the meeting, which was fairly attended. Songs were given by Mrs. Abel, "London bridge ;" Miss Emily Hewitt, "She wore a wreath of roses;" Mr. Brearley, "Jack's yarn ;" Mr. William Rhodes, Mr. Abel, "Leaf by leaf ;" Mr. J. Lyon," Polly." A pianoforte duet was given by Misses E. and F. Hewitt; a violin solo by Mr. C. Hewitt; a pianoforte solo by Miss Dinah Pennington, "Caprice ." a song and chorus "Evan- geline" by Mrs. Abel and choir, and "The policeman's chorus," by the choir. Readings were given by Miss Coupe. on picture galleries, Miss Ada Shaw, "The house where we were wed,'. and Miss Lyon, the" The Shunamite." A most enjoyable evening was spent.—The Chairman said it was not usual with the association to pass votes of thanks, but as that evenings proceedings could not be considered ordinary they would suspend the rule—Mr. T. Brown was sure that all present were ready to express their thanks as they had had a most enjoyable evening. (Applause.) What they bad heard that night made one feel proud of their society; they had such an amount of talent in connection with it, both instrumental, vocal, and elocutionary. Without at all disparaging the musical entertainment, the readings bad been of a very high class, and showed that they had as good elocutionists in St. Helens as'ulsewhere. (Hear, hear.) Re had,therefore great pleasure in moving that the best thanks of the meeting be given to those who contributed to the evening's entertainment. (Applause.)—Mr. H. L Riley seconded the motion, and said there was only one remark of Mr. Brown's that he felt disposed to qualify, and that was . . . . .

that they had as good elocutionists there as elsewhere. From the ability displayed by the ladies he felt that in their society they had a great deal better elocutionists than in many places. (Applause.) The motion ,was carried with acclamation.

BT. HELENS PRESBYTERIAN SUNDAY SCROOL.-A.111.4•- cellaneous concert was held on Thursday night in the Presbyterian Sunday schoolroom, Hardshaw. street. The concert was got up by the choral society connected with the church, which society has now existed for two years. It was, a short time ago, found necessary to extend the school on account of insufficient accommodation, and in July last the work was begun. The front portion of the school was extended so as to admit of a farther accommodation of 500 scholars, the additional ground floor accommodating 250, and the second floor over it a similar number. A wing has also been added,_and is used for the Purposes of a library. Previously there was inadequate spa-ce, and the books, which otherwise would have been obtained from the Sunday School Union, did not make their way into the library on this account. Now, however, the library has been increased by the addition of books from the Union, and will no doubt be farther in- creased.. The work of extending the premises has ben car- ried out by Mr. William Harrison, builder, Cotham-street. To cover the cost of building, and furnishing, subscriptims have been promised ; among the subscribers being Mr. hfcKechnie, who takes an active interest in the welfare of

the church and Sunday school. He has promised £lOO. To assist the movement, the concert of Thursday night was "a given nd the attendance was very large. Vocal and instru- mental music was given by the choir and Misses Robinson, Finney, Hall, Mort, Murray, Watkinson, T. Murray; Messrs. Russell, McEwen, Wilson, Williamson, Walsh, Milne Duck. worth, Sutherland, Skaife, and W. Atkins. Mr. J:Morton performed the duties of conductor, and Mrs. Cranston those of accompanist.

greatly augmented quantities upon recent years; and for the first time since 1875 or 1876, the coal trade has become in the latter months of this year decidedly brisk and, we may take it for granted, satisfactorily remunerative to those colliery-owners, at any rate, whose mines contain coal of recognised high quality. Although the output of coal has increased greatly ;since the development of the principal manufactures of the country recommenced, the consumption of this indispensable fuel has grown so fast, that the price of coal has been rising, until the margin of profit for the colliery companies must be considerable. Whilst we should not like to see coal advance to a I=4 price again, for that would both check many znagufacturers and infliet hardship upon the Poorer classes of housekeepers who need coal for their kitchen fires equally with the rich, still it would not be nnpleasing to know that the coal trade had ceased to be a losing business to those whose capital is in- vested in collieries. Other proofs that the country's commercial condition is sounder than it has been, and the vitality of its trade and industry replenished, are presented in several directions. The rolls of pauper- ism shew fewer names upon them than they did in most of the centres of population. The numbers of men and women and young persons able to work, Willing to work, yet denied the privilege of working by reason of the dearth of employment, are much diminished from what they were from 1877 to 1879. Our readies cannot have forgotten what thousands of decent honest people were reported as without work and destitute for weeks and months of the winter season, at the worst stage of the depression within the Period we have named. In Manchester, in Sheffield, and in other large towns the impoverishment of the Population through the contraction of the ordinary sources of employment was shocking, and the misery ‘rlag-apread. But where do we find such a state of things existing now? Not anywhere in the manu- facturing and mining districts of England and Scot- land. It is natural for our workers to regard plenty of work with fair wages as a thing of course when they have it; and expressions of thankfulness are less common when times are good than of complaint when times are bad. We do not bid working men to be Profuse in their thanksgiving to the peace-making, commerce-fostering Liberal Government under which the trade of the United Kingdom has so happily re- 717ed. Perhaps it is a pure accident that trade im- proves when a Government comes in which avoids l'zars and reduces taxes, and worsens when a Govern. 'tent accedes which makes needless wars and increases taxes and the public debt. The relation of cause and effect may not be traceable in this instance. Anyhow, the working men of England will do well to remember the coincidence—the striking coincidence—of the dis- appearance of hard times with the exodus of a Tory administration ; and the rapid recuperation of our ex- Port trade and the great increase in the demand for lab Our since a Liberal administration pursuing ettea,t;t ; --..Y the policy of Free Trade and of non-interven- :n came into power. We ask them simply to make mental note of the circumstance that for the gen..'ra I, •41, uY prosperous year British labour has passed rough Conservatism, with all its presumption, aan.not lay claim to the smallest particle of credit, renig that during the year the party of reaction has no more to do with the fiscal and foreign policy teand the protection of the external commercial in- of this country, than with the government of the • „ Inhabitants of the moon, if that chaste orb is really Lae abode of intelligent beings.

I hear that very considerable alterations are to be made at Widnes docks by the firm of Messrs. Hutchinson. The con- tract for the work will be a very heavy one, and as this, and the making of the Widnes sewer (to cost about £12,000) will, in all probability, be proceeding together, it seems that next year ought to be a brighter one in the annals of the town than the last has been.

The quarterly meeting in connection with the Wesleyan Methodist Runcorn circuit shows an increase of 10 upon the quarter, and that there are 48 on trial. This does not em- brace the fruit of the late revival services; and must be very satisfactory to the Runcorn Wesleyans.

Mr. Arthur T. Nowell, son of the Runcorn Wesleyan Methodist superintendent, has carried off the first prize in connection with the Manchester School of Art for drawing from the antique. Is it correct that at the next meeting of the Runcorn Board of Commissioners, the Market Inspector has recom- mended that a summons be taken out against the vendor of hot potatoes who wanders up and down the streets with his patent machine, with the object of cheering the souls of the various "dead beats ?" .

At various times within the past few years, celumns of matter have appeared in The Exam- iner upon the advantages which a free library would prove to Runcorn; but I think I may safely say that even the most hopeful amongst the promoters of the movement had not any grounds for believing that the Acts would be adopted on the Cheshire 'before the Lancashire side of the Mersey. Such, however, has proved to be the case, for whilst the ratepayers of Widnes have scornfully rejected the proposal to establish such an institution in the town, the Runcornians have, by a startling majority, carried the suggestion. Mr. William Handley, Dr. McDougall, and other hard workers in the cause, deserve the thanks of the public. Victors can afford to be generous, and it would probably not be wise to fire off the battery of sarcasms with which some of those who oppposed the resolution, the other evening, at Runcorn, might be greeted. Some who voted against the motion would undoubtedly have at the present time been far better off in the world if, when battling with poverty, and members of the great body of working men, they had had access to good books. It is very well known that when a man arrives at middle age, however anxious he may be to make up for the defects of early training, he will find that his brain has not that ductility which that of the young man possestes, and to the end of life's journey he will, when in the company of educated men, be ever and anon making some egregious mistake which it will require all their reserve power to keep from letting their friend know that they are quietly chuckling at him. The true man, of course, never cares who knows from whence he sprang, as he feels the fact that he has been enabled to "battle with his evil star," and "breast the blows of circumstance" suc- cessfully, to be his highest honour, whilst there are beings of another class to whom it is "as vinegar to the teeth" to have the slightest reference made to the days when they were not so fortunately situated. It is very gratifying to read of the manner in which Mr. John Simpson, of Frodsham, supported the movement. Though he is now in possession of, perhaps, one of the finest libraries in Cheshire, he was not ashamed to say that he could remember the time when he was a young man, and when the ability to obtain access to some of the valuable books often to be found in a Free Library, would have been of the greatest value to him. In earnest tones he pleaded with the ratepayers not to let the small expense which would necessarily follow the adoption of the Acts stand in the way of their doing so. How many 1 there are even in a small town like Runcorn wha have no pure source of enjoyment because in their early days they never walked "the glorious court" where a reader may hourly converse with kings and emperors, and sometimes with philosophers, "weighing their councils." Of them I may say with Gray,

"Knowledge to ,heir eyes her ample page, Rich with the spoils of time, did ne'er unroll," How many there are to-day who find their sole enjoyment in the bar parlour or the billiard room, who might have been saved from the weaknesses too often engendered from such associations, especially when carried to excess, if they had had a taste for reading ; for to him who loves literature the grand old masters of prose and poetry never grow dull, and, as one somewhere has said, these friends never meet you with a gloomy face, or refuse to hold sweet converse with their admirers. Now that the Acts have been adopted in the town, it behoves all to work together in an amicable manner to see that they are properly carried out, and not to throw needless impediments in the way. I believe, juVng from what I have heard, that there is no desire to enter into the slightest unnecessary ex- pense. If the Library is once started, and the Board of Commissioners are responsible for its maintenance, there are many such friends as Mr. John Simpson, who has promised £2O towards it, and Mr. G. S. Hazlehurst who offers his £5, that will come forward to help it in various ways. I am confident that in coming years there are many in- habitants of Runcorn who will look back upon the rather stormy meeting in Bethesda Congregational school-room last week, as one of the sunny spots in (their local history. This will make the total number of volumes already posses- sed by the town upwards of 1,000, reckoning the books +ft•of hp fho inotiflato anti horttiod nvol• to the Commissioners. The Runcorn Free Library will thus be enabled to make a very fair start.

Judging from the prosecutions at Runcorn Police Court last week, it is quite evident that Superintendent William- son is determined to make it rather lively for those milk dealers who will persist in adulterating the genuine article. I wish him all success in his admirable efforts.

Shopkeepers are at times brought up at the police courts in this district for having defective weights, concerning whom great astonishmeit is expressed that they should have placed themselves in such an unenviable position. The other day, Superintendent Barker, of Widnes, made a few remarks during the heating of one of these cases which, if taken in a proper spirit, may prove very useful to some of the shopkeeping class. Ha said it was no uncommon thing for assistants or lads in shops, when in want of a hammer, to use the first weight they came to for this purpose, and to resort to a variety of other plans which inevitably tended to destroy their exactness. lam able, from personal obser- vation, to support this statement of the Superintendent's, and the reference to it may make some owners •of grocery and provision stores more watchful to prevent such silly con- duct on the part of their workmen. Of course, these re- mks apply to the honest tradesmen, and not to those rascals who are to be found in all businesses, to whom a false balance, or defective weight, is a delight. I regret to see how often the Runcorn Board of Guardians have to proceed against able-bodied men, who permit their parents, who have arrived at that time when the grasshopper is a burden, to become a burden to the ratepayers. Even some civilized Englishmen, whose cultivated classes say that we had better have fifty years of Europe than a cycle of Cathay (or China), are found to be sadly wanting in that kindness to parents which is so distinguishing a feature of the disciples of Confucius. A believer in the Christian religion wjio is unwilling to help his parents in a difficulty, ought to be ostracised by his fellows, in order to give his soul time to grow a little larger. FLACCUS.

div.head: EZAIIINER, SATURDAY, DECEMBER 31, 1881.
div.p: THE EZAIIINER, SATURDAY, DECEMBER 31, 1881.

PROMOTION OF I WIDNES POLICE OFFICER.—PoIice Constable Clarkson, of IVidnee, has been promoted to the rank of sergeant. HALTON PARISH CHURCH MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY.—The weekly meeting of this society was held on Tuesday evening, when Mr. W. H. Thompson occupied the chair. The Vicar gave a reading, explaining the meaning of " Christmas," "Christmas boxes," "New Year's gifts," "Carols," "Wassail bowl," eke. RUNCORN BRANCH OF THE MERSEY MISSIONS TO SEA- MEN.—On Monday evening, a tea party will be held in the Mission Room, Bottom Locks, after which addresses will be delivered by several friends. An entertainment will follow. The Rev. Canon Barclay will preside. On Tuesday evening, a tea party and Christmas tree will be held for the boat chil- dren attending the Sunday school. For further particulars see our advertising columns. A NOVELTY IN CHRISTMAS CARES.—Christmas, says the old rhyme, comes but once a year, but when it comes it gives good cheer. This good cheer is of various kinds, one of which takes the form of cakes and confectionery. Messrs. Kirkland Brothers, of Lord-street, Liverpool, have intro- duced a novelty in Christmas and New Year confectionery which is not only of a very superior description, but is ornamented with very chaste and artistic devices and mottoes, formed in sugar' and suited to the season, the cakes thus ful- filling the double duty of pleasing the eye and administering to the appetite. WESLEYAN BAND OF HOPE MEETING AT WIDNES. On Thursday evening, a Wesleyan Band of Hope meeting took place in the Lacey-street schoolroom, Widnes. The Rev. J. H. Cummings occupied the chair, andedelivered an address on the subject of temperance. A programme of the usual description was then proceeded with. Among those who contributed to the entertainment by giving recitations, songs, drc., were Miss A. Kirkham, Miss Alice Ramsey, Mr. H. Wright, and G. Berrington. Among the recitations was the popular one at meetings of this class, "The Drunkard's Wife." In the course of the evening, an address was given by Mr. S. Owens. PRESENTATION AT HILTON PARISH CHURCH SUNDAY SCHOOL—On Sunday afternoon, the teachers and scholars in connection with this school assembled to present one of their teachers, who has recently left the parish, with an illuminated album bearing the following inscription : "Pre- sented to Mr. John Povey, by the vicar and teachers in connection with Halton Parish Church School, as a small token of their esteem and regard. Halton, Cheshire, Christmas, 1881." The vicar made the presentation with a short address, and spoke highly of Mr. Povey's services, and the loss all had sustained by his removal. Mr. Povey briefly replied thanking the donors for their kindness. PRESENTATION AT HA.LTON PARISH CHURCH SUNDAY SCHOOL.—On Sunday afternoon the teachers and scholars in connection with this school assembled to present one of their teachers, who has recently left the parish, with a neatly illuminated album bearing the following inscription:— "Presented to Mr. Povey, by the Vicar and teachers in connection with Halton Parish Church Sunday School, as ' a small token of their esteem and regard. Halton, Cheshire, Christmas, 1881." The Vicar made the presentation with a ' short address suitable to both teachers and scholars, and spoke highly of Mr. Povey's services and the loss all had sustained by his removal. Every good wish having been accorded him, Mr. Povey briefly replied thank- ing the donors for their kindness and good feeling. ST. JOHN THE EVANGELIST'S, WESTON, (RUNCORN.)— The annual congregational tea party in connection with this mission was held on Wednesday evening last. The attend- ance was very large. A miscellaneous entertainment follow- ed, at which the Rev. Canon Barclay presided. One pleasing aspect of the entertainment, which included songs, trios glees, and readings, was that it was given entirely by mem- bers of the congregation and choir. Texts and ecclesiastical designs suitable for the festival of Christmas, tastefully worked in holly on crimson bickgrounds ; festoons of fir, ivy, and holly profusely decorating window and arch and spanning the room, contributed in no little degree in stirring up those feelings of goodwill and cheerfulness aasociated with this season. The promoters feel themselves specially indebted to the following ladies and gentlemen, most of whom were present, for their donations of tables: Mrs. Aaron, Adcock, Armstrong, Mr. T. Bankee, Mrs. Barclay, Barrow, Bryant, Clander. Ford, Griffiths, Lightfoot, Morses, Poole, Miss Rougier, Miss A. Rougier and Mrs. Vose. DARESEURY PE.= SESSIONS.—At these sessions on Tuesday, before Messrs. Edward Greenall and James Mar- son, Thomas Hindley, of the Cat and Lion, Stretton, was cllarged with having on his premises for sale, on the 18th November last, a quantity of gin, the same being unduly diluted with water. Constable Bosson submitted the gin in question to the county analyst, and received a certificate statir'ne that it contained 13 per cent, more water than al- lowed by Act of Parliament. Defendant, who said he did it in ignorance, was fined ss. and costs.—J. D. Meakin was charged with having, on the 3rd December, allowed a boat to be used as a dwelling without having had the same duly registered. It appeared that when the boat was built it was registered, but lately it had been repainted, and the builder had neglected to number it as before. Defendant was ordered to pay the costs.—Terence Fitzpatrick, a farm labourer, was charged with Laving, in Whitley, on the 20th November, stolen a bag of flour, the property of Peter Lees, grocer.—Prosecutor said he left the bag of flour in a basket inside a gate, and while he was absent prisoner took it away. The prisoner admitted the theft, and was com- mitted to Knutsford gaol for a month. DRAMATIC BALL AT WIDNES.—It Will be seen from our advertising columns that a grand dramatic ball, under distinguished patronage, will be held in the Volunteer Hall, Widnes, on the evening of the 2nd January. During the evening the celebrated actor and author, Mr. W. S. Branson, who has won golden opinions in various parts of the coun- try for his elocutionary powers, will give selections from various English classics; and Mr. E. Sansom, stationmaster to the London and North-Western Railway Co., will act as auxiliary to him. The Farnworth Glee Party will also take part in the proceedings. The prices will be :—Double tickets for lady and gentleman, 25.; single tickets, lady's 2s. 6d., gentleman's 2s. Oct., which may be had at The ,Examincr office, or from Mr. Edwards, registrar, Simm's Cross. Judging from the gentlemen who have the matter in hand, we think we are quite safe in prophesying that the ball will be conducted in a thoroughly respectable manner, and be a thorough success. ALLEGED Frur.,)s ON I..rn LIVERPOOL D,cx BOARD.— At the Liverpool City Police Court, before Mr. Raffles, John Jones, aged 54, and Jno. Beckett, aged 58 (of Runcorn), were charged with obtaining money by false pretences from the Mersey Docks and Harbour Board. Jones was employed as a weigher by the Board, and Beckett had for some time con- tracted with the Board for the.supply of gravel. Mr. Carver (instructed by Mr. Pinfield, deputy solicitor to the Board,) prosecuted. Mr. R. Bremner defended Beckett, and Mr. Moore (Messrs. Moore and Spence) defended Jones. Mr. Carver stated that for something like three years the prisoner Beckett had been a contractor to the Board for the supply of gravel at 3s. 9d. per ton, which he engaged to deliver at either the north or south works. The gravel was brought in a small vessel, and Beckett paid the freight. It was then put into trucks and weighed by Jones and other employes of the Dock Board. Suspicion was aroused as to the quantities which were being delivered, and on the sth the cargo of a vessel called the Tarleton Lass was put in a place where it would not be touched. On the 20th, Jones weighed it, and gave a return of its weight at 211 tons and 11 cwt., inclu- ding 61 tons and 17 cwt, for the tare of thirty-one waggons, or a net weight of 149 tons 14 cwt. This gravel was after- wards re-weighed, and it was found that Jones had returned a weight of 14 tons in excess of the real weight. Beckett thus obtained £2 12s. 6d. by the misrepresentation of the weight. A remand was asked for, and the prisoners were I admitted on bail of two £25 each.

LlNcasunzE ANNUAL SESSIONS.—Tho annual general session of the justices for the county of Lancaster was held at Preston, on Thursday, under the presidency of the Earl of Derby. The estimates of expenditure for November 30, 1881, to August 31, 1882, which exceeded the estimates for the corresponding period in the previous year by about 44,000, were approved. The increase 1r1.3 said to be due to the enlargement of the county police force, for which the Home Secretary's sanction has been obtained, to the extent of two inspectors, 14 sergeants, and 102 constables. THE BIRTH AND D RATH RATE OF Wannurarox.—For week ending December 24th.—The mean temperature was 31.6 Fahrenheit, and therefore 1 degrees higher than the preceding week. The maximum temperature 42.5 F. was recorded on the 21st inst., and the minimum temperature 145 F. on the 23rd inst. The rainfall measured 1} inches. The general direction of the wind was north-west. During the week, which was the 51st of the current year, 30 births and 29 deaths were registered. The death rate from all causes was equal to 35.9 per 1,000, against 29.2 the average of the previous four weeks, and against 18.2 the corresponding week of last year. The deaths included 1 from measles, 2 from scarlet fever, 2 from diptheria, 1 from croup, 4 from brain disease, and 10 from lung diseases. The higher death rate is due to the increased number of deaths from infectious diseases old affections of the organs of respiration amongst young children. Seven cases of infectious disease were reported under the requirements of the Act of Parliament, viz: 3of diptheria, and 4 of scarlet fever.—Joux 11. GORNALL, Medical Officer of Health.

TUE PAMIR Idnusrun.—On Thursday, Mr. Glad- stone completed the 72nd year of his age, haying been born at Liverpool on the 29th December, 1809. Having been elected for Newark on the 13th December, 1832, the right honourable gentleman has entered upon the fiftieth year of his public life. Of the members of the Cabinet of Earl Grey, then in office, not one survives. Of the 658 members, of the fir,st reformed Parliament, to whom the speech of King William was addressed on the sth February, 1833, the Prime Minister is the only one who, with a seat in that assembly now, then began his political career. There are in the present house only two representatives who were in the unreformed Parliament—Mr. Christopher Talbot, who has sat continuously for Glamorganshire since 1830, and The O'Gorman Mahon, first elected for Clare in 1830, but whose parliamentary experience has not been unbroken.

LIVERPOOL PRINCE OF WALES THEATRE PANTOS/USE. —The pantomimes usually produced at the above theatre have obtained more than a local popularity, and the pro- babilities are that the one of this season will be visited as in past years, by great numbers of persons from the towns within reasonable distance of Liverpool, such as Warrington, St. Helens, Widnes, and Runcorn. The legend dealt with this time is "Aladdin and the Wonderful Lamp," the author of the pantomime being Mr. J. F. M'Ardle, whose experience in such work is a guarantee that the composition is blight and entertaining, only needing good artistes to interpret it, and proper stage appointments to render it altogether the kind of entertainment to charm and to delight both young and old. The first performance of the pantomime came off on Thursday before Christmas, and our Liverpool contem- poraries speak highly of it. The Mercury, in its notice, ' states that all the points in the well•known story are retained but they have been set by Mr. 111`Ardle amid such a brilliancy of wit as to be more striking and attractive than ever. The company is well selected and versatile, the ballet various and well trained, and the scenery splendid. In short, the management in the production of " Aladdin and the Wonderful Lamp " have all the elements of success.

SAD DEATH OF A FOREMAN AT WADETNGTON.—At the White Hart Inn, Sankey-street, on Tuesday, Mr. Barker, deputy-coroner, held an inquest touching the death of a young man named John Preston. From the evidence it appeared that deceased, who was 21 years of age, lived with his mother in Guardian-street, and was empl...yed at the chemical works of Messrs. Lonshaw and Son, Sankey Bridges. He went to work on Saturday morning and worked all day, continuing work at night. About three o'clock on Sunday morning he complained of being rather sleepy to the night watchman, James Wood, who said that he had better have a sleep. Deceased went and 13y down in the bottle shed. The watchman went to speak to him about a quarter- past four, and deceased followed him. He had been standing at the still for about ten minutes, when it filled and ran over. He told deceased they had better shift the cask, as it was full. Deceased said "all right," and, as he shifted the cask, slipped his foot into the well. He ran to the tap with him and turned the water on his foot. He also ran for a can of oil and applied the oil to the scalded foot. When asked if he felt any pain deceased said he had bad worse burns than that before. Wood then left him and went to his work. Deceased went to him again about five o'clock, and he noticed that he seemed very sleepy and tired out. About six o'clock he seemed stupefied, and the watchman told a man to go for Hewitt, the foreman. Deceased was taken to the Infirmary, and Wood went and stayed with him about a quarter of an hour. He was then quite ineen- Bible, and continued so until his death. He was attended by Mr. Parkinson and several doctors. His right foot was very badly scalded. All was done for him that could be done for him to bring him round, but he died about one o'clock in the afternoon. Mr. Longshaw, one of the proprietors of the chemical works, said the deceased had been in his employ for about three or four years. He was foreman of the carbolic acid department, where he had full control. He was a steady man and quite competent. He (Mr. Longshaw) saw him about one o'clock on Saturday afternoon, when be was then quite well, and he left him in charge. The still he had charge of worked about 80 gallons an hour. The work the deceased was at was light, he had only to remove the casks as they filled, and he could go and lie down in the intervals. He saw deceased again at the works about eight o'clock on Sun- day morning; he was then unconscious. He gave him some whiskey and milk and sent for a doctor and a cab to take the deceased to the Infirmary. On examining the still at which deceased was working he found that the manhole ha. burst, and in order to repair it deceased must have inhaltt the fumes from the still. He ought to have drawn the fire before trying to repair the manhole. The jury returned a verdict to the effect that the deceased came to his death "accidentally and by his own act of incaution."

div.head: CHRISTMAS IN RUNCORN DISTRICT.
div.p: CHRISTMAS IN RUNCORN DISTRICT.

Christmas Day this year happened upon Sunday—one of those days of which quaint George Herbert says : "The Sundays of man's ive Thre.de 1 together on Time's string, Make bracelets to adorn the wife • Of the et,rnal glori ,us King. On Sunday Heaven's gate stands o;e.; Blessings are plentiful and rlps More plentiful than hop."

We are, therefore, gratified to be able to report that the 1 time was Sot devoted to jollity, and that there were but few incidents to be witnessed in the streets to which even the most strict in their ideas of the day could have taken ex- caption. Certainly when the shadows fell, and the moon C 3.1110 out, that is what little could be seen of her, owing to the fog—there were certain streets in the town where num- , hers of young men who appeared to have a greater love of I discord than harmony, went about trying their lungs on How beautiful are the feet," or " Hark the herald angels sing.", Some of the principal choirs visited the houses of their friends on Saturday evening, notwithstanding that rain was falling heavily, and their sweet tones mingled with the shouts of the shopmen in some of the thoroughfares. Appropriate sermons were preached at the variOns places of worship on Sunday, when the attendance though very fair in the morning, was but scant in the evening. Earl's' on Monday morning the town was alive with plea- sure-seekers, and people who were intent on taking journeys for the purpose of grasping the hands of some trusty friends On the highway of life. The trains were splendidly filled, as the weather was of so mild a description that numbers who would otherwise have been kept within doors, ventured out for a "constitutional "or to pay visits Hundreds went to Liverpool, Manchester, Warrington and neighbouring towns, whilst the places of the absentees were filled by the country cousins and relatives who thronged the streets from every quarter. A multitude came from the Lancashire side of the Mersey; and the sun which had been absent from sight for so many days in the district, shed a blessing on the scene. As the day advanced there was a fair sprinkling of men to be seen who had worshipped too long at the shrine of Old John Barleycorn, but ,not so many as in previous years. The efforts of the total abstinence party and the educationalists are beginning to boar some fruit and the publicans are crying out hourly that they are not doing the business they did in former times, though trade is acknow- ledged to be considerably improved, as compared with last year, even by the most inveterate grumblers. The shop- keepers in the district speak with much more hopefulness as to the future, and those who of late years have been loud in their prophecies that the country was going to the dogs, and that we were never to see prosperous times again, have "taken back seats" in public affairs.

THE PARISH CHURCH. was, as usual, beautifully decorated by a number of friends, amongst whom we may mention Mesdames Armsnn, Barker, Bryant, Crosby, Toule, Lightburn, Stanway, Steele, Whit- taker, the Misses Barclay, Carr, Cawley, Crosby, Hartley, Rouoier, A. Rougier, Statham, Ward,and Williams; Messrs. Brundrit, W. and L. Crosby, Davies, Dykes, Greaves, Tonle, Sutton, Shaw and Torkington. The evergreens were supplied by Mr. Robert Dagßah, of Ashton Hall, and Dr. Steele, of Heath House. Over the west door was a scroll containing the words "God sent forth His Son made of a woman," and the compound nature of the Saviour was also alluded to in the mottoes "God incarnate" and "Man divine" above the north and south entrances. In the spaces between the central and side lights of the east win- dow were the words, "Hark, the herald angels sing glory to the new-born king ;" and the name " Emmanuel," wrought in holly gemmed with berries in mediaeval capitals, occupied the place of the reredos. On Sunday, communion service (choral) took place at mid-day, being Dykes in F. The anthem in the evening was the appropriate one of "Sing, 0 Heavens," by Berthold Tours.

div.head: HOLY TRINITY CHURCH.
div.p: HOLY TRINITY CHURCH.

Upon no former occasion has Trinity Church presented a prettier or more elegant appearance in its Christmas decora- tions. The window-sills are ornamented with the test "Unto us is born this day in the city of David, a Saviour which is Christ the Lord," worked in white, Church text on a red ground and bordered with evergreens. A border of evergreens goes round the entire church; and festoons of evergreens with shields ornamented the gallery. The pulpit has in front the initial Greek letters of the name " Christ " on a red ground embosomed in evergreen; and the chancel has over the table "Emmanuel" in gilt letters, the back ground being crimson relieved with white lattice work and a border of evergreen. The whole exhibits much artistic taste and reflects great credit on the executors, who were Mesdames Preston, Buckley, Robinson, .Misses Annett, Preston, Smith, Martin, 'Bird, Lea, Hamer, Stubbs, Williams, and Isherwood; Messrs. Buckley, Rogerson, West, Worthington, Sefton, Annett, Fletcher, Broughton, Hankinson.
