div.head: CHRISTMAS AT WIDNES.
div.p: CHRISTMAS AT WIDNES.

This year Christmas Day at Widnes was marked by an unwonted peacefulness, as it fell upon the Sabbath; and the weather was of a character more in unison with that generally experienced in November than the ice and snow which, generally speaking, are to be found in this district at this season of the year. Indeed the difference between this 25th of December and last was wonderful indeed. Then we had to speak of the Mersey as ice-bound; hundreds of people out of work, and gigantic icicles on Runcorn railway bridge —weather which would not ,have been out of place at Quebec or on the St. Lawrence. Old stagers whose lungs are as sound as a bell, and who are fond ef skating, may talk of the glories of old fashioned winters as they please; but such terrible weather means scarcity, sometimes semi-starvation, in the workingman's home, and, therefore, comparatively little money circulating amongst the shopkeepers. Business matters in the town are looking considerably better than they were twelve months ago, and as several new works are to be commenced at the new year, there is a fair prospect of better times. On Sunday, special sermons were preached at many of the places of worship. At the Parish Church the Rev. W. H. Duggan, curate, preached in the morning from Luke ii. 10; and in the evening the Rev. J. Wright-Williams dis- coursed on "He hath visited and redeemed His people." There were good congregations at both services; and the sacred edifice presented a beautiful appearance, much care having been bestowed upon its decoration by the ladies of the congregation. On Monday, the Wesleyans had a capital day at their sale of work and Christmas tree, in Lacey-street School-room. On this day the mighty chimneys ceased te send forth their huge volumes of smoke, and the town was comparatively free from the vapours which tend to render it so full of curious flavours. The railway stations did a splendid business—especially the London and North Western, which had such a run of business that one of the leading officials was constrained to give vent to his satisfac- tion in the sentence, " They may say what they like about the state of trade in Widnes, but all the money's not gone out of the town yet." Hundreds left for Liverpool, War- rington, and places even still more remote' and during the early part of the day the streets were full of holiday seekers. Tuesday was considerably quiter, as some of the working classes then started work. We regretted to see such a con- siderable number of semi-drunken people about in the even- ings, who were full of that maudlin sentimentality and jollity which seems to be one of the chief characteristics of the (tiddler's brain. Many of these blocked up the footpaths whilst they swore eternal friendship, under the exhilirating influences of Bacchus, and the police dealt kindly with the poor souls and refrained from locking them up under the exceptional circustances of the time.

div.head: WARRINGTON POLICE COURT.
div.p: WARRINGTON POLICE COURT.
FRIDAY.—Befde Captain Reynolds, Mr. John White, and Mr. Ziba Armitage.

DEFAULTING APPRENTICES.—Mr. George Aspey, master fustian cutter, summoned his apprentice, Elizabeth Sankey, for leaving her work onithe Bth October, whereby he bad sus- tained a loss of 7s. 6d.—An order was made for the payment of the claim and expenses, at the rate of is. 6d. per week, and to return to work.---A similar charge was made against Mabel Gandy, and she was ordered to pay the claim of 17s. 6d. and costs, and to return to her work. THE FIGHT IN BEWSEY.—SERIOUS CHARGE AGAINST BEERHOUSE.KEEPER. James Worrall, keeper of the Bewsey Inn beerhouse, in Pitt-street, was charged with having unlawfully allowed gambling to be carried on in his house on the 17th December.—Mr. Robert Davies ap- peared on behalf of Messrs. Whitley, Greenall 8; Co.—Mr. Hunt said this case arose out of evidence given a week ago, in regard to a fight where a man had died. It was stated that a game of chance called "shove penny" was played, for pints and quarts of beer, in the defendant's house from half-past six in the morning to half-past twelve at noon.— James Hassell said he was in the defendant's house at the time and date named, but he never saw any games going on. Mr. Worrell would not allow R.—Captain Reynolds : Ar'n't you saying something different to what you did last Friday ?—By Mr. Hunt: There was n 3 betting going on.— William Bradford, a forgeman' said there was "some sort " of a game being played but he couid not tell what. The " regular " game was "push penny." He was talking to a man and did not see the game being played, but he heard them crying out the numbers. He did not see Mr. Worrell in the room that morning, but he had seen him on many previous occasions stop the men from playing.—Mr. Davies said the defendant had been a police constable 11 or 12 years, and if lie allowed any gaming in the house it was contrary to the instructions and wishes of his landlords, Messrs. Greenall. He (Mr. Davies) did not think a man had a more difficult task than the defendant had, in managing his house. His customers were chiefly forgemen, who were very difficult to get under control, and he had witnesses to prove that he attempted to check the gaming. The men took chalk of their own to the house and made marks on the table and then struck a penny with the side of the hand, and the man that lost paid for the beer. The law required that there must be a certain amount of knowledge on the part of the landlord, and the defendant was not in the room when the gaming took place. If the Bench considered the evidence of the witnesses incontrovertible, he would ask if there wap any evidence to connect the defendant with the gaining, ar_d he suggested that Mr. Hunt withdraw the charge, and the defendant would pay the costs, and he (Mr. Davies) would be glad to enforce any special opinion on the subject upon Worrell, who, if be allowed the gaming, would be liable, and the conse- quence would be very disastrous to his license. Captain Reynolds said it was distinctly stated by one witness, a week ago, that games were played for half gallons of beer, and that Worrall was himself in the room watching the game.— Mr. White and Mr. Armitage concurred with that statement. I —The Magistrates' Clerk remarked that he understood that the defendant was in the room, but did not know about watching the games.—Captain Reynolds said the summons would not have been taken out but for that Statement. The men spoke very clearly last Friday and to-day they were shuffling.—Edward Cartwlight, was then placed in the box and said he was a forgeman, and was in the defendant's house on the day named. "Shove peony" was being played, and he had one game himself for a pint of b7er. I.lt defend- ant brought in the beer, bat be did not se hiin in the room whilst the game was being played. —1 Captain Reynolds : What made you say last Friday that he was in the room? I didn't your worship.—My memory is very treacherous if you didn't.—Mr. Armitage : He did say it. There is no doubt about it.—Captain Reynolds said there was no evidence against the defendant, and Mr. Hunt withdrew the charge. —Captain Reynolds remarked that the Bench had heard of a good deal of gaming being carried on. No doubt it was a very difficult thing to keep these men from gambling, and he hoped the present proceedings would be a caution to the defendant. .

_ PROCEEDINGS TO RECOVER AN APPRENTICE. Colonel Henry D. Renzi Pigott, commanding officer at the Bar- racks, was summoned to show cause why an order should not he made upon him to deliver John Brogan, who had en- listed in the South Lancashire Regiment, over to his employers Messrs. I'ilkington Bros., glass manufacturers, St. Helens, with whom he was apprenticed. Mr. J. 0. Swift appeared for Messrs. Pilkington, and said Colonel Pigott, who did notitippear, had no objection to the Bench making an order for Brogan to return to wmk.—The order was made. "HE FORGO', Iharszt.v."—George Povey, a respectable looking young man was charged with having, on the 26th December, assaulted Mary Ann Taylor.—Mr. Robert Davies, who represented the complainant, said the defendant had apologised to her, and if the Bench would bind him over to be of good behaviour, the complainant would be quite satisfied. Defendant "forgot hinlself "when he committed the assault, and was, he believed, rather in liquor.—Defendant pleaded guilty and he was bound over to be of good behaviour for twelve months, in his own recog- nizance of £lO.

EMBEZZLEMENT BY RAILWAY POI:ITEM—Jan Wm. Paggater, a railway porter at Arpley Station, was charged with having on the 3rd December stolen Td.; and at various other times, divers sums of money, the property of his employers, the London and North-Western Railway Company. Prisoner pleaded not guilty.—Mr. Preston re- presented the company, and said this was an unfortunate case in which the company endeavoured to stop a practice which was too common in many parts of their railway. Passengers very frequently taavelled by train without ob- taining a ticket, and paid their fare on arrival at their des- tination. It was for the convenience of the travelling public that it should be so, but it opened a wide door to fraud. The money so received for fares was called excess. and it was the duty of the collectors to account for it. It was difficult to prove whenever they did so or not, and it had become the duty of the company to test the honesty of their servants by test cases. It was not the seven pence, nor the shilling, but the pounds which very often found their way into the pockets of individuals, that was the cause of these prosecutions. In 'this case the company instructed I test cases to be undertaken by the detectire department, and there were four occasions on which defendant had received fares for which he had not accounted. The object the company had in view by bringing these cases was to inform their ser- vants generally that their conduct was overlooked, and that they could not perpetrate frauds without some danger of dis- covery. Thomas Hollingsworth, head booking-clerk at Bank Quay Station, proved that it was the defendant's duty to collect tickets from the train arrivingin Warrington from London-road at 11.30. In the excess book there was no entry by the defendant of the receipt of any excess fares on the 3rd December, or on the 14th, 15th, or 17th Decem- ber.—Sarah Cleaver, wife of John Cleaver, detective officer, stationed at Warrington, deposed to travelling, with her son, from Lyrnm to Warrington, by the 11.15 p.m. train, without tickets. The defendant, at Warrington, demanded her ticket, and that of her son's. She paid him 7d., the fare he demanded. On Wednesday the 14th December, she travelled in the same train, and in the same manner, and again paid defendant 711—The son, Herbert Cleaver, cor- roborated.—The wife of a railway constable, residing at Manchester, said she travelled from Lynam to Warrington by the 11.15 p.m. train on the 15th December. She was without ticket, and she paid sd. to the prisoner who demanded that sum as its equivalent.—Elizabeth Barlow, also the wife of a railway constable, stated she paid the prisoner sd. on the 15th December, the fare from Lynam to Warrington charged by him.—Henry Allcock, detective officer, of Long- sight, said that on Saturday the 17th inst., he arrived at

( Warrington by the 11.15 p.m. train from Lymm, without a ticket. The guard of the train, John Husband, demanded his ticket, in lieu of which he paid 5d., and he saw the guard hand the money to prisoner.—Wal tor Timperley, book- ing clerk at Arpley, said it was the collectors' duty to band excess fares to him, but he had received none from the prisoner on:the dates named—.'When apprehended by the detective Cleaver, prisoner said "I know nothing about it." He now said he remembered none of the transactions.—Captain Reynolds said the evidence had been so strong that there was no question of the prisoner's guilt, and he would be committed to 'gaol three months, with hard labour.— Another porter, named William Clayton, was then placed in the dock charged with having, on the Bth December, stolen 711, and other sums at various times, the property of the London and North-Western Railway Company, his em- ployers.—He pleaded not guilty.—He was proved to have received 74d. on the Bth just, 10d. on the 21st, and 71d. on the 23rd, for which he had not accounted. He had, how- ever, unlike the other prisoner, entered several sums which he had received in the book.—ln answer to Captain Rey- nolds, Mr. Preston said there was a bye-law which prohibited riding without ticket, but if it were strictly enforced, a barrier would have to be erected at each station at which to examine tickets, which would be a great inconvenience to the public.—Mr. John White remarked that parties travel- ling without tickets were then liable to be summoned.—The Magistrates' Clerk : There must be the intent to defraud. It is the intent which constitutes the offence.—Prisoner said he had always given up what he had received, and had paid money out of his own pocket to the Company.—The Bench did not regard this case as serious as the former one, and sentenced him to two months' imprisonment with hard labour.
A DESERTER.—John Brown was charged with having deserted from the 2nd battalion of the Bth Regiment of Foot, in January, 1875.—He pleaded guilty, and was handed over to the military authorities.

div.head: WESLEYAN METHODISM AT WIDNES.
div.p: WESLEYAN METHODISM AT WIDNES.
CHRISTMAS TREE AND SALE OF WORK.

On Monday afternoon, a Christmas tree and sale of work were held in the Lacey-street schoolroom, Widnes, for the purpose of defraying a circuit debt amounting to about VO. The proceedings were opened at two o'clock, and as the weather was of a rather pleasant character, there was a capital attendance. Amongst those present on the platform were:— The Revs. J. H. Cummings, J. Tessyman ; Messrs. It. H. Davies, R. Fogg, T. Robinson, Benjamin Brown, S. Sadler, T. S. Swale, and P. Speakman. The proceedings were commenced with devotional exer- cises, the Res.. J. H. Cummings giving out a hymn, and Rev. J. Tessyman offering prayer. The Rev. J. H. CUMMINGS then remarked that he was very happy to see so large a gathering upon that interesting occasion, and also to introduce to them Mr. R. H. Davies, the gentleman who had so kindly consented to attend there that afternoon and open their sale of work and Christmas tree. (Applause.) He was glad they had received the mention of Mr. Davies' name with so much enthusiasm, and that gentleman would now make a few remarks to them. Mr. DAVIES, who was warmly received, said he did not suppose they would have seen him there that afternoon at the opening of their beautiful bazaar, had it not been that he found it impossible to withstand the deputation of fair ladies wha waited upon him to request him to be present. When he came to consider what he should say he became puzzled. He at first thought that it would probably form part of his duty to cut down the Christmas tree,—(laughter)—and he had considered the desirability of sending to Her Meet Gracious Majesty the Queen to ask for the golden axe which was sent to her the other day by an African prince. He, however, came to the conclusion that if he did so he should only meet with a refusal—(laughter)—and so they would have to do without it. Then his mind carried him back to the time when the yule log, which burned so brightly I at Christmas time and shed its genial warmth upon every I one was so popular; and when they were all welcome to I partake of the good things upon the festive board. He sup- posed that the Christmas tree he saw before him bore all sorts of wonderful things Upon its branches, and to any of these any one of them was welcome if he would onlj pay for it. (Laughter, and hear, hear.) He hoped thlt all present had come well supplied with money—with pockets well lined—and that they were in an anxious state of mind to part with that money. (Laughter.) He understood that the sum raised there on that and the following day would be employed in extinguishing a small debt of about £6O, which remained upon the circuit. He had every confidence that they would raise the amount; and he must call upon all the rank and file of the Wesleyans in the circuit to rally round those who had for some time been labouring for this object. In conclusion, he had to declare the Christmas tree and sale of work open. (Applause.) Mr. BENJAMIN BROWN moved that the best thanks of those present be given to Mr. Davis for attending there for the purpose of opening what he might call.their bazaar. He had known Mr. Davis for many years, and he knew that he had a natural feeling of diffidence against taking part in public demonstrations. Being quite aware of this, the only way which he could see to get Mr. Dayis to attend their bazaar opening was to bring before him a deputation of ladies. This proposal was carried into effect, and that , genlleman succumbed to their persuasiveness. (Laughter and applause.) Mr. Davis had attended there at consider- able personal inconvenience, and he had no doubt that they would show their appreciation of his kindness by darry- ing the motion with enthusiasm'. Mr. FOGG, in seconding the proposition, remarked that he was happy to say that was not the first time he had met Mr. Davis on a Methodist platform; and though be was not a Wesleyan Methodist, he belonged to the great body of Non- conformists. (Applause.) Mr. Davis must, consequently, know something as to what voluntaryism meant, and that I every membn of a chirch Cottoned in accordance with these principles had to put his band into his pocket. (Hear, hear.) He was very gratified to see that Mr. Davis had managed to attend there at such a time as Christmas week, and he had no doubt that he had done so at no little mown- ' venience to himself—(applause)—in order to help the Wealevan Methodists.

Mr. ROBINSON, Who was received with applause, observed that he had great pleasure in supporting the proposition, and he could very easily enlarge upon it, but he was under the impression that it would not be wise to do so. He could bear personal testimony to the fact that Mr. Davies was worthy of all their thanks; and he had no doubt he would prove this assertion to be true' before he had done with them. (Laughter.) On ouch an occasion, he (the speaker) could not help going back to the old times when Martin Luther used to assemble his children on Christmas eve, in his own house, around the Chirstmas tree. The candles were kept burning, and it was a great celebration with them. He, however, considered that the one they saw before them was as improvement upon the great 'reformer's Christmas tree. This was an age of money getting, and to their Christmas tree they had superadded what they might very fairly des- cribe as a bazaar. In the gathering together of such a great number of things there must have been a deal of kindness of heart manifested on part of the ladies, and much expansive- ness of soul on the side of those who had given the goods. In getting up such a display as that, it seemed to him that the ladies were going through a kind of educational course. which gave them a capital acquaintance with the construc- tion of articles which they'might themselves need in after life. (Laughter.) That appeared to be the most effectual way of raising money which they were acquainted. In con- clusion, be would say he thought they might all congratu- late themselves that they had such a display, and such gentlemen to open their bazaar. (Applause.) Mr. Davis, in reply, said he could only hope they would have a very successful day, and be should be glad to do any- thing he could to assist them in the good cause they had at I heart.

The ladies in charge of the stalls were as follows: Mesdames B. Brown, Cummings, Fogg, Houghton, Hulme, Robinson, T. Sadler, and Stringer. The Christmas tree was superintended by the following :—Mesdames Cooper, For- shaw, John Sadler, the Misses Abbot, Balshaw, Butler, Gorst, Jones, Sadler, and the members of the select class. The two refreshment stalls were in charge of Mesdames Proctor, Rowlands, S. Sadler, Seed, Shaw, Swale, Duxbury, J. Duxbury, Lawrinson, S. Robinson, Spencer, Miss Gerrard, Mr. Houghton, Mr. T. Robinson, jun., Mr. Stringer, and Mr. Lawrinson. The room was decorated with banners, mottoes, and paintings in oil and water-colours, which gave it a very pleasing appearance. The chief stall, which occupied the centre of the space, was a very handsome pavilion, in the construction of which great taste had been shown. We have seen many Christmas exhibitions of a similar character— indeed, the writer scarce cares now-a-days to recollect the exact number—but we never saw a more charming specimen of a similar stall, where the amount expected to be raised was so small.

The Christmas tree, which was a fine one of its kind, was placed near the door, and was powdered wish imitation snow and decked with nearly every imaginable kind of toy such as Santa Claus brings to his friends at this holiday time. A recent magazine article states that the Christmas tree is without doubt of German origin. The Teutons con- ceived the world to be a great tree whose roots were hidden deep under the earth, but whose top flourished in the old German paradise—Walhalla--with which that rugged soul, Thomas Carlyle, has made modern readers so familiar. The Christmas tree was first fitted up in honour of Bechta, the goddess of spring; but was subsequently transferred to the birthday of Christ, who, as the God-man, is "the resurrec- tion and the life." The evergreen tree, and emblem of spring time, became the symbol of an eternal spring. The burning lights usually put on such trees were to act as a shadow of Him who is " the Father of Lights," and the gifts to remind the spectators of the gift of his son. Such was its origin ; and now the Christmas tree is not only to be found through- out Germany, but has taken root from the Alps to the Uiral,—alike OD the banks of the Neva and the Po, the Thames and the Mississippi. The workstall contained more articles of the useful than the ornamental class, and in this the promoters of the sale showed their good sense, for those who purchase things at similar exhibitions have too often to complain, like Frank- lin, the American philosopher, that they have paid far too much for their "whistle." Amongst the goods were some very nicely-dressed dolls, presented by Mrs. Booth, which would no doubt delight the hearts of any of theriyoungsters who were fortunate enough to secure one. For the "children of older growth "and the gentler sex, were well-made anti- macassars, presented by Mrs. Sadler, Mrs. Fogg, and Mrs. Brown; and several beautiful shawls, some of which were attractive enough to have served for a present from some rich Indian Nabob, such as William Makepiece Thackeray took such pleasure in describing to the literary world. The I rest of the goods consisted chiefly of clothing which would
be pretty sure to find a ready sale amongst the crowd who I thronged the room. the I

The other attractions included &general art gallery, con- sisting of oil paintings, water colour drawings chroos, and oleographs, lent by Mr. T. Gill, of Widnes-road, m Simm's Cross, for the purpose of adorning the room. They embraced a pair of landscapes by W. Williams, valued at eight guineas, a cabinet painting by R. Burrows, (limner to the Prince of Wales), a very pretty view on the Ribble, by Robert Evans, a landscape by-moonlight in Essex; four scenes on Winder- mere—the loveliest of English lakes, whose praises have been sung in such bewitching language .by Wordsworth; and a very fair portrait of the Premier. At intervals, miscellaneous concerts were given, in which the following ladies and gentlemen were announced to take part :—Mrs. Robinson, Misses Evans, Harrison, Rose, Row- lands, Taylor, and Messrs. Chadwick, Fogg, A. Jackson, J. Jackson, J. Robinson, T. Robilkson, Rowlands, Swale, Taylor, C. Taylor and Thomas. A singing bee was held, the competition being for a small prize offered by Mr. B. Brown. The Reverends J. H. Com,. mings and J. Tessyman acted as judges. There was like- wise a speaking bee, in connection with which Messrs. Fogg and Joseph Robinson were judges of the candidates for oratorical bays. Signor " Robinsine," assisted by Messrs. W. Nixon and Makin jun., had the management of a "Tour round the world," which was conducted in No. 6 classroom. Judging from the comments heard from visitors, Messrs. Hamilton, the famous dioramists, have no need to look out for their laurels at present; but the exhibition contributed its mite to the day's receipts. In the infants' classroom was shown a magic lantern by Mr. J. Hargreaves, assisted by Messrs. Stokes and Evans. The other attractions were :—a microscopic entertainment, by Mr. John Robinson, assisted by Mr. J. Sefton; a weighing machine, by Messrs. Peet and E. Wright; and a galvanic battery by Messrs. W. L. Bal- shaw and Joseph Birch. _. .

, The sale was also continued OD Tuesday, and met with the success which it thoroughly deserved. The result of the sale from a finacial point of view, has been exceedingly satisfactory, the proceeds being about £122.
LATEST NEWS.

Yesterday, William Griffiths was charged at Wrexham—, with attempting to murder his mother. He was remanded I Yesterday, the Birmingham Watch Committee decided not to encourage military applicants for the office of Chief- constable.
_ --- Yesterday, at Ushaw Moor Colliery, neat Dunham, the miners were being evicted from their homes. They had a dis- pute, and gave ;mice in a body.
List night, barns and stables on a farm belonging to a Mil named lluggim., living near Neale, were burnt down. The cattle were injured, but one animal escaped through the open doorway.
Jane Johnson was charged at Bradford yesterday with being drunk. She was eighty-three years of age, and had been before the magistrates on one hundred and sixty-nine occasions.

On Thursday a discovery was mule in a house in Chorl. toa-o:-Medlock, which leads to the belief that a shocking tragedy has been committed. A girl named Harcourt, 10 years of age, was found dead in bed, and lying on the Boor was the dead body of a man named Lestrange. Poison was discovered in the room, and appearances seem to indicate that Lestrange has poisoned the girl and then committed suicide.

The Lord Mayor has received from the Earl of Courtown, as the President of the Property Defence Association (Ire- land), particulars as to the object and past work of the Association, from which it appears that since the com- mencement of the organization in December last year, 357 writs and notices had been served, 629 sheriff's sales of farms attended, and 79 sales of cattle, 410 caretakers had been supplied for farms, other agricultural services to land- lords and tenants had been rendered, and the efforts of the ' association had been directed to seeing that the rights of all classes were fully and fearlessly manifested. The expenses of the work had been heavy and almost exhausting, but the committee felt that they had no choice but to per- form it. Over five hundred cattle, the property of grasiers who have taken boycotted farms, near Boyle, were last night turned off the land, and have not since been hear u of. Threatening and prohibitory notices have been posted in the district.

Sr. JOHN'S PHEstIYTIMALV Salon, RubroonN.--The annual meeting of the teachers and elder scholars belonging to this school took place on Monday. Mr. James Pritchard and Mr. James Kirkham were elected superintendents; Mr. James Dobson secretary; and Mr. J. E. Warburton and Mr. J. Richardson librarians.

ON NEW YEAR'S DAY (Sunday) special services, to which all classes are invited, will be preached in the Wes- leyan Chapels. The Rev. J. Eglinton will preach morning and evening in Bold-street, Chapel, and at Bewsey-road Chapel the pulpit will be occupied at each service by the Rev. Thomas Rippon.

LO.G.T.—TsarrErtaxcE MisstoN Longr.—The mem- ber s of this lodge held their annual Christmas party at the Mission Room, Academy-street, War- rington, on Wednesday evening, when 75 members sat down to an excellent repast of hot joints, with season able accompaniments. The room was gaily decorated, and appropriate mottoes adorned the wars After let a variety of games were engaged in, the W.C.T, George McNaboe presiding. Brother Hall, H.D., gave an excellent address en the objects of the order, and the evening was enlivened by the singing of songs. At the conclusion a very hearty vote of thanks was tendered to the friends who had subscribed to the expenses of the tea, and to Messrs. Milling and Co. for their most acceptable gift of fruit. ENTERTAINMENT AT,BEWSEY-ROAD CRATEL.—Last even' log, a tea party and entertainment was held in the Lecture- room of Bewsey-road Chapel, in connection with the Rev. T. Rippon's Juvenile Bible Class. Mr. Rippon commenced the class, which embraces the children of the people attend- ing Bold-street and Bewsey-road chapels, in October, and there are now 130 members. There was a large attendance at tile tea, which was thoroughly enjoyed, and afterwards recitations were given by the children, and the Rev. J. Eglinton and the Rev. J. Agar Beet delivered addresses. Religious songs were also sung by some members of the class. Mr. C. Plinston gave a magic lantern entertainment of miscellaneous views, concluding with the illustration of Banyan's Pilgrim's Progress. The children enjoyed a very pleasant evening. SANKEY BRIDGES WESLEYAN SUNDAY SCROOL —On Monday last the fourth yearly meeting was held, when a substantial tea was provided. The chapel was well filled. • After tea a public meeting was presided over by Mr. Sum- mersgill, and an interesting programme gone through. From the report given by Mr. Summersgill, in the absence of the secretary, Mr.Snoddy, it appeared the school is in an efficient working condition, and the funds of the school: are healthy. Two new vestries have been added, furnished, and paid for, and are found useful for select Bible classes. One of the vestries can be easily thrown open to the chapel giving 60 additional sittings. Several scholars received prizes for good behaviour and regular attendance during the year. The Wesleyan catechism was in use in some of the classes and was strongly recommended in forming a settled belief and fixed principles among young people. Sixty monthly periodi- cals are circulated amongst the teachers and scholars A library is in preparation and a library case has already been contracted for, by Mr. John Lloyd, joiner and builder. A Band of Hope is in connection with the school. The meeting wasafterwards addressed by Messrs.J. Corradine, W. Summerfield, G. Savage and W. Webb. The following songs were given at intervals :—Mr. Brough, "Not now my child," and "Safe with the master." Miss George, " Caller herrin," and "Where's my Eva gone ;" Miss Taylor, "From the heavens above," and "Angels ever bright and fair." Mr. Tomkinson gave two voluntaries on the harmonium. Recitations were also given by Messrs. F. Braithwaite, J. Lewis George, senior, and Clement Geome. At the close of the meeting votes of thanks were given to the managing committee, Mr. Sunamertiold, and Mr. Grice, to the singers, and the chairman.

------- THE CHIEF CONSTABLE OF WARRINGTON AND STAFFORDSHIRE MEN. Sir,—In looking over your issue of last Sattrday, I could I1)t help making a note of what Mr. Hunt, chief constable, said relative to the Staffordshire men. New, sir, no one more than myself deplores the shocking termination of that quarrel, and I am joined by hundreds of Staffordshire men in their expression of sorrow at such a terrible event. But I, along with these men, desire to express through your Medium, our regret that Mr. Hunt should so far forget him- self, and cast aspersions upon a body of men whose only desire I 3 to do all is their power to live peaceable and sober lives. We admit, sir, that there are exceptions, but when Mr. Hunt said in a public court that the Staffordshire men had "no . Sort of control or dlicipline, had no behaviour whatever," he was cu..sfepping his duty as a public officer. Let me ask Mr. Hunt if he will publish a statement for the past one or two years setting forth (for the public of Warrington to judge from), bow many Staffordshire men have had to answer in the court before the magistrates for either drunkenness or disorderly conduct, and whether they cannot compare favourably with the rest of the inhabitants of the town. If such is the case that they can compare favourably, then I maintain that Mr. Hunt was taking advantage of his position in casting a stigma upon the Staffordshire people which he bad no right to do. Let rue remind you that in all the forges a large preponderance of Staffordshire men are work- ing, and a public meeting has been talked of to express their indignation at, and refute the statement made by Mr. Hunt, but let us hope the excitement undw which the men are labouring will be allayed, and a better feeling will be shown by those in office towards those who have to work night and day for their daily bread, and have often to wring, through ' - their CHECK CAPS. ____.--------•"-^-

THE NEW YEAR AND THE OLD. A STORY FOR BOYS. Years ago, when the writer was a boy of fourteen winters literally—for he was born:upon a winter's morning—his father was sexton of the village church in a New England town. The church was the old white structure of tke "standing order," the orthodox. It stood upon rising ground at the head of the main street, and all other buildings had ever kept at a respcctful dis- tance; nothing dared to invade the sacred precincts of the "church green," save the horse-sheds in the rear, which were tolerated apparently as body servants about the persons of great men. Hence the antique structure was awful, solemn, and lonely in the extreme. It was the last day of December, and it was evening. My father and I went up to the "meeting house" as the sun went down in the low south-west. We were to make prepara- tions for ringing the midnight bells. It was the custom of Old England, brought over to New England, to ring the old year out and the new one in. The Puritan villagers would have thought they bad begun the new lease of time all ill- fated, did not this steeple tocsin rouse their slumbers on the stroke of twelve. But my father found the bell-cord worn so thin that it would hardly bear the strain of a joyous pull. After some examination he must needs to the village store for rope; whence, after many creeping minutes lengthening into hours, he came; and after that as the Clock struck ten, I must up the attic stairs, along the narrow path beneath the rafters, up again the ladder, upward still and higher, to splice the rope while father rested down below. Father was an old man; I was the child of his age, the youngest, and the pet! Father slept by the fire-place in the parson's study, rested and slept, as he afterwards confessed, as I went aloft. I was not asleep, oh, no; but broad awake lam sure as I paused a moment by the first open:window. The wind had grown most boisterous rough, and swirled like mad through the paneless port-hole, so that one heard the old timbers groan, amid the shrieks of the wind, on hurrying past and upward. I could not have been asleep, for I now could see the village lights that twinkled like a firmament beneath in answer to the firmament above. The stare! How friendly near they seemed, like laughing eyes that mocked me with some lure sinister. Not sleeping, for I saw the clouds that rolled up from the east as if from out the sea, which in its turn Was loudly knocking that same night upon the shore. The rope was spliced, lam sure. The frayed length was just beneath the great bell. I was looking curiously info its iron throat; I noticed, startled, that its heavy tongue was on the swing. I remember all that distinctly. I crouched close down upon the belfry floor to escape the yelling winds and thickening flakes of the gathering storm, to get my breath before descending, but mainly to see if it was indeed the blast that swung the tongue. Then and there he sat, a figure who did actually walk out from the rusty gul- let of that bell! He sat him down upon the further side, a little in the shelter of the huge old yoke and wheel. He was older than my father; to him my father was a youthful man. I saw the few stars yet unclouded shine through and through him quite. I saw the hour-glass in his hand, the scythe across his shoulder, and the empty water.jug of a pilgrim at his girdle. It was the Old Year. He was speak- ing unto some one whom I could not see. I am sure as that I was not dreaming, that it was the young New Year upon the other side of the bell. And Old Year said:— "Take the scythe; the list of names is writ upon this Scroll. Cut them down." "Not I; the New Year dawns with joy," replied a young and cheery voice. "Nevertheless you are the year of death to many. Take the scroll and be ready; be ready to strike even as the joy- bells of thy birth are pealing. Se is the work appointed unto us years." From the oaken floor I strained all my vision to bend the line of sight past the serrate lips of the old bell, and scan that scroll; to read if father's or my own. name were there; and whose among the many scores of village lads and lasses whom I loved. Would not you,-kind reader, with leaflets from the book of fate se near, have almost snatched to gain them? I dare not; I was afraid to see, and cowed again to the wind-swept floor. Then the Old Year sail: "I give you lists of birth as well. Behold, all these shall begin to be while you hold sway ! " And there fluttered out upon the winds a catalogue so long that it wound the weather-stained timbers like an angers veil—the names of thousands yet to be. But, strange to say, though I might, I did not care to read a name. The earth seemed already crowded to Us poor folk; and many mouths there were with loaves so few. "Here is the budget of surprises for the sons of men. Startle,_ thrill, awake, and make men wonder! Make rich poor, Young Year; the poor rich. Rain disappointments on the miserable and make them strangely happy ; on the happy, and, never having thought such things could chonce to them, behold, they are most miserable. Here wars and rumours of wars. Here unexpected peace. Here earthquake, fire, and the discovery of new mines of gold. 1-lee accidents, Indeed, to set the world shuddering; and, while they weep, here overflowing harvests from the fields of hopeless drought. Here the king dies. Here the birth of a new and latest nation on the globe. Ay, ay," said the Old Shape, chuck- ling through his toothless gums; "make them wonder!" Much more there was of this strange charge from the dying year to the newly born; things that concerned the slumbering world beneath me, from the hamlet to the proudest capitals. I was filled with speechless awe. It seemed to me I scarce drew breath for fear of the tell-tale sound thereof. la hen abrupt as the buffet of the latest storm-blast, the Old Shape turned upon poor me to say; "Here, now, is this small lad, Young year, no bigger than thyself is he. Almost the same growth Washe when myself was young. A year is not much in the stature of the human kind. I have blessed him much. Is it nothing that I've made sunrises on his path so oft? I have set before the boy both good and evil many times. I shall never see him more. My handiwork upon the lad is ended here, whether for marring or for mending. You have him now. See thou handle him well New Year, for thou must give account for him to thy successor—unless be is appointed for thy sythe upon the lists. You must write a few things in his memory; run thy graver lightly, very lightly, along the fair, smooth brow where are many pencilled lines to guide the wrinkle- making years that follow us. Young Year, these later years shall grave upon the ontside; you and I upon the inner man, the untaught soul. The Fiftieth Year from now will think he does much mightier things because he shall beri the boy's back, shake his tottering feet, dull his eye, and make his hooked nose to meet his scarred chin. But thou and I have the making ef this boy. We work upon the immortal part in plastic youth. What we tell him he will never quite forget. What sights of good or ill we shall show will keep for ever in the mind; while the older years shall speak with thunder tones or hang most startling lessons up before him all in vain. Work carefully on the child." Then I thought the New Year, beautiful as cherubs are in pictures, clasped me like a playfellow, pressing his rosy cheek against my own. We laughed, in jocund glee that rang upon the wintry air, while he caressed me kindly. So rich was he, and I so poor; so strong, so full of hopes was he, and so yr; I ; I can hear his merry laughter yet ; and he was my friend and the "Happy New Year." I remember that we vowed together to keep innocence, the Happy New Year and I. But he did not prove true thereto, nor I, who have lived to vow such high resolves with many after him. _We vowed to do good deeds and kind; but failed far oftener than we did achieve. We planned out blessings on a thousand human friends of his and mine. Thank God, we have somewhat here succeeded. I remember that the New Year prompted me at last to pray Great God to bless both him and me. "For," quoth he, "YOU deathless men can talk with God and plead His benediction. But we, poor years, are nothing but an empty name for little spans of time. It is thou and God, the living God, clear child, who shape thy destiny. A year is nothing but an empty name. Post sae ?" And even while I looked the Elder Shape was vanished, and the younger, too, as father struck the midnight bells,

Belege clesing my account ot Dames/zees:l neteAsmention a Visit we paid to the houses ,of two Jewish inhabitants in the higher ranks of life. The first was that nt the Vice- Consul of Denraark. When we stepped teat +A the winding porch of his house into the open court within, the young dignitary, a stout, handsome man, was pacing the quadrangle lin his loese Turkish dressing gown. He bowed graciously, and received the introduction of our guide in a quiet easy manner, with hands clasped before him. He then led the way into a gorgeously furnished room on one side of the arched recess, which I have said was common in these Eastern residences, and which in this case had not only a broad divan stretching across it, but had mirrors at the back reflect- ing the entire court, with its fountain and orange trees. The reception rooms are entered from the recess on each side. The first of the rooms was exquisitely decorated and fur- nished; the floor, occupying about two-thirds of the apart- ment, was in beautiful marble mosaic, with a marble foun- tain in the centre, while the rest of the room was taken up with the dais, covered with thick carpet, and around which were placed richly figured satin divans of Oriental pattern. The walls were cevered with Arabesque panels and fluted pilasters most chastely carved and decorated, while the ceil- ing seemed as beautiful in design and elaborate as art could make it. After we had feasted our eyes en the exquisite picture it presented, we were introduced very graciously to the father of our host, who then led us across the recess into the opposite room, and requested us to be seated. As we sat on the dais, one or two steps above the floor, a servant ap- peared with confections, of which we partook sparingly. I while we were informed that we should have been enter- tained with coffee and narghillas if it had not been the Jewish Sabbath. While the Consul entered into conversa- tion with Miss R—, who spoke to him in French, his wife came in with a baby in her arms, and sat down just within the door. She and her daughter, who closely followed. seemed deeply interested in their strange visitors, and in the conversation. Her husband was inquiring of Miss R-- hew it was that the English people were so fond of their Danish princess, and her answer that the princess was "so good" appeared to give great pleasure. The second man- sion we visited was even more elegant and chaste in the get-up of its reception rooms than the. first, yet all was precisely on the same plan.. I often thought we must have presented a curious tableaux to Eastern eyes; but of course the effect on beholders only came out as we were viewed by unmannerly fdk, among whom, I am afraid, the Jewess and her daughters must be placed, for in truth there were no marks of refinement or culture in the ladies at all in keeping with the exquisite taste displayed in all the surroundings of the feminine trio. Probably, had we seen the lord of the mansion, we might have beheld a man as polished and easy in manner as the Danish Consul. But it would seem that in abutting the women from all society, as the Jews evidently do, in con- formity with Eastern custom, they become mere toys and playthings, without mind, without information, and by and 1 bye degenerate into the gawkish and boorish creatures we ' saw. It is pitiable to think how degraded and abject the condition of the women in the East is, even under the most favourable ciroumstances. We had four full days in Damascus, and felt greatly invigorated as we mounted our ponies on Monday morning, 10th April, greatly joyous, too, to think that we were turning our faces homeward, after having persistently placed 3,000 miles between ourselves and those we loved best on earth. Damascus, with all its social and municipal drawbacks—and to the European they are many—had furnished us not only with bodily vigour, but with mental pabulum enough to feed upon and ruminate for many days. Orientalism flourishes so perennially in this grand old city, and brings down from the past so many customs and forms of human life illustrative of sacred history, that memory must ever love to liuger on what we Saw during these four interesting days in Datnaseus—so in- ' teresting that I fear the demon-life lurking beneath the surface became myth-like and shadowy, although the ghostly memorials of inhuman deeds of times stared us in the face. The abhorrent nature of those deeds forced itself, however, most powerfully upon our attention as we left the city and passed around its walls on the day of our departure. We felt that, des- pite all its ancient glory and unfading Orientalism, a black and ineffaceable curse rested on r amascus, in view of the dreadful tragedy that made its streets and houses stream with blood in 1860, when no less than 6,000 un- offending Christians were slaughtered by their Moslem neighbours and fellOw subjects, while more more than 14,000 fell butchered on Syrian ground. We passed the cemetery in which the multitude of mangled victims were buried; and, as we thought that the city was still rife with the same dark and infamous spirit of hate and jealousy, we felt it a relief as we passed up between the mountains and lost sight of Damascus for ever. Was it not a symbol of the savagery that still lingers in the open plain, a dead camel, over whose well picked ribs two or three vultures were still hovering ? After leaving Damascus we travelled for nearly an hour and a half along the excellent macadamized road which the French:Diligance and Carrying Company have made , between Damascus and Beyrout. The road winds by the , bed of the river Barada, as it flows through the deep gorge I that leads up to the anti-Lebanon range, dividing the barren mountains on each side by a broad line of foliage as fresh and green as trees planted by the river side in Eastern countries could make it. After we left the main road and I turned to the right, passing out of the Barada gorge, our way for two hours lay through very fine but rugged barren scenery; Hermon, with a fresh covering of snow, giving glory and beauty to the distant landscapes. As we again descended into the valley of the Barada, the verdure that clothes its banks on both sides burst upon us, and continued to charm us all the way until we came to the Fountain of Fijeh. Sometimes the rocks were towering above our heads on the right, while on the left and below us were orchards which displayed a variety of foliage perfectly enchanting. From the dark olive, with its silvery lining, to the deep brown of the pomegranate, every variety of shade was spread out befere us. Then the walnut, with its rich fragrance, vied with the hawthorn in throwing its odours on the air; while blossoms of brilliant purple and white and pink gave an additional charm to the scene. We lunched by the side of the swiftly flowing Barada, with the rugged cliffs rising high above us on each side, then rode along the narrow pathways on the sides of the rocks as far as the Fountain of Fijeh, which is one of the chief sources ot the Barada. It is the most wonderful spring of water I have ever seen. Within a cavern, covered at the bottom with loose rocks of immense size, the water comes boiling up 'hundreds of tons per minute, and, rushing forth with a tremendous roar, spreads out into a wide torrent, which joins the Barada at a few yards distance. We encamped for the night on the site of the ancient Abila, sur- rounded with ' every kind of natural beauty. It is in the ancient province of Abilene, which Luke says was placed under the government of Sysanias, and afterwards of Philip the Tetrarch. Proceeding next morning we passed through a glen of exceeding ruggedness and romantic beauty, and came to a Roman road which had been hewn out of the rock. Upon the walls we saw Latin inscriptions, recording that the road was constructed during the reign of Marcus Aurelius and his successor by Julius Verus, at the expense of the inhabitants of Abila. Not far from these interesting records we saw and travelled by the side of a Roman conduit, which had also been cut ot t of the solid rock. That evening, after passing through scenery which no pen can describe, we found out selves in the circle of rocky hills, between the central and western , ridges of the anti-Lebanon range, at a place called Turgagha. Through the whole of this day's journey we had a succession of gorgeous views. One or two pictures cling to the imag- ination as things of unfading beauty. The vision at lunch- time of tall mountain cliffs, with their sharp outline tower- ing thousands of feet against the blue vault of heaven, which Iwas like rarefied crystal in its clearness, had a more powerful 1 influence in lifting the soul upwards than I ever felt natural I scenery to have before. Both the Lebanon and the anti- Lebanon mountains have a beauty and a grandeur all their ONVIII. As we turned out of our tents next morning at Surgagba, the mountain tops were coveted with snow, which descended to a certain point, and formed a straight line along the entire range,leaving the rest of the mountains in their garb of summer green. een Bain fell in the morning, and for the first tffne since we left home our waterproofs were brought into requisition. The rain soon passed off, and early in the afternoon we en- Camped in the centre of Baalbee's wonderful ruins, respect- ing which I shall have something to say in my next. (To be continued nest week.)

They felt assured that it would be advantageous to the society to make known, not only to the members, but also to the public the present sound condition of the society's affairs. The report con- cluded with a word of praise for the admirable manner in which the books were kept by Mr. Henry Makin, the secretary, who has filled the office since 1887, when the society was only worth between £BOO and £9OO. The election of officers for the year was then proceeded with, the result being as follows :—Mr. William Ashcroft was re-elected \president ; Mr. Richard Mercer was elected vice- president in the place of Mr. Edwin Rimmer; and Mr. H. Makin was re-appointed secretary. The following gentle- men were appointed a committee for the year—Messrs. Wm. Rigby, James Case, Edmund Range, James Bixter, John Ackinson, and Joseph Rigby. _

tion: January 6.-Visit of Dr. Thorne, Local Government Board Inspector, to Infectious Diseases Hospital. January 11.-Fatal accident to James Eaton, a farmer's son, at Grappenhall. Chairman of the 1 Warrington Board of Guardians "Boycotted." IFebruary 3,-Presentation to Rev. J. Clelland on his resig- nation from the ministry of the Presbyterian church. ebruary 5.-Rebecca Clarke, a Penketh woman, indicted at FeLbirvuearrpyogl. Ais3suizrsetsing o for bigamy. f Sankey Canal. Discussion in Town Council on the representation of the ratepayers in the Council. March 7.-Branch of Church of England Temperance Society formed at. Heath Side school. Richard Greenall, at St. Thomas's Church, Stockton Heath. October 24.-Puddlers' strike at Pearson and Knowles' BewseY Forge, Warrington. November 3.-Sad suicide of a farmer's aen at Buttonwood. November 16.-Action by Warrington Waterworks Com- pany heard at Wigarr; verdict for defendant, Mr. Long- shaw. November 19.-Death of Mr. W. E. Winstanley, of Newton. at Runoorn. Jai/nary 21.-Great distress at Runcorn through the severity of the weather. January 29.-Michael Tulleyl drowned in the canal at Halton. Sad fatality to Joseph Inglesfield, at the Big Pool, Runcorn. January 30.-John Burke, of Widnes, killed by the fall of a hoist. February 3.-Mysterious disappearance of Thomas Wilson, a Runcorn sea captain. February 5.-Gallant rescue from drowning of named Murray by Mr. Edward Kennedy. September 29.—Fourth arn:.ual soiree of the Choral Society. October 4.--Agitation for a. 'res Library commenced. October B.—Mysterious tragedy at Widnes: Harriet Pen- dleton and dames Hague shot. ST. HELENS. January 1.-Westfield-street Coffee Rooms opened. January 20.- Jonadab Prescott, relieving officer for St. Helens, convicted of having robbed his employers, the Board of Guardians. -Strike of colliers at St. Helens. January 27.-Local Government Board inquiry at St. Helens, relative to an application to borrow money for works of water supply and street improvement, a survey of the borough, and for an infectious diseases hospital. February 1.-Prosecution of Whiston colliers for leaving work without fulfilling the terms of their notices. February 19.-The St. Helens Town Council rejected the offer of a park by Mr. S. Taylor. March 9.-Annual meeting of Lancashire Congregationalists at St. Helens. March 18.-Government inquiry at St. Helens relative to the application of the Council for sanction to borrow £3,200 for works of street improvement. April 27.-Commemoration dinner of the formation of the 47th Lancashire Volunteers at St. Helens. April 30.-Prescot Conservative Club opened. Sudden death of James Tomlinson in Randon-street. May 18.-6-Holy Cross Bazaar, St. Helens. May 21.-Alleged manslaughter of William Miller, labourer, by Bryan Conroy, 67. Conroy committed for trial by magistrates June 2. June 4.-Murder of a wife at Prescot. The prisoner, James Fitzpatrick, committed for trial June 14; and sentenced at Liverpool Assizes to 15 years' penal servitude July 30. June 7.-Conservative demonstration at St. Helens. June 8.-James Keenan, a boy, killed by express train at St. Helens. June 13.-Funeral of the late Mr. Thomas Lea, of Whiston. June 30.-Laying the foundation stone of the new chapel at Prescot Workhouse. July 4.-Death of Superintendent Brindle, Prescot. July 11.-Shocking attack on a wife at St. Helens. Edward Foy, the husband, committed for trial for manslaughter July 10. August 2.-Lamentable railway accident near Prescot. An engine fitter named Scott, of Crewe, cut to pieces. August 3.-John Foy, charged with the murder of his wife, was sentenced to 12 months' hard labour at Liverpool Assizes. September 7.-Motion for a borough bench of magistrates carried at St. Helens Town Council. Opening of St. Paul's Church, St. Helens. September 20.-Stanley Corn Mill, Blackbrook, burnt down; £1,600 damages. October 3.-Rainbill Liberal Club opened.' October 10.-Primitive Methodist Bazaar, St. Helens, this and two following days. October 24.-Elopement of a baker's wife with a Welshman at Huyton. October 28.-First car run on St. Helens Tramway. November 6.-Religious census taken in St. Helens. November 0.-Death of Richard Swift, collier, through fall of coal at Carr's Colliery. November 14.-Escape of a prisoner named Glynn at St. Helens. November 15.-Fall of a house in Brown's-square,Eccleston- street, Prescot. November 16.-Shocking death of Father Sebastian, of Sutton Monastery, at St. Helens Junction. November 19.-William Fillingham (16) suffocated at St. Helens Chemical Works. December 6.-Mrs. Holcroft, wife of a Wigan tailor, killed at St. Helens station. December 7.-Swiss bazaar in St. Helens Town Hall in aid of St. Paul's Mission Church.

div.head: WARRINGTON POLICE COURT.
div.p: WARRINGTON POLICE COURT.

• Sarunne.v.—Before Mr. Z. Armitage. SHOWING WILLT HE COULD DO.—George Miles was charged with being on the premises of James Henderson, Mill-street,for an unlawful purpose on the previous afternoon. P.C. Boyne said prisoner went into Mr. Henderson's shop on Friday afternoon and asked for something to eat. They re- fused to accede to his request, and he said " I will show you what I can do "and picked up some bread which he commenced to eat. Prisoner stated he was in the Work- house on Thursday night and before leaving the followingll morning asked to see the doctor as he was suffering from, rheumatism. This the porter refused to allow him to do, and put him out without breakfast. He (prisoner) said he I said he should do something and would then be taken before Ile magistrates and would have an opportunity of telling the truth.-1-risone was remanded so that inquiries might be made. MONDAT.—Before Major Cartwright (chairman), Coun- cillor Fairclough (ex-mayor), and Captain Litton. A TRAMP'S TRICK.—George Miles was brought up on remand and was now charged with stealing from the shop of James Henderson, Mill-street, on Friday afternoon, a two- pound loaf value 3cl.—Prisoner, who appeared very ill, stated that on Thursday night he applied at the police station far a ticket for the Workhouse, which was granted. He went to the Union and was admitted, and a pauper searched him. He told the searcher he was unwell and that it would be impossible for him to get up until he had seen a doctor. The pauper pulled off his clothes and opened all the windows and he (prisoner) was left in the cold for nearly six hours. No one came to see him until two o'clock in the afternoon when a pauper came and advised him to try to get up and go to the office. lie dressed and went to the lobby where a little boy told him he could go to the big room and the relieving officer would come to him. The porter—at least, he did not know whether it was the porter or the governor, came to see him. He said to him "I have been weak all day. Tell me who you are. I want to see a doctor." The man "bully ragged" him (prisoner) to try to get him out of the place. He told, the man he had had no meat, and that he should bring the matter under the notice of the magistrates. He then went to a shop and said to the woman in charge "my good woman, could I get something to eat. lam going to take a piece of bread." He told her to "send for a policeman as he wanted to see the magiStrates." He was ar rested in that way.—The Ex-Mayor: Do you say you did not have anything to eat at the Union, and that you remained there all night ?—Prisoner: I received a portion of bread when I went up to the house from a pauper.—Captain Litton: What is to be done? Is not this a matter for the Guardians to deal with ?—The Clerk: Yes; but what is to be done with him in the mean- time? It is a matter strictly for the Board of Guardians. —Captain Litton: I think he did perfectly right.—Major Cartwright : To get locked up ?—Captain Litton: Certainly; to bring the case 'before the magistrates.—The porter, on being called, said the prisoner was admitted at 6-30 on Thursday night by the portress. He had something to eat. The following morning one of the paupers went to get the men up at 7-30. There were about 30 casuals in the ward, , and the prisoner was one of them. No one told him the I prisoner was sick. He cut the bread and laid it on the table. The men were marched into the room, and no bread was left. At ten minutes to two o'clock witness was at the hall when he saw a pauper going away with a dinner. He asked him who it was for, and he said it was for a casual. Witness went into the room and found it was the prisoner. He said to him, "What are you doing there? If I had known you would hays bean down before this." The prisoner asked permission to go, and it was granted. As , prisener left the place he said, "I will go and steal a loaf of bread go to prison." Prisoner said nothing to him about being sick.—TWO paupers were called, and they stated that prisoner did not complain to them of being ill until two o'clock in the afternoon.—Mr. Mackey (the master) said the prisoner did not even wait for his dinner.— Major Cartwright said be certainly failed to see thaVhe prisoner had received any abuse. On the contrary, the officials of the workhouse were very kind to him.—oooo- , oilier Fairclough thought there was a la k of something as , the man was left in the room until two o'clock in the after- noon without anyone seeing hirn.—Captain Litton: That is where the mistake was. They ought to have known he was \ there. There is something lax somewhere.—Major Cart- , wright failed to see that any injustice had been done to the ' prisoner.—Prisoner : I might have been found dead in the room.—The Master said he visited the lodge four times dur- ing the previous night, and no complaint was made to him. —Prisoner was sent to gaol for seven days, Councillor Fairclough remarking that the complaints against the officials was a matter for the Board of Guardians to inquire into. REMAND CASES—Frank Minton was remanded until Wed- nesday on a charge of stealing from the shop of Mary Booth, Buttermarket-street, on Saturday, three pairs of boots, value ss. pd.—John Williams, charged with stealing four hens and a cock from the house of Richard Holland,Mersey- street, on Sunday night, was remanded until Wednesday. ASSAULTS ON Tux POLICE —Thomas Mellor was charged with being drunk in Crosfield-street, on Sunda". afternoon, and assaulting P.C. Hennessy. Fined ss. and costs for being drunk, and 10s. and costs for the assault.—Richard Jackson was fined 40s. and costs for being drunk in Horse- market-street on Sunday, and assaulting P.C. Hardy. WenexEsteay.—Before Alderman Chandley and Coancillor Fairclongh. A " SUSPECT."—John Williams was charged on remand with stealing five fowls from the hencote of Robert Hol- land, of Massey-street, on Monday last. The prisoner when apprehended had fresh blood stains on his hands, shirt, and clothing, and in his clogs were a number of feathers. His clogs also corresponded with the marks made near the hen- cote by the thief.—Mr. Hunt said it was a case of strong suspicion, but he couli not produce sufficient evidence to convict the prisone,r, who was, therefore, discharged. A CONSTABLE COMPLIMENTED.—Frank Minton, a dis- charged soldier, was charged with stealing three pairs of boots, value ss. Pd., the property of Mary Elizabeth Booth, ' 29, Buttermarket-stteet.—The prisoner was seen by the prosecutrix's son, Arthur, to snatch a pair of boots from the shop door, on Saturday night, about 9 o'clock. Prisoner then ran away, and the boy followed and caught hold of him, but he managed to escape. Sometime afterwards P.C. Crickett. when in Percival's-fold, noticed the prisoner acting in a suspicious manner, and he captured him in the Pelican public-house vaults. There three pairs of boots (produced) fell from under his clothing on the pavement.—The pri- soner, who had been many times previously convicted for felony, was committed to take his trial at the Liverpool Quarter Sessions. Councillor Fairclough complimented P.C. Crickett for the manner in which be had arrested the prisoner, and said it showed he was equal to his work. THURSDAY.—Before Alderman Webster, and Councillor Milner. TETE " ANXIOUS " FATHER.—William Owen was charged with having on Monday, used mall cious threats toward his wife, whereby she was afraid he would do her some bodily harm—The proeecutrix said her husband had been separated from her" on and off" for two years. On Monday when she was on her way home, the prisoner met her in Mersey- street, and said he would dash her head against the wall, and that he would "hang for her." When she arrived home he broke two window panes and kicked the door. He had illused her many times.—Prisoner, in defence, said he had been married 22 years and he only wanted to see the claildren.—He was bound over to keep the peace for six menthe, or in default of finding two sureties, go to gaol for a month. VIRTUE ITS OWN REWARD.—WiIIiaM Quinn, a fine look- ing young fellow, was charged with being a deserter from the 7th battery of the 22ad brigade of the Royal Artillery, hav- ing deserted in IS7s.—James Reynard, a staff sergeant at the Barracks, said he was returning to the Barracks at 6-30 on the previous evening when he saw the prisoner stagger- ing under the influence of liquor, in Marsh House-lane. He told him to keep to the middle or he would fall in the pool behind the hedge. Witness had scarcely walked on a dozen yards when he heard a splash, and calling for help he ran back and saw the prisoner in the water. With the aid of four men witness rescued the prisoner, who stated, on re- covering consciousness, that he was a deserter. He was consequently locked up.—Prisoner pleaded guilty and he was remanded to Walton gaol to await an escort.—Sergeant Reynard asked for the usual reward, and said if the prisoner had been in the water another minute it would have been a "case with him."—Councillor Milner : Virtue has its own reward. (Laughter.)--Alderman Webster: Its more a case for the Humane Society. (Laughter)

div.head: PRESCuT BURIAL SOCIETY.
div.p: PRESCuT BURIAL SOCIETY.

The annual meeting of the Prescot Burial Society was held on Tuesday at the Engine Inn, Sewell-street, for the purpose of passing the balance-sheet and auditor's report, and to elect officers for the ensuing year. Mr. William Ashcroft, president of the society, occupied the chair, and there was a good attendance of members. The balance sheet, as presented to the meeting, showed that in the`funeral fund account a balance of £2,090 16s. 64. was brought forward I from last year, which with £3Ol IN. 44., contributions and I other receipts, made a total of £2,392 15s. 10d. The ex- penditure amounted to £214 ss. 01 made up by allowances for 67 funerals; leaving a balance of £2,178 10s. 10d., a gain of £B7 14s. 4d. on the year. The receipts in connection with the management fund amounted to £45 Os. 21; balance from last year, £ll5 2s. 01, total £l6O 2s. 21.; the total expendi- diture was £44 15s. 01 including,. the expenses of a valua- tion of the society ; bal'ance, £ll5 7s. 24., being an increase of ss. 2d. on the previous year. The total work of the society last year was £2.205 18s. 61.; total worth this year, £2,293 18s. Od.; being a gain of £B7 19s. 6d. during the year. The number of members in 1850 was 516, and there had entered since, 25; total 541; suspended, excluded, and dead, 26; leaving the present number at 515. MR. GLADSTONE ON THE COMING SESSION.—Mr. Sym- onds, secretary of the National Reform Union, on Wednesday received the following letter from Mr. Gladstone's secretary: —lO, Downing-street, Whitehall, December 26, 1881. Sir,— Mr. Gladstone is in receipt of the resolutions which were passed at the meetings of the National Reform Union, held on the 16th ipst., and he desires me to thank you for for- warding him copies of them. He is gratified to learn from Mr. Herbert Gladstone that the meeting was attended with so much success, and its proceedings with so much enthu- siasm. With regard to dealing with the Land Laws, to which special reference was made, I am to say that Her Majesty's Government are sensible of the importance of the subject, but with respect to this and other legislation much must depend as to the time taken upon the reform, which it may be possible to effect, in Parliamentary procedure. Mr. Gladstone is glad to observe that the principles of so-called Fair Trade were so emphatically denounced at such an im- portant gathering at Manchester.

_ January 22.—Jervais Merriclss frozen to death at Widnes. January 25.—Suicide of Henry Digby Mann at Widnes. January 27.—Thomas Craig killed on the railway at Farn- worth. January 30.—Fenian panic at Widnes. January 31.-3ano Unsworth found dead in a cesspool at Farnworth. February B.—Fire at the shop of Mr. William Findlow, grocer, Widnes; damages, £250. Februar 26.—A11eged Fenianisna at Widnes. Important seizure of arms at a dwelling-house in Market-street. March 20.—Patrick McGuire drowned in the canal at . Widnes. March 20.--Thrible railway accident at Widnes: two men

_ March 27.—Opening of the Stations of the Cross at St. I Michael's Church, Ditton. April 2.—Railway accident at Widnes: one man killed. April 4.—Census taken at Widnes. April 11.—Death of Mr. Robert Barrow, of Farnworlh. May 14.—Death of Mr. James McClelland, of Widnes. Jane 17.—Death of Mr. William Gill. August 24.—Ferry boat accident at Widnes : George Treacy drowned. September 25.—John Walskkilled in a chemical vat.
