burst's bedroom. He found one drawer had been cut and damaged with some sharp instrument. Prom what he vrs told he went to the left hand back door, and between there and the stack-yard he found footpriats. He took the prisoner into custody on suspicion of having committed the robbery. Witness brought prisoner into the house and told him to take off his boots. Prisoner did so, and witness compared the boots with the footprints and found them to agree. Witness then searched the prisoner, and found the pocket knife produced upon him. The point was slightly bent. -Prisoner said that he had been to the Red Cat, but hearing some people say there was a fire he ran across the field to it. Witness took prisoner to Sergeant Lawless in lierrington-lane, and they all three then went back to Mr. Middlehurst's house. Prisoner pointed out where he had crossed the field when going to the fire, but witness found no foot marks of the prisoner. Witness then took prisoner to St. Helens. On the way witness charged him with steal- ing four cases, one gold watch, and one silver watch, one gold chain and one gold locket; one gold cross, one gold necklet, one gold brooch, and a pair of gold ear-rings, and a number of small articles in one of the boxes. Prisoner replied "That's to be proved yet; I am not going to tell things I know nothing about. You'are paid for :finding things out." At 9-30 p.m. on the 23rd inst., he was with ' Sergeant Lawless. He saw the Sergeant find the boxes and jewellery produced in a corn stack in Mr. Middlehurst's yard. Sergeant Lawless gave corroborative evidence.—Sergeant Whittaker said he had the prisoner brought from the cells into the office on the 23rd, to ask him where his friends were. Prisoner said he had no father or mother, but his friends lived about London-road, Liverpool. When going back to the cells prisoner asked if Mr. Middlehurst had been there. Witness said be had, but had gone back. Prisoner said he wanted to ask Mr. Middlehurst if he would forgive him, as he had stolen the watches and hid them in a corn stack. He then set fire to the hay stack to get Mr. Middle- hurst out. Prisoner said he did not wish to burn the stack, and expected Mr. Middlehurst out before he came. Witness then went to Rainford to assist in searching for the articles, but the articles were found when he arrived.—Prisoner, on being formally charged, said, "I did take the things, and set fire to the stack. I went into the house as soon as they came out by the left back door. I went for the purpose of getting money. I did not go for anything else, as I have been work ing in Mr. Middlehurst's quarry, and he has not given me any pocket money for the last fortnight. I wanted some money. I did not intend to damage the stack; I expected them sooner out. That's all I have to say."—Com mitted to the A Ssizes..

WIDNES POLICE COURT. Morenase—Before Mr. F. H. Gossage. A WARRINGTON MAN'S ADVENTURE AT WIDNES.—EIIen Hunt, Esther Williamson, Elizabeth. Peacock, and William Garrity were charged with having, on Saturday, stolen from the person of Patrick Burke, forgeman, Factory-field, Warrington, a silver watch and 7s in money.—Prosecutor stated that on Saturday night he came to Widnes for the purpose of visiting a woman with whom he formerly lived. When leaving he went up Queen-street, and asked a woman who was standing at a house door to give him a light for his pipe. She asked him to enter, and he did so. Some proposal of an improper character was made to him, and he replied "he was not a man of that kind." The prisoners then set upon him, knocked him down, and beat him about the head with a poker. He bled very much from the wounds, but he could not say which of the prisoners it was who used the poker. Whilst he was upon the floor the prisoners stole his watch and 75. He had never seen any of them before, and he gave them no provocation to com- mence the attack.—Mary Clarke, of Queen-street, said atm was in the house of Mary Ann Jessop about half-past nine on Saturday night, and whilst in the back kitchen the pri- soner Hunt, who was also there, asked her to change aprons. She enquired her reason for the request, on which Hunt replied that she had taken some money "from a fellow," and though she had nest robbed him she did not wish him to know her again. She took the apron now produced home, and it was covered with blood.—P.C. Clarkson stated that on Saturday night he was on duty in Warrington-road. when the prosecutor came up to him and complained that he had been robbed and assaulted. Witness then went to the house of the prisoner Williamson' ar.d found the skirt produced, which was covered with blood. He took Hunt and William- son into custody. He afterwards charged the three women at the police station, and Williamson replied, " I will take all the blame on myself." Hunt's answer was, "I never SW his money."--P.C. Pitt said he apprehended Peacock in her own house in Oakland-street, and charged her with I being concerned in stealing the watch and the money. She denied her guilt —Mr. Gossage said there was a very strong case against the prisoners, and they would be remanded until Wednesday.—On Wednesday, the prisoners were brought up, on remand, before Messrs. Holbrook Gaskell junior, and Mr. George Prlkington. Complainant gave evidence at length, the principal facts of which are detailed above. He now added that he was going out of the house when the prisoner Hunt came in. She told him that he should not leave until they had murdered him, and taken his money. ehe then struck him with her fist. Whilst the struggle between him and the women was going on, he heard one of them say that they were too long about the business, it being about tinae to finish him. All the time this was going on, the male prisoner was standing near the fire. One of the women tried to close his mouth. He bled profusely from his wounds. There was no light in the kitchen, which was, therefore, in semi-darkness. Besides his face and head were covered with blood, and the crimson stream got into nis eyes, and prevented his distinguishing objects clearly. He scarcely remembered getting out of the house, aq he was in such an exhausted state from loss of blood and the savage manner in which he had been treated.—I 0 cross-examina- ion, witness said he was sober when he entered the house. His injuries were such that he had not been able to work since. He could not exactly, say whether Garrity struck him or not, but he was present all the time the assault occupied, but never offered to save him, though he called upon him to do so.—By the prisoner Peacock: He never offered to pay for a pint of beer, or to give the woman a shilling.—Mary Clarke, P.C. Pitt, and Sergeant Clarkson gave evidence.—Dr. Cooper said he examined Burke on Monday. He found his shouldier bruised- that there were several serious wounds we his head; that his legs were bruised, and one of his fingers had apparently been bitten. The wounds on the head. had probably been caused by a poker. Complainant had lost a deal of blood, and might not be able to return to work for SONiC little time—After being ' formally charged, the prisoner Williamson said thee Burke hit her and than she struck him again. Garrity said he told the complainant he had better leave the house, and then he went out, and saw no more of what took place.—Prisoners were all committed to the Liverpool Assizes for trial. WEDNESDAY.—Before Messrs. Holbrook Gaskell (chairrnan) and George Pilkington. AN INTERESTING COUPLE.—Thomas Barrows, licensed victualler, Ditton, and John Corns, carter, of the same place, were each charged with having been found drunk whilst in charge of a horse and cart—Evidence was given by Sergeant Coutts and another officer to the effect that at about a quarter to six o'clock on the afternoon of the 20th inst. the two men were seen going along Birchfield-road, each being in charge of a horse and cart. One of them was , so druak that he is-reneged to get his horse and cart in the ditch, and broke the shafts.—Barrows, who did not appear, I was fined 10s. and costs, and the other defendant 7s. 6d. and costs. Detesie ON LICENSED TREMISES.—WiIIiam Milton and Thomas Burns were summoned for hewing been drunk and disorderly on the licensed premises of John Gould, of the Swan Inn, Elizabeth-street, on the 17th inst—A constable stated that at about eleven o'clock at night he noticed a large crowd of people opposite Mr. Gould's public-house. He went in and saw the two defendants fighting in the front vaults. He got the assistance of another constable, and put the men out of the house.—Each defendant was fined 7s. Od. and costs, A 33an APPEARANCE.—FINED £5 FOR SHOOTING A Pneesaerr.—William Miller, a powerful looking fellow, was charged with having, on the 7th October last, at Allerton, unlawfully taken a pheasant without having a licence.— Mr. Swift, jun., appeared on behalf of Mr. Thomas Brockle- bank, of Allerton. On the date mentioned Mr. Sockett, farm bailiffe-was near a field belonging to Mr. Brocklebank, on the public road leading from Woolton to Gersten, and saw the prisoner and another man. He concealed himself, as his suspicions were aroused in reference to the men; and in a few minutes they turned off the public road into a private one, leading up to Mr. Brocklebank's farm. They walked along for some yards, and then stopped at a field gate. One of the men placed two stones upon the gate, which is in the occupation of Mr. Gorst. After this the second man got upon the stones and fired a gun at one of nine pheasants which were feeding in a field, and killed one. Then the prisoner now before the Bench went into the field and took the pheasant. Mr. Socket spoke with the men, and a few days afterwards a warrant was issued against them. One of them, named Oldbury, was taken into cus- tody, but Miller took his flight from the neighbourhood.— Superintendent Barker said this was the 33rd appearance of the prisoner, who had been convicted 20 times for poaching. —Mr. Swift observed that the prisoner had once been fined £.5 for an assault on a gamekeeper; and had alsn suffered three months for night poaching. In November of last year prisoner was sentenced to three months for night poaching,, and was bound over for 12 months; and in Sep- tember of this year was fined 108 for game trespass, but was slot cot when he was wanted to pay the money.—The Chairman remarked that the Bench were convinced the pri- soner was guilty, and he would be fined £5 and costs, and, in default of payment, be sent to gaol two months with hard labour.

FOUND DEAD IN BED AT Si. HELENS.—Elizabeth Jennings, 196, Westfield-street, Eccleston, a married woman, 72 years ol age, was found dead in bed by her husband at ten minutes to six on Monday morning. Deceased had always enjoyed good health, and on Sunday evening took her supper, which consisted of bread, pork, and a glass oi I beer. She retired to bed with her husband at ten o'clock. At half-past five the following morning she asked her hus- band if it was not time to get up, and he replied that he I would lie a little longer. At ten minutes to six he spoke to ; her, but getting no answer ho found she was dead.—An ; inquest was held on Tuesday by Mr. Barker, and a verdict I of "Died from natural causes" was returned.—At 20 Iminutes past 11 on Saturday night, Martha Houghton, 4, Liverpool-road, 81 years of age, widow, was found dead in bed by her granddaughter. Deceased had been bed-fast for i the last 12 months, and had suffered from rheumitism and weakness. She had otherwise enjoyed good health, and had taken her food regularly up to the Thurslay prior to her death. Since then she gradually declined. Verdict, •• Died from natural causes.',

div.head: ST. HELENS POLICE COURT.
div.p: ST. HELENS POLICE COURT.

Fumas.—Before Colonel Gamble, and Dr. Iwyford. ROBBING a. DRUNKEN MAN.—Hugh Mooney, between 30 and 40 years of age, was charged with stealing the sum of 15s. from the person of Peter Carney.—Prisoner pleaded not guilty, and neither side was professionally represented. Prosecutor said that on Sunday morning he went to chapel, and about half-past twelve went with prisoner and some friends to the house of Mr. Durkins, a private house in Hardy-street. After dinner prosecutor went out, g•Ot more drink than was good for him, and returned to Durkin's house at half-past two. Later on he missed his money and gave information to the police.—Hannah Oakes, in service at Durkin's house, said that on the day in question prosecutor and prisoner were in Durkin's house. All in the house, with the exception of herself andprisoner, fell asleep. Pri- soner asked her for a pipe, and she said there was not one in the house. He then put his hand in prosecutor's pocket, pulled out a pipe, and, at the same time, a purse. Witness said "Don't take it ; put it back." He made use of a foul expression to her, but afterwards pretended to place the purse where begot it, saying For sake don't tell." —Prosecutor said he did not 'want to press the case, as he was drunk at the time, and it was quite probable that the prisoner did not take the purse.—P.C. Kendall apprehended prisoner at his own home in Hardy-street, and at the office searched him. He found some money upon him. Prisoner I pulled out a shilling and said "Keep that separate; that is Carney's." He charged him with stealing half-a-sovereign in gold and five shilling pieces. Prisoner replied "It's right "—Prisoner was fined £2 or a month. A GREENMAN% WOUNDING CASE.—John Crilooley was charged with unlawfully wounding Dennis Connor.—ln applying for a remand, Superintendent Johnston stated that a quarrel arose at Greenbank, between the prisoner and a third party, and Connor interfered. Gilooley ran into the house, leaving Connor and the other man in the street, but he shortly afterwards sprang from a window, and renewed his attack upon the third man. Connor went between them, and in doing so received two wounds.—P.O. Kendall stated that he apprehended the prisoner at one o'clock on Sunday morning. On searching him he found a pocket knife marked with blood in his overcoat pocket. In answer to the charge of unlawfully wounding Connor, the prisoner said that "before he would-be killed he would use fists, feet, I dagger, knife or pistol." He added that he "did not stab Connor wilfully, but the knife accidentally went into him when he (Connor) was pushing him (the prisoner) from the other man."—Dr. M`Nicol stated that he was called in to I see Connor at eight o'clock on Sunday morning. • He was suffering front one serious wound. All danger from hemor- rhage or shock had passed, but it would be days or weeks before the man would recover, and he was in danger from inflammation of the bowels or peritonitis setting in.—The prisoner was remanded for a week. STEALING AND SETTING FIRE TO HIS DUSTER'S FRO- PERTY.—John Mars was charged on remand with setting fire to a stack of hay, the propetty of Mr. John Middlehurst, farmer and quarry-owner, Crank, for whom he was working, and also with stealing from Mr. Middlehurst's house four watches and some jewellery, of the total value of £B3. About half-past seven on the evening of the 22nd inst. Mr. Middlehurst was sitting in his kitchen, when he perceived a smell of burning, and on going out to ascertain the cause he found one of his hay stacks in flames. He raised an alarm, and went to Red Cat Village for assistance, and after some thne the fire in the stack was put out. On returning home after the alarm had subsided Mr. Middlehurst found that a drawer in his house had been forced open and the watches and jewellery above mentioned bad been stolen. Suspicion attached to the prisoner, who was subsequently taken into custody. 'The prisoner was further remanded till Thursday. THURSDAY.—Before Mr. H. S. Hall. TILE ARSON AND JEWELLERY ROBBERY IT RAINFORD.— John Mars was again charged with setting fire to a hay stack, and stealing £5O worth of jewellery, the property of John Middlehurst, Rainford, on the 22nd instant.—Prose- cutor said he was a farmer, residing at Higher Crank Farm, Rainford. Prisoner was a stonemason's apprentice, and had been with him about five years. Prismer came from the Industfial Schools. During that time prisoner had lived with him, and occupied a bedroom next to his own. At a quarter-past seven on the 22nd he waS in the house with his sister-in-law, they being the only two persons ia the house at the time to his knowledge. He perceived a smell of burning, and he went out to see what it was. He found a hay stack on fire. Prisoner was in the house about an hour before, and about half an hour after be discovered the fire. Prisoner came and assisted him to extinguish it. Witness told prisoner to stand back or he would get wet. Prisoner replied that he was already wet through. Witness was afterwards told that his house had been broken into, and a number of things taken away. The articles produced were his property, and were worth £5O.— Mary Smith, prosecutor's sister-in-law, said that she fol- lowed prosecutor out of the house to see what was burning, and returned shoitly afterwards to bolt both back doors right and left of the back kitchen. Witness did not see anyone in the house at the time and soon left to go to the fire, leaving the front door unfastened. During the time the stack was burning witness visited the house several times going in at the front door. She saw the prisoner at the fire, and again visited the house. She found the right hand back door closed, but the left hand back door open, although she had fastened it. Soon after that she saw Mrs. Middle- hurst who gave her a bag of money to take care of. Wit- ness took it upstairs and placed it in a drawer in Mr. Middlehurst's bedroom. She found the drawer open and in- formed Mrs. Middlehurst of the fact in about ten minutes afterwards. Prisoner was in the kitchen about an hour before the fire broke out.—Elizabeth Middlehurst, wife of John Middlehurst, said on the day in question, about half- pi natsnt ht he rr e he nos'hc leoncdk ihne dttheen n f tfeerrn osoewnt some she obey. .o c clat swi °ens to hge no all right. Witness kept her jewellery in the same drawer, and that was r ight also. She locked the drawer after getting what she wanted, and then went to a shop at the Red Cat. She returned the same evening at half-past seven, and saw a fire in the stack yard. She saw the last witness there, and gave her a bag a money to take care of Soon after that, from what last witness told her, she went into her husband's bedroom and found some studs and boxes scattered about the room floor. The drawer was open and she missed the whole of the jewellery produced. She gave information to the police.— P.C. William Duerden, stationed at the Red Cat, Rainford- said, at 7-30 p.m. on the day in 'question, he saw a fire in Mr. Middlehurst's stack yard. He went across a field to it. At eight o'clock he saw the prisoner there, and was told that a robbery had been committed. He examined Mr. Middle.
