div.p: _ IitINCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS. \ At the meeting Of this Board, on Tuesday, there were pre- sent the Rev. J. W. N. Tanner, Messrs. 7ohn Mclntyre On the chair), Charles Rigby, James Darbyshire, Jost= Mid- wood, Thomas Andrews, John Weir, Thomas Norraan, Fisher, John Challoner, William Whittaker, H. Linaker (clerk), and W. H. Linaker (deputy clerk).

THE YACCISATIOI•7 AND FAY ST.TIONS. A letter was read from the Local Government Board, ill which it was stated that they regarded the proposal of the Guardians to have Bethesda school-room for a vaccination station as satisfactory. They requested that the change of station may be endorsed on the vaccination contract for the district and that the contract he forwarded for the Board's approval.—The Local Government Board, in a communica- tion dated December 24th, stated they were prepared to assent to the hiring by the Guardians of the Runcorn Union, of the house in Church-street, Runcorn, at a rental of £l4 per annum, provided there were no special conditions in the lease or agreement which would interfere with the use of the premises by the Guardians for their intended purpose. On the proposition of Mr. FISHER, it was decided to rent the house for a pay station on a seven year's lease. Tem STORAGE OF BOORS.—WARM DISCUSSION. The committee appointed to consider the best means of providingaccommodation for the books and documents belong- ing to the Union, held a meeting on the 22nd inst.,. Canon Barclay presiding. The committee, after considering the question, deemed it desirable that all the books and docu- ments connected with the Union business be kept at the Clerk's office, and recommended that the Clerk make arrange- ments to find accommodation for them, and that a certain rental, to be fixed hereafter, be paid for the use of the room, or rooms, which may be requiend for the purpose. The com- mittee had requested the clerk to prepare a plan, showing how such accommodation could be provided at his office, and to prepare an estimate of the probable cost as well as to state the rent which he will require for the portion of his office so appropriated to the service of the Guardians. Mr. NORMAN moved, and Mr. CHALLONER seconded, the adoption of the report. The former remarked that the Clerk had said he should require £2O a year for the room and fire. Mr. RIGBY : £2O a year! Mr. CHALLONER : The committee thought that very reasonable. If you build an office you will have to have fire in it. If you have no fire to keep them aired the books will be in as bad condition as at present. As it is now, we have no Clerk's office. We thought he would want £3O

a year. Mr. JAxS DmanysnißE said the matter had been looked at from every point of view, and a place could not be built in that house under .£SGO. Mr. RIGBY: Monstrous! Mr. DARBYSHIRE : That is the conclusion we came to. I wish you could see what books and papers there are accumulated. Mr. RIGBY : Would they fill this (Board) room? Mr. DARBYSTURE : Thev would half fill it. The CHAIRMAN : I think we have been trespassing on Mr. Xinaker for many years. I don't know whether there is any introspective account taken into consideration, tut if there Is not I think he is letting us off very well. (Hear, hear.) The CLERK: I would sooner the whole thing was removed hom me. Mr. RIGBY asked if the Guardians were bound to find an Office for the Clark? - The DEPUTY CLERK said they were bound to find Union offices. Mr. RIGBY: Do other unions find offices? The DEPLTY CLERK said the Prescot Guardians had spent a considerable sum in building offices. Mr. RIGHT: I think we might put up a place for £5OO. : The DEErry CLERK: You would have to pay it back at 71 per cent. per year. Mr.BIGBY: We could build offices for £3OO. Mr. CHALLONER ; There are the expenses afterwards— light, fire, and cleaning. The CLERK said the Board had just arranged to pay £l4 and provide light, fire, and cleaning for a room that would only be wanted once a week. It was painful to hear these expressions when one only wanted to do justice to the rate-

payers. Mr. Nonares said be was told, the other day, that the clerk of a union, not half as big as theirs, had a salary of £l6O a year. Their clerk only got £9O. "And then talk about £2O rent! " A member remarked about the £2O being only a small expense. Mr. RIGBY observed that it was the little expenses that add up. The report was then adopted, all the members voting for it pith the exception of Mr. Rigby. 'min DIVIDED PARISHES. The CLERK said he had received the following letter: —Local Government Board, Whitehall, S.W., 22nd Decem- ber, 1881. Sir,-1 am directed by the Local Government Board with reference to the inquiries hold on the subject on the 22nd June last, and the 2nd ultimo, by their inspector, Mr. R. J.Dansey, to forward to you the accompanying copies of four orders which they have issued under the authority of "The Divided Parishes and Poor Law Amendment Act, 1876," and " The Poor Law A ct, 1879," relative to the town- ships of Antrobus, Seven Oaks, Kingsley, and Norley, in the Runcorn Union, and the township of Crowton in the Northwich Union. lam to add that owing to difficulties which have arisen in the matter, the Board do not propose to deal at present with the townships of Frodsham, Halton, and Runcorn, and the lordship of Fro4sham.—l am, sir, your obedient servant, Hugh Owen, assistant secretary. To H. Linaker, Esq." After quoting the sections of the Act, which empowered them to deal with the question; the orders stated the Local Government Board had decided that it was expedient the isolated part of the township of Antrobus should be,arnalga- mated with the township of Seven Oaks, in which it was locally situated; and, the Education Department having given their sanction thereto, the amalgamation should take effect on the 24th March, 1882. A detached portion of Norley was ordered to be amalgamated with Kingsley, and another portion to Crowton. Mr. RIGBY : Well, that's something. THE STATE OF TEE norsx. The Master, in his report, stated there were 196 inmates in the house • corresponding week last year, 159. There were 16 imbeciles in the house and 33 belonging to the Union in Asylums. 33 boys and 30 girls were in attendance at school and 12 boys and 19 girls were receiving industrial training. During the week 644 persons had been relieved at a cost of £62 7s. 66., compered with 643, at a cost of £62 6s. ld. during the corresponding week last year.

div.head: • RUNCORN POLICE COURT.
div.p: • RUNCORN POLICE COURT.

MONDAY.—Before Messrs. William Bankes (chairman), and S. B.:Chadwick. OFFENCE UNDER THE CANAL BOATS' ACT—James Gerrard, of Chester-road, Northwich, was summoned by the Runcorn Herat Sanitary Authority, for having, on the 15th Mat., at Weston, used a certain boat called the Constance, upon the river Weaver canal as a dwelling, without having it registered in accordance with the Canal Boats' Act, 187 7. —Mr. Farrington, inspector to the Authority, proved finding defendant's boat near the chemical works at Weston, and it was not lettered, marked, and numbered, as required by the Act. From information given to him afterwards, it appeared that the vessel was registered in 1879, but owing to some neglect on the part of the captain, who was the owner's son, I and had since been dismissed, the boat had been lying up nine months. Owing to defendant being an invalid, he had not been able to see about the matter.—Defendant was rep- resented by Mr. William Topham, who made a similar state- ment.—Mr.Farrington thought that under the circumstances a nominal fine and costs would meet the case.—The Chair- man said defendant would be tined is. and 11s. ed. Mts., THHRSDAY.—BeIote Mr. William Banks. SAVAGE THREATS BY AN AMERICAN MEAT BrTCHER.— John McAvoy, a butcher keeping an American meat store, in Church-street, was summoned for having, on the 28th inst, used serious threats towards a man named -William Brown, a bailiff employed by the Runcorn Loan and Dis- count Co —Mr. Lake (Messrs. Day and Lake) appeared on behalf of the complainant, and prisoner, who is a young man, and had been taken in custody under a warrant, was unrepresented.—Mr Lake, having opened the case, asked that McAvoy might be bound over in substantial bail. It was very necessary that bailiffs, who had often such un- pleasant work to do, should be nrotected from men like the prisoner, who threatened to cut open their insides.—Com- plainant, who was then called, said he lived in Wellington - street, and on the previous afternoon, he was employed by the manager of the Union Loan and Discount Co., to take possession of all the things in the house at No. 89, Church- street, in the occupation of the prisoner.—He produced the bill of sale under which he was empowered to act. When he entered the premises, the prisoner said "Be clearing out of this, or I will throw you out," and be then pulled his apron off in 'wrier that he might have more free use of his limbs. McAvoy next struck him, on which he told him he had better be quiet or it would be worse for him. Prisoner's only reply to this, was to get a large knife, shout out that "He was the boss there," and that if he did not go out, he would cut his liver out! Mr. Yarwood, auctioner, then came, on which the prisoner did not proceed to any further violence, but contented himself with cursing and swearing what he would do to anyone who touched anything in the place. McAvoy was somewhat under the influence of liquor, but not very much so. He was certainly in fear that if he moved anything prisoner would do him some bodily harm.—Prisoner I am going to put you out of posses- sion as soon as I get out—ln reply to Mr. Banks, he said he did not remember doing any thing to the complain- ant, and he was sorry if he used the expressions which had been imputed to him. He had not signed any bill of sale to the society.—Mr. Charles Houghton was called for the defence, and stated that he was present when Mr. Yarwood entered the prisoner's and offered to read the bill of sale to McAvov ; but he added that he did. not' hear anything take place between the bailiff and the prisoner.—Mr. Johnson, deputy-magistrates clerk, ruled that Mr. Houghton's evi- dence did not affect the point at issue.—Mr. Lake :I am prepared to prove that what took place occurred before this witness was on the scene at all.—Mr. Houghton maintained that he did not lose sight of the prisoner during the whole dispute.—Mr. Yarwood (pointing to Mr. Houghton): His evidence is simple perjury.—George Lee, a youth, was called for the defence, but his statements appeared rather to favour the complainant.—Mr. Bankes said the charge against the prisoner was a very serious one. It certainly appeared that he was in drink at the time he was guilty of it, but that was no reason why he should assault the officer in charge Of the goods and utter threats to him. He should, however,

deal as leniently as he could wlth the prisoner, as he had I not been before the Bench on a drunken charge before. He would have to enter .into sureties, himself in £2O and two in £lO each, to keep the peace for si months, and in default of payment, would be sent to gaol 14 days.

div.head: WIDNES POLICE COURT.
div.p: WIDNES POLICE COURT.
_ Coatiettecl from page 6. WEDNESDAY.—Before Messrs. Holbrook Gasketl (chairman) and George Pilkington.

--- - STEALING A CANT LOAD OF COAL.—Jeremiah Sullivan, a young man, was charged with stealing a cart load of coal, the property of Messrs. Fletcher, Burrows, and Co., colliery proprietors, Crown-street,Liverpool.-Superintendent Barker, having briefly opened the case, called Mr. John Thomas Hayes of 64, Hardy-street, Liverpool, who said he was manager to the prosecutors. ,A few days ago he sent a load of coal to the Huyton station, so that the prisoner might deliver it to a lady on the day following. Having had reason to suspect the young man's honesty, he (witness) went to Huyton himself on the following day, and found that he had disposed of the coal to a Mrs. Lowe who lived near the rail- way goods' yard, but it had not been delivered when he got to the place. The load weighed bewteen 25 and 30 cwt., and was worth at least 15s.—Prisoner had no authority to sell it, and on finding what he had done, he gave him into custody.--Margaret Lowe, the wife of Edward Lowe, Pen- nington-place, linyton, stated that on the evening of the 20th inst., Sullivan came to her and asked her if she would bay a load of coal, which she had not then seen. She agreed to give him 6s. for it, and paid him 2s. 6.1. towards it.—Mr. Lewin, magistrates' clerk (to the witness) :Is not that a low price to give for a load of coal?—Witness: I had not seen them when I bought them.—The Chairman said that if the prisoner had been before the Bench previously, he would have been dealt with far more severely. He would be sent to gaol two months, with hard labour. A ROUGH CIISTOILEIL—MichaeI Loftus was charged with having been drunk and disorderly at Much Woolton, and as- saulting two police officers.—P.C. Noble said that about twenty minutes past seven on the previous afternoon, he was on duty at Much Wootton, and saw the prisoner, who was offering to fight another man. He (witness) attempted to take Loftus home, on which he attempted to kick him, and was so voilent that three other constables had to assist be- fore he could be taken to the station, and even then the man had to be put in a wheelbarrow.—P.C. Steele also gave evi- dence as to the prisoner striking him several times.—Loftus said that all he could say in defence was that he was drunk at the time.—Superintendent Barker said the prisoner only came out of gaol on the 22nd inst., where he had been serv- ing three months for assaulting the Woolton inspector. Ile had been twelve times before the magistrates, and this was his seventh appearance this year. He hoped that the Bench would inflict such a punishment upon him that it would be a warning to others that they could not treat the police hr such a brutal manner with impunity.—The Chairman re- marked that it was quite evident the prisoner was a man of such a violent disposition that it was scarcely safe to permit him to be at large, for he had only just come out of gaol, where he had been incarcerated for a similar offence, when he was at his old game again. He would be sent to gaol six months, with hard labour. ALLEGED Assanur WITII A PONER. .—Michael Tobin was summoned for threatening Michael McDonnell, a chemical labourer at ,Messrs. Sullivan's. From complainant's state- ment it appeared that defendant had struck him with a poker, on the evening of the 24th inst. As Tobin did not ap- pear, the Bench issued a warrant for his apprehension. THIIRSDAY.—Before Messrs. F. H. Gossage and Holbrook Gaskell. - - -

------- STEALING lEON.—Thomas Fyldes was charged with steal- ing on the previous day a quantity of old iron from Widnes Marsh.—Prisoner was seen coming away from the locality in question with a bag over his arm. He was stopped and the bag examined, when its contents were found to be old iron, and as he was unable to give any satisfactory account as to how he acquired it, he was handed over to the police.—The Bench sent him to gaol for a month with hard labour. A WEAE CASE.—Arthur Brown, a boy, and Elizabeth Brown, his mother, were charged with stealing, on the 28th December, a drake value 25., the property of Joseph Ford. The drake had been seen to stray into his yard, and a boy named Lloyd had observed a woman there kill a drake and take it into the house. P.S. Robinson afterwards searche4 the house and found the head and entrails of a drake. Lloyd, however, could not identify the female prisoner as the woman he had seen killing the bird, and the case was dismissed. A BATCH OF VecatArrrs.—Charles Burns, James Shannon, John Lappan, and Simon Kilroy were charged with sleeping out luau engine shed, on Widnes Marsh, on 'the previous night.—P.C. Laing proved the cases.—Burns was sent to gaol for seven days, and Shannon and Lappan each for a month, all with hard labour. In the case of Kilroy it was stated that the prisoner, who was ahoy about 14 years of age, had two months ago been sent to the Beacon-lane Industrial School, Liverpool. About six weeks after his committal the boy escaped, but was immediately recaptured. A few days ago he again decaqiped, but has since been caught. He was sent back to sch 001.

WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS. At the fortnightly meeting of the Baard held at the Workhouse, on Wednesday,:there were present: Mr. Joseph Harrison (chairman), the Rev. J. Yonge. Rev.G. F. Roberts, Messrs. Derbyshire, Cartwright, Hall, Blackhurst, Hough- ton, Greene% Hunt, Fairhurst, Cooper, Kilahall, Mackie, Greening, Garnett, Gibson, Woolfall, Jeans, and J. C. Sutton ( clerk). THE WARD AND THE CORPORATION. The CLERIC read the following letter, the first part of which refers to the complaint about the removal of pails by the Corporation during the day time :—Town Clerk's Office, Warrington, 17th December, 1881. Dear sir, lam directed by the Sanitary Committee to inform you that the subject of your letter on the 6th inst is under their careful con- sideration. Your Authority may be assured that every effort is and has been made to prevent such a nuisance as you complain of.—Removal of paupers: I am in receipt of your letter of yesterday's date, on this subject, which I will lay before the committee at their next meeting.—Yours faithfully, Wm. H. Brook. THE REWARDS FOR ArmuntwttstoNs. Mr. BARBYSItIrtE moved that the following resolution, passed in 1880, be rescinded: "that the sum of 55. be paid to the police officers, as a reward, in each case of arrest of I persons for neglect of family, and an iocreased reward of any sum not exceeding 20s. according to the recommenda- tion of the chief constable on his ceport and the vigilance of the officer." He said his attention was called, a month ago, to the case of a man named Peter Swift who left his family chargeable to the Union, and for whose apprehension a warrant was issued. That man went into the police station without any exertions being used by the police to get him there, and gave himself up, and consequently he could not be said to have been arrested. If a person gave himself up voluntarily, there was no apprehension, and he thought in that case the reward which the Board offered ought not to be paid. He was curious to know who would have the reward, seeing that there would be more than one officer at the police station when the man went in, and he found, on looking at the bill sent in that P.C. Neil would get it. He also found that of the last five cases in which rewards bad been paid by the Board, fortunately for Neil, four fell to that constable and one to P.C. Bowen. P.C. Neil must be a very superior officer, or the other police officers, if they had the same facilities, were very dilatory, as they seldom got the rewards. The system et giving rewards had not worked beneficially for the Board or for the ratepayers. It had really prevented the Board's officers from obtaining the rewards. Some time ago the Board appointed an officer who be understood at the time was to be warrant officer. That officer, however, had never apprehended any one that he had heard of or taken any trouble to do so because of this resolution by which the war- rants were entirely in the hands of the police officers. He , thought that ought not to be the case, but that the Board's officers when they saw in the street a man against whom a warrant was in existence, ought to be able to apprehend him, and have the reward for so doing. He therefore proposed that the resolution be rescinded, and the following substi- tuted :—" That our OWR officers be requested to use their utmost endeavours to arrest people who have deserted their familie, or any other person who should lead to the arrest of the.delinquents should participate in the rewards as given by this Board." The Rev. J. YONGE : Wnat do I understand was the regu- lation before that? Mr. DARHYSHIRE said that the police constable who arrested a person wanted by the Board appeared before the Board and made a statement of the extra exertions required to arrest such person, and the Board decided whether he should have ss. or 20s. Now the applications came from the Chief Constable without any report; but he would have been glad of a report of Swift's case from the constable. As it was the Board could not judge for themselves whether the reward had been earned or not. The Rev. J. YONGE, merely as a matter of form, in order that the question might be discussed, seconded the proposi- tion. It did not appear to him to be necessary to pay a reward for the apprehension of a man who gave himself up voluntarily. He was struck that one officer should get four fifths of the rewards that were offered, according to the last account that had come in and he would like to know, if Mr. Sutton could tell, whether previous accounts showed the same sort of thing. P.C. Neil must be a magnificent officer or the other constables must be particularly unworthy of their position. But it did appear singular that one officer should get four out of five rewards in one account. Mr. BLACEIVCRST said the question seemed to him to be whether offering the rewards had had the effect the Board intended them to have. As to one officer getting more than another, he did not think that was a question the Board should enquire into. It was nothing to them how Mr. Hunt carried these things out. If by these rewards the Board facilitated the apprehension of the persons they wanted, he did not think it mattered to them how it was done. No doubt some officers were far more energetic than others in what they undertook, and this must be a case of that sort. Unless Mr. Darbyshire was prepared to propose a better plan to facilitate the apprehension of people for neglect of family he felt bound to vote against the motion. Major CARTWRIGHT was glad to find Mr. Derbyshire had taken this matter up, because he ventured to say none paid greater attention to the apprehension of deserters of families, which became chargeable to that house than he did. Even, if it was from that alone, he should be inclined to support
I

div.head: EXAMINER SATURDAY, DECEMBER 31, 1881.
div.p: THE EXAMINER SATURDAY, DECEMBER 31, 1881.

any resolution that Mr. Darbysbire might bring forward, if I he could show clearly that these cases would be better I attended to thsat they had been. He did not hesitate to say there had been negligence in cases where apprehensions ought to have been made sooner, but whose neglect it was he could not tell. Warrants were executed not only by the officers of the borough but by those of the county as well. There was a case in Latchford, the other day, where a warrant was in the hands of the officer for some weeks before the appre- hension took place, although they had informa- tion of the man's whereabouts. If any plan could be adopted to secure an improvement in the apprehension of deserters he would be very glad indeed to I support it. He stated the other day that there were some- ' thing like 85 children chargeable to the Union through desertion, but he was glad to say now that in consequence of recent activity the number had been reduced consider- ably. He believed there would be a greater diminution if the warrants were promptly, executed. He should like to know whether Mr. Derbyshire was prepared to propose a resolution that would meet the case. Mr. MACSIE suggestei that it would be well for the Board not to be in too great a hurry in moving in this matter, which practically amounted to censure upon the police authorities. (Major Cartwright: No, no). It was not intended, but it practically came to that, and that class of persons in whom the police were most interested, and who took the greatest interest in the police, were very likely to interpret the saying and doings of the Board that morning in a way they would scarcely like them to be in- terpreted. It so happened that he had had submitted to him a very long, full, and particular account of the dif- ferences which had taken place between the police and the Board's officers, and he would strongly recommend, with- out passing the slightest reflection upon anyone, that a committee be appointed to bold a conference with the Chief Constable, and to call in any others they thought necessary to consult in the matter. Mr. DARBYSHIELE said he would be satisfied if the motion was not carried if some course of the kind suggested was adopted. He did not move in the matter in a spirit of opposition to anyone, but simply to perform what he felt to be his duty, and to get negligent parents apprehended as soon as possible. Because if a man deserted his family for three or four months, and they became chargeable to the I Union, the Board could only get the amount that had been paid for the maintenance of that family from the time the man was apprehended, so that it was essentially necessary apprehensions should be effected as soon as possible. He therefore proposed to add to his motion the following "That our officers be requested to use their utmost en- deavour to arrest people who have deserted their families, or any other persons who should lead to the apprehension of the delinquent participate in the rewards given by the

Board." Mr. BLACKHURST thought the Board's officer could not apprehend anyone- unless he had the warrant in his pos- session. Major CARTWRIGHT said it was the relieving officers' duty if a person had deserted his family to give all the in- formation he could to secure his apprehension. The CHAIRMAN said supposing the relieving officer happened to be in Manchester and met a person whom he knew was" wanted" ha would be perfectly justified in giving that person into cnstody. If he did not lay himself open to being called a partisan, he could not help saying , that he thought Mr. Derbyshire's proposition should be met with a direct negative. In the first place, when a gentleman stood up there and asked the Board to rescind I resolution which had been deliberately passed by the Board twelve months previously, he ought to be able to show some substantial reason for endeavouring to cancel it. He did not think Mr. Derbyshire had adduced a single reason in justification of the course which he had proposed. All that he had told the Board was that out ef five warrants held by the police four had been executed by P.C. Neil. •He really did not see much grievance in that. As Mr. Blackhnrst had said, it was no matter to the Board by.whom these persons were arrested so long as they were arrested; and was it not going out of their way to criticise the manner in which the Chief Constable chose to arrange how the duties of his position should be performed? Surely the Chief Constable ought to be the best judge. He thought Mr. Derbyshire's resolution came at a very inoppor- tune period. A complaint was made, he thought, at the last meeting by Mr. Derbyshire that there had been great neglect in arresting the persons who were wanted. He was not in a position to contradict it at the time, but he had now some figures which he thought would not help Mr. Derbyshire to induce the Board to pass the resolution. In 1879, for the , year ending 29th September, there were 20 arrests; for the year ending 29th September, 1280, there were 11 arrests; and for the year ending 29th September, 1881, there were 38. (Hear, hear.) Surely if an argument could be used to show the undesirability of passing the resolution, he thought it was to be found in those statistics. He thought the reso- lution, if passed, would only nomplicate matters, and that the best way to meet it was by a direct negative. Mr. DAREYSHIRE claimed a right of reply. The CHAIRMAN maintained that Mr. Derbyshire had already replied. Mr. DARBYSHIRE said he had not replied, and did not wish to do so until he had heard the Chairman's speech. After some conversation, Mr. DARBTSIIIRE was allowed to reply, and be said he was surprised that the Chait man attributed as the results of the resolution the Board were acting upon at present the figures he had quoted. He looked upon them in a different light altogether. Last year and the year before there were many more desertions than ever the Board had experienced before, and it was from this fact that there had been more apprehen- sions. Looking at the matter in that way, he was surprised the Chairman should qaote the figures in the way he had. The Chairman told them a fortnight ago these rewards were confirmed or otherwise by the Watch Committee of the Town Council, and if that committee did not think it right that the police officers should have them they could be handed ever to the superannuation fund. He did not wish the I rewards to go to that fund, as it was not for that purpose they were offered. The CHAIRMAN: I trust I can make an observation? z Mr. DARBYSIIIRE: It entirely depends upon what you have to say. (Laughter.) I think you have made your speech, and I do not think you are entitled to make two any more than any other member of the Board. (Laughter.) T conveyi s remarks was abtohua tt theth sup e final disposition of rewards given to police officers for having reference to to to h exercised their vigilance in arresting persons the Board ehreanCnilulatTillo3n Is fund all he ef wanted rested entirely with the Watch Committee. He happened to say if they thought fit they could confiscate it to the superannuation fund, but he was not aware of a single instance in which that bad been done. The Rev. J. TONGE thought the best way would be to adopt Mr. Mackie's suggestion. Mr. MACKIE proposed that a committee be appointed to enquire into the whole disagreement existing between the police and the Board's officers. Mr. B LAM:MIST seconded the proposition. Mr. JEANS did not see what the committee were to enquire into. The simple question was whether the Board were I going to give a reward for apprehension or not. On principle I he thought it was wrong to reward police officers. Why should they be rewarded for doing their duty in these cases ; more than in any other ? The CLERK, replying to Mr. Carleton, said there seemed I to have been a much larger number of warrants applied for this year than in the previous year. Major CARTWRIGHT said, this was the result of the Board's , determination to prosecute deserters of families. The CHAIRMAN stated that in regard to Swift's case Mr. Hunt waited upon him the previous day, and assured him that in no instance had a reward been asked for where the person had given himself up. Mr. Hunt showed him a document he had received from the governor of the gaol where Swift was, containing several qeestious that had been submitted to Swift, and in one instance he stated he was not aware there was a warrant out for his apprehension. He admitted going to the police office, but he distinctly denied that he went there to deliver himself up. He then referred to a letter signed "Jack," which appeared in The Warrington Examiner the previous Saturday. Mr. DARBISHIRE I don't think it is before the Board. The CHAIRMAN said he only wanted to allude to one matter which he thought was before the Board. In that letter the Watcli Committee were accused of having done a gross injustice to the Board's officers, and he was accused in the first instance of being a strong partisan, which he declared he was not. If the Watch Committee could have done 'what was stated in the letter they would have been unworthy of the confidence of the public, and he declared he would never have eat down and been a witness of such an act of injustice. The letter distinctly stated while the Watch Committee permitted Mr. Hunt and a host of his witnesses, police-officers ktc.,to be examined and heard on his side of the question the Committee positively refused to hear Mr. Harbourne, Mr. Garnett, and other persons. He assured the Board that in that assertion there was not a par- ticle of truth. (Hear, hear). He was present at the Com- mittee himself, and they refused to hear any witnesses. They said "We will hear no witnesses. 'We have the fullest confidence in Mr. Hunt; we believe his explanation ; " and the Watch Committee were about to pass a resolution t ,:that effect. • Mr. 131.actitnnsT : I think, gen tlemen, this is not fair. The Curansuor : You have no right to interrupt me. Major CAUTWEIGHT This is an attack upon the chair- man. I intended to have brought it forward myself, and I think he ought to be allowed an explanation to an attack like that. Mr. BLACICTIIIRST Our chairman has an opportunity at the proper place and proper time. This place is not the Town Council. The Cwatnimor : Mr. Blackhurst is tint of order. The Rev. E. C. CARLETON : The whole question is certainl under discussion and no difficulties ought to be brought in. Major Carerwwwwr : You would not allow the chairman to be attacked under an assumed name? The CHAIRMAN said he was accused of having acted in a partizan spirit as a member of the Committee and as chairman of the Beard, but be declared such an accusation was as un- truthful as the assertion made regarding the Committee. If he hacl,sot been on the Committee they would simply have passed a resolution saying that they had full confidence in their officers and that the charge was unfounded. He there- fore suggested to the Mayor that they should effect a com- promise, and that while expressing confidence in their officers they should say that Mr. Harbourne and Mr. Garnett a taint moat n disagree- able had no intention to mislead, but had been mistaken in oesup- posingither the informations to be warrants. That was what he hoped business,w ouldbe withoute n amicable n g the arrangement f slightest one side or the other. But at the last Board meeting, Mr. Harbourne put in a letter addressed to him and he had to read it. That anfortunately reopened the question and at the last meeting of the Watch Committee they passed such

a resolution as they would have passed at the previous meeting had it not been for his interposition—that they had the fullest confidence in Mr. Hunt and his officers, and they believed the charges made against them were entirely un- founded. He thought Mr. Blackhurst's conduct was ex- tremely discourteous to him, attacked in the way he was by this dastardly production. The writer ought to be ashamed of himself. He was told it was a member of the Board but he hoped not. Mr. BLACKRUEST did not wish to be discourteous, but it was very mach to be regretted that gentlemen should go there to defend themselves of paragraphs in the news-

papers. The CnianateN : I have referred to nothing but what is appertaining to myself. 'lle Rev. J. Yoe un supposed the last remark of the Chairma n was aimed at him ,but he wished to give him and everybody 'else the most emphatic denial. (Hear, hear.) His habit, whenever he wrote to the newspapers, was to put "John Yonge " at the bottom of the letter. (Hear, hear.) I Major CARTWRIGHT said when it was suggested to him he at once said Mr. Yonge would never do anything of that

sort. Mr. JEANS thought the Chairman was quite right in refer- ring to the letter. He had not read it, but it happened he had read the letter signed "Joseph," and be assumed "Jack" and " Joseph " were the same person. He never saw a more complete misrepresentation of facts of law than was shown upon that letter, and he could say the subject upon which "Joseph" wrote was one " not for Joe." (Laughter.) It was an entire perversion of the facts of the law. Mr. DARZYSHIRE said the Chairman had been out of order in occupying the time of the Board in defending him- self against an anonymous writer in the public papers. He thought the Chairman's proper course, if he thought it necessary to take any steps at all, was to defend himself through the newspapers. The CHAIRMAN was very much obliged to Mr. Darby- shire for his fatherly advice—(laughter)—but he was sure he was perfectly in order. If it had been an attack upon him without any reference to him as a member of the Board he would not have alluded to it. But he felt it was a duty incumbent upon him to exonerate the Watch Committee from the foul aspersion cast upon them. He was sure what had been done by him that morning was only what would I have been permitted at the Town Council, and he would be very sorry if any gentleman thought he had abused his power as Chairman of the Board. After a pause, the Chair-. • man said: Now, Mr. Clerk, how does this matter stand ? (Loud laughter.) Major CARTWRIGHT : I cannot tell. Mr. Mackie will perhaps be able to sieve it. (Laughter.) Mr. Mackie's motion was carried, Messrs. Blackhurst, Greening, and Garnett being appointed a committee to inquire into the question of rewards granted to the police for arresting persons for neglect of family, and to report as early as possible.

THE NURSE'S SALARY. On the motion of Major CARTWRIGHT, the salary of Miss Pugh, nurse, was increased from £25 to £3O per annum. THE BARRACKS WATER SUPPLY. The minutes of the Barracks Committee stated" that the Clerk attended to explain the proceedings taken by him in the matter of the supply of water for domestic use. The correspondence between the Secretary of the Waterworks Company and himself was laid before the Committee, and a notice by the company to cut off the water supply on and after January Ist, 1892, and that if the Guardians were desirous of having a supply of water on the basis of the old Barracks being a private-dwelling house, they were at liberty to require a fresh connection, according to the provisions of the Waterworks Clauses Act, 1847, section 50, which limited the bore of the pipe to half an inch. The Superintendent reported that although such a pipe might afford a supply of water to pne wing of the barracks, it would fail to supply the whole of the premises with sufficient water for domestic use. The Clerk was of opinion that the premises were dwel- ling-houses, and that the Guardians were entitled to a supply of water in respect of each one or more of such dwelling- houses. The Clerk further reported the aggregate annual value of the premises to be fixed on the Overseer's Valuation List at £lBO gross, and £153 rateable, and that in his opinion this sum admitted of considerable reduction to arrive at the actual annual value. The Clerk was also of opinion that, according to the 68th section of the Waterworks Clauses Act, 1847, the magistrates' court was the proper tri- bunal to fix the annual value, and that proceedings in that court were a condition precedent to proceedings in the County Court upon any question that might otherwise arise in that court. The superintendent was instructed to apply for a supply of water for domestic use, to such separate por- tions of the premises as might be necessary' and to make the necessary tender of money, and that such other proceed- ings be taken by the Clerk in this behalf as to bring the matters in dispute to a settlement." The CLERK explained the position of affairs, and said that Mr. Mines had made the requisite tender of money, but the Waterworks Company refused to receive it. Replying to Mr. Jeans, he said the Act of Parliament stated that the bore of the pipe should not exceed the prescribed limits, but where no limits should be prescribed, the pipe should not exceed half an inch except with the consent of the undertakers. He contended the barracks was not one dwelling-house, but a series of dwelling-houses. The CHAIRMAN said it was quite clear the law contem- plated the Company putting a supply pipe of such dimen- sions as was necessary to meet the requirements of the inhabitants of the house. Mr. DARKYSHIRE said it seemed to be a pity some arrange- ment could not be come to considering the short time the Board would occupy the Barracks. The Water Works Company so far had treated them in d very sisters manner. The CLERK read the following letter :—" Waterworks Office Warrington, December 27th, 1881.—Dear sir,—Yours of 24th instant. As already stated you have all requisite information. You demand water to the barracks upon the basis as to a private house, and in order to obtain that domestic supply, certain provisions of the public statutes with regard to the pipes to be laid most be observed. All householders have had to do this and it can be no hardship upon you to do so likewise. Rule 3of the printed fittings, regulations, specifies the size and weight of the pipes, and , rule 8 informs you that each premises or house will be allowed one supply pipe and no more. In your letter of the 20th inst. you yourself refer to a workhouse as a house, and you add all the paupers are one family,' and in support of that definition you cite the Liskard case. The Barracks, as you are aware, are now, and always have been, one premises or tenement, and in one occupation, and they shall new as hitherto be treated. As the special pipes by which the Barracks are now supplied will shortly be cat off, I would remind you while it is yet time that the. fresh com- munication pipes for domestic supply should be aid with- out delay. This, of course, forms no business or mine. I merely refer to the circumstonce, and I would add that the Company's officers will give constant attendance te facilitate and expedite your work of obtaining that domestic supply which the Guardians now require.—Yours truly, JOHN Ross." After some conversation the minutes were adopted, on the motion of the Rev. J. YONGE, seconded by MAJOR CART- WRIGHT.

div.head: CHRISTMAS FESTIVITIES.
div.p: CHRISTMAS FESTIVITIES.

THE CARISTMAS DINNER. ] The Master and Matron on behalf of the inmates begged to acknowledge with gratitude the receipt of a box of oranges from Mr. Robert Heaton, which it had been his custom to send for the last 13 years. Also a box of Christ- MRS cards from Miss Grimes, of ths Elms, Thelwall, which I was very much appreciated by the children and sick inmates. He was pleased to be able to report that the Christmas festivities (on the 26th inst.) had passed off most satisfactorily. and that both young and old enjoyed them- selves thoroughly, and not one at the workhouse appeared the worse for drink upon the occasion. Several Guardians and friends visited the house during the day, notably the , Chairman (Mr. J. Harrison), and chairman of the House Com- mittee (Major Cartwright), Mrs. Cartwright, Mr. and Mrs. R. Garnett, and family, Mr. Robert Heaton, and Rev. S. Wilkin- son. Mr. Harrison and Major Cartwright addressed the I 'people assembled in the large hall ,and the addresses were I ,much appreciated and loudly cheered, the more so as Mr.t Harrison was the only chairman who had come amongst them for years on this particular day. The CitatrotAW remarked that as far as they could judge the festivities certainly passed off with great spirit, and he did not think there was any person the worse for having taken the beer. He dared say they would all be the better ' for having drunk it, because he believed a small supply of beer had a stimulating effect, and they were better men than without it ('question '). He believed they were much happier than if they had taken tea or coffee ('question '). The Rev. J. YONIIIE said, if a member next year, he would again move in the matter, fortified by the fact that the Manchester Union on Christmas Day followed its practice of some years standing not to allow beer, and the inmates, so the report said, enjoyed themselves exceedingly. Mr. GREENING said nine-tenths of the inmates were brought to the house through beer, and it ought to be entirely discountenanced. The Rev. E. C. E. CARLETON, who had been for 25 years a total abstainer, but was not one at the present time, thought it was not inconsistent with the principles of tem- perance to allow the inmates one glass of beer in 12 months. He thought it was the wrong time to raise the question of economy at Christmas time, as they never thought of it. If they did there would be no Christmas dinner. Major CART WRIGHT remarked that no coffee was made.

Christmastide, the great festival of the year, was cele- brated in Warrington with wonted hilarity. Each succeeding year the display made by the tradespeople, in preparation for the events seems to eclipse its predecessor, and the ingenuity exhibited in the art of window dressing this year has had the desired effect. Crowds of persons lined the streets on Saturday, and viewed with delight the various shop windows, resplendent with Christmas goods of every conceivable description. The markets, too, decorated with prize beef, splendid mutton, and tempting poultry, were thronged throughout the day, and the appearance of the stalls in the evening showed that the holders had reaped a harvest. Christmas Day fell this year upon Sunday, and the festival was ushered in unaccompanied by the weather usually associated with it. The meteorological conditions were, in fact, dispiriting. Rain commenced to fall on Satur• day evening and continued to do so for several hours; and , as the wind increased it was extremely disagreeable out of doors. Still the "Glad tidings of great joy" were conveyed by numerous bands of mdsicians who showed a determina- tion to take their accustomed part in the festivities; and , when the rain had ceased, in the small hours of the morning, I Christmas greetings were exchanged between drowsy house- holders and the choirs which had turned out to pay their annual visits. Very few persons were seen about the streets on Christmas Day, so unfavourable was the weather. The I episcopal churches were decorated as usual, but the evening services here, and also at the Nonconformist places of wor- ship, were very poorly attended. This was doubtless owing to family parties being held on that day. The general merry-making was, however, deferred until the following day, and the enthusiasm with which the festival was then observed was as great as on any previous occasion. Monday was a general holiday, and as the weather lead improved upon that of the previous day, large numbers of holiday makers were strolling about the streets wishing their acquaintances the "compliments of the season." Many persons went to Manchester and Liverpool to see the panto- mimes in those cities, and at home the performance of " Cinderella " at Harmston's circus was witnessed by a crowded house. Numerous tea meetings and other enter- tainments were held in the evening, reports of which will be found below. Business was almost entirely suspended on Tuesday, the greater portion of the works being stopped and the shops closed. Very few persons were locked up for drunkenness, a circumstance arising no doubt from the lenity exercised by the poliae upon holiday occasions. THE MARKET STALLS. The greengrocers in the new market shed had, on Satur- day morning, elaborately decorated their stall with mistletoe and holly; and to encourage them in their attempt at artistic designing the Markets Committee decided to give prizes to the four persons vrho exhibited their goods to the best advantage. Alderman Chandley (chairman of the Markets Committee) and Councillor Litton were appointed judges, and these gentlemen, in the presence of a large number of people who had been attracted, by the display, examined the stalls on Saturday morning. Their awards were as follow :-Ist prize, 10a., Mr. David Plinston ; 2nd, ss. 61, Mr. James Longshaw ; 3rd, 3s. 6d. Mr. Edward Lewis; 4th, 25. 6d., Mr. Thomas Holland. The last named, it is stated, and the unsuccessful stallholders, questioned the justice of these awards, and they secured the services, as judges, of a pumber of country gardeners, whose decisions were directly antagonistic to those of the appointed judges. But each stall' holder appeared to be fully convinced that his or her stall was deserving of the first place—" nothing less and nothing more." They each, therefore, obtained a card with "First prize " printed upon it in bold letters, and purchasers were considerably amused to see almost the whole of the stalls ticketed "First prize." After the manner in which the greengrocers have received the generosity of the Committee, we scarcely think the prizes will be offered another year. THE WORKHOUSE. In consequence of Christmas Day falling on Sunday, the customary festivities were held at the Workhouse on Mon- day. The dining hall was gaily bedecked with flags, mottos, and evergreens, and had a very cheerful appearance. The inmates assembled at twelve o'clock for dinner, which consisted of roast beef and plum pudding, and the feast was heartily enjoyed. Altogether the festival was celebrated with far greater enthusiasm than last year, and this is doubt- less to be ascribed to the presence of visitors and, it may be, the supply of beer, which was prohibited last Christmas. Certain it is that on the present occasion, in marked contrast to last year, the inmates were stimulated to indulge in cheers, and they seemed to be far mere hilarious. Amongst those present were Mr. Joseph Harrison (chairman of the Board). Major Cartwright (chairman of the House Com- mittee), Mrs. Cartwright, Mr. and Mrs. Robert Garnett, Mr. Robert Heaton, Mr. and Mrs. Mackey (master and matron), Mr. Curry (porter), and other officials of the House. Suit- able addresses were delivered by the Chairman, Major Cartwright, and others, and, after dinner, cheers were given for the visitors and the master and matron. The remainder of the day was spent in an enjoyable manner. At the Barracks, 180 children were regaled with roast beef and plum pudding, and oranges and apples were afterwards dis- tributed. Mr. J. Harrison, the Rev. J. Yonge (chairman of the Schools Committee), Mr. William Darbyshire, Mr. C. N. Spinks (medical officer), and others visited the schools and delivered appropriate speeches. Dancing and singing were indulged in during the evening, and cheers were given for the various officers connected with ls",s,,schools. THE BARRACsis S. Next to the sailor, the soldier looks forward to Christmas with feelings of the most pleasurable anticipation, and at Orford Barracks great preparations had been made for its advent. In the building known by the name of" Prince," occupied by the first and second battalions of the South Lancashire Regiment, four rooms had been decorated, and they presented a very gay appearance. There was con- siderable similarity between the rooms and a description of one will suffice for all. Running round the top of the wall of Room No. 3, was a chain of evergreens, studded with roses, and suspended across the room from almost every point, were festoons, some made of holly and mistletoe, and others of coloured paper. The wall above the fireplace was draped with red cloth, bespranglect with silver stars, having in the centre a portrait of the Prince of Wales. The portrait was encircled with the scroll,ivritten in blue letters on a white ground, "Success to the Prince of Wales, and success to his Volunteers." At the top end of the room the wall was hidden with banners with a star formed of bayonets in the centre, over which was the motto of the volunteers "Defence, not defiance" and beneath "God save the Queen." Othr appropriate mottoes also adorned the walls, and that of " Our comrades in India," showed that their absent brethren in arms were not forgotten. The regiment has taken an active part in 21 engagements, and the names of several of these, in gilt letters, ornamented each room. Amongst them were, Luckloef, Peninsula, Sevastopol, Monte Video, Vittoria, Egypt, Candabar, Cabul, Maharajpoor, Nivelle. The men on Christmas Day were provided with a capital dinner (to which the militia were invited) of roast beef, turkey, goose, drc., with the indispensable accompaniment of plum pud- ding but the merrymaking was reserved for Monday, when a ball was held. The music was supplied by a band com- posed of men from the several companies, and the devotees of Terpsichore `.‘ tripped it" until four o'clock on Tuesday morning. HILL CLIFFE BAPTIST CHAPEL. There was a large attendance at the annual tea meeting in connection with this chapel, which took place on Monday evening. Afterwards a public meeting was held, under the presidency of the pastor, the Rev. W, Pilling.—The Chair- man having explained the cause of the absence of Mr. Mc- Minnies, M.P. (who was to have occupied the chair), and several other gentlemen who were expected to take part in the proceedings, Mr. Garden, of the Baptist College, Man- chester, spoke en the subject of "A living church." A living Church, he said, was a band of men and women who had been renewed by the Holy Spirit, who had been born again, who had consecrated their lives to the service of God, every one of whom should try to infuse spiritual life into the Church. As to the characteristics of a living Church. In the first place a living Church was an active Church. Another characteristic of a living Church was that it was fruitful; and if there were life, activity, and fruitfulness, there would also be progress in the Church, and its influ- ence would be felt. The members ought to be like finger' pests, to guide fallen humanity to "the Lamb of God, which taketh away the sins of the world."—Mr. Lewis, student of the Baptist College, Manchester, delivered an address upon "Progress," reiturking that if young men who wished to become useful members in the Church and in the world, would make the Bible their special study, they would progress not only in this life but in that which was to come.—The Rev. J. Yonge (Congregationalist) spoke of the growing laxity of the population in attendance upon public worship, contrasted the attendance of the present day with what it was 30 years ago, and pointed out that the remedy lay very much in the band's of the individual mem- bers. He denounced the prevalent idea that the minister, and he alone, was to do all the work. They had heard much about progress that evening, and if they were to make progress each individual member must use all his efforts to bring those outside the Church within the sound of the gospel.—Mr. Guy Harvey also briefly addressed the meeting.—The choir was in attendance, and sang several pieces very effectively at intervals.—On the motion of Mr. Jepson, a vote of thanks was accorded to the choir and others who had contributed much to their entertainment that evening; and a similar compliment having been paid to the chairman, the proceedings terminated with the Bene- diction being pronounced. THE CLUBS. Politicians have as keen an enjoyment of the jovial time of Christmas as other people, and there'is no reason why their clubs shoald not be made as attractive as possible at this period of the year. The Liberals at least, appear to take this view, and their club in Bewsey-street, reflects, by its decorations, the cheeriness of Christmas, and the buoyancy of the party. Entering the large billiard room, there is at once seen the wish "Long lif e and prosperity to our e r eod On capitalsthe rigohnt member, J. G. McMinnies, Req., M a dark ground, with a fringe offvF"yl neiayselsv. side uof nttyh ef rarnocohmi sea,l,saonidn vr eeer etdralde ett,,e,rwi nhg, il satr conspicuously the mottoes on the left is the watchword of the party " Peace, retrench- ment and reform." The numerous pictures which adorn the walls of the large room are decorated with evergreens, Wily, fir burs, &ea extra attention havins, been bestowed upon the oil painting of Mr. McMinnies. 'When leaving the room, there comes prominently into sight, the question "Should old acquaintance be forgot ?" and immediately is supplied the answer in the words "Majority 529." The refreshment room is decorated with holly and evergreens, and on the walls are "Success to our club" and "Compliments of the season," which wish is also expressed on the wall leading

to the subscription billiard rooms. No decoration was needed for the newsroom, the splendid wall paintings which it contains having recently been cleaned, and the room painted. The decorations were in charge of Mr. Norman, the club keeper, who has discharged his task with credit. —At the Conservative Club no attempt had been made at decoration, a few sprigs of holly placed in the newsroom and billiard room being the only evidences of Christmas.

THE INFIRMARY. The patients in the Infirmary, although separated from home and friends, were not allowed 'to forget the advent of Christmas, nor denied the enjoyments of some of its atten- dant pleasures. At this season of the year home is almost invariably decorated with evergreens, and the nurses by their aid imparted to each ward a bright and cheerful appearance. The chandeliers were adorned with holly and misletoe, and at the head of each bed were tastefully arranged evergreens and parti-coloured roses. On Christmas day a dinner of roast beef, potatoes, and plum pudding was provided, fol- lowed by a plentiful dessert of fruit, nuts,cakes,:&c., and the patients, as far as their state would allow, thoroughly en- joyed themselves. The Mayoress (Mrs. Pickmere), sent a large Christmas hamper, Mrs. Stubs, a quantity of evergreens and a Christmas card for each patient; and Dr. Richmond presented some wines. The Ladies' Committee also provided a considerable quantity of the evergreens by which the wards had been rendered so attractine. THE OLD MEN'S DINNER. It is pleasing to note that those who have the means of pro- viding for themselves good Christmas dinners do not forget, in the midst of their festivities, their poorer neighbours. By the subscriptions of kindly intentioned persons, the aged poor are annually treated, the men to a substantial dinner, and the women to a capital tea. The dinner took place in the Public Hall, on Thursday, and the hearts of the subscribers would have been gladdened could they have seen the ex- pressions of delight upon the countenances of the 214 men who assembled to partake of the feast so bountifully pro- vided by their contributions. The ages of the men ranged from 60 to 87 years, and, although several seemed to be in possession of fall manly vigour, most of them bore evidence of the effects of time, the company including the lame, halt, and partially blind. At 12 o'clock, steaming joints of roast beef were placed upon the tables, and after grace had been said the committee acted as carvers, and the feast com- menced. In a short time the beef was transferred to the plates of the diners, and a large number of waiters were kept fully employed for about an hour, in attending to the wants of the old men. After the plum pudding had been disposed of, the patriarchs were supplied with church-wardens and half ounces of tobacco with which to charge them, and the room was soon filled with the fumes of burning incense. While the devotees of Bacchus were paying tribute, Council- lor J. Pierpoint (presideAt of the committee), proposed the health of the Queen, Prince of Wales, and the rest of the Royal Family, and the toast having, been drunk, cheers were given for the Queen. The "Army and Navy" was next given, and Mr. J. Whittaker responded. He joined the Royal artillery in April. 1847, and was sent to the Crimea, but was not in any engagement ; and on his return home he was kicked by a horse, and was discharged in July, 1855, after serving eight years and three months. The Rev. S. Wilkinson afterwards addressed the assembly. He remarked that he was glad to find the ladies and gentlemen of Warrington still took an interest in the proceedings, and that he was glad to see those present. Their appetites had certainly not altered, but were very good inAeed. (Applause.) He could not address them so near the close of 1881, and so near the beginning of 1882, without saying one or two solemn words. They were just ending the old year with all its privileges, with all its mercies, and with all its sins. They were just going to enter upon the new year, during which they might depend upon it a great number of them would pass away. Therefore, he said to every one of them "Prepare to meet your God." He knew he was addressing that day people of different religious persuasions. They had many present connected with the Church of England, many connected with St. Alban's and St. Mary's Churches, and a number connected with the various Nonconformist bodies in War- rington ; and although they differed on many points, still they had this one great object in view—to live to the honour and glory of God here so that they might meet with Him hereafter. Therefore, let each one strive during the coming year to live nearer to God than they had done before, and then he could promise they would all have a happy and prosperous new year. He wished them all in God's name a happy and prosperous new year. (Applause.) The Rev. THOMAS RIPPON said he was going to ask them to accord to the president and committee their heartiest thanks for the dinner they had provided. He was sure as a visitor he had been delidted to see them all enjoy them- selves as they had done. He dared say if one of them rose to respond they would be in sympathy with that old alderman who was called upon to respond at the Lord Mayor's ban- quet and could only articulate "My Lord Mayor, I am too f all for utterance. (Laughter.) Perhaps they had not arrived at that high state of feeling, but he dared say they had enjoyed the good cheer and would go away with the kindliest feelings towards those who had been so liberal. He hoped they would remember Mr. Wilkinson's remarks, and having wished the new year would be to them one of the happiest and one of the brightest they had ever experienced, I concluded Dy calling upon them to give a hearty cheer for I the president and committee. The cheer having been given, Councillor PIERPOINT, in replying, said their thanks would be received by the committee viith a great amount of pleasure and considered a sufficient reward for the onerous services they rendered in procuring the feast for the benefit of those assembled in the hall. (Hear, hear). The com- mittee were not the only persons who provided them with amusement. They had many friends who came from Liver- pool, Birkenhead, and Manchester to affad some amusement to the old folks, and more especially in the evening. Mr. Sheridan, proprietor of the Prince of Wales Theatre, had also sent an invitation for the old men and women to visit his performance on Saturday afternoon. In addition to that Mr. Harmston, proprietor of the large circus in Sankey street, had sent an invitation for them to attend the perfor- mance there on Monday afternoon—(applause),—and he hoped as many as could possibly do so would avail them- selves of the great favours bestowed upon them by the proprietors of these establishments. He thanked them most cordially for the vote of thanks, and hoped their remaining years would be very happy. (Applause). Amongst those present were, Councillor John Pierpoint (president), Messrs. T, Morris, J. E. Wright, S. Jones J. Smethurst, W. Horton, N. Legge, P. Chrimea,W. Dooley, committee; Rev. S. Wilkinson, Rev. F. W. Cory, Rev. E. C. E. Carleton, Rev'. E. St. A. Duke, Rev. T. Rippon, Rev. M. Schonberg, Mrs. J. Pierpoint, Mrs. Seed, (of Preston), Mrs. P. Chrimes, Mrs. T. Morris, Mrs. Skinner, Mrs. Smeth- hurst, Mrs. Wilkinson, Mrs. Carleton, Mrs. Venn, the Misses Geddes, tke Misses Horton, Miss Townsend, Miss Guy, Miss Fraser, &c. BUTTERMA.RKET-STREET WESLEYAN SUNDAY SCHOOL. _ . .

A tea party, followed by; conversazione, promoted by the teachers of the lhove school, was held in the Workmen's Club, Market-place, on Monday. About 150 persons were present at the tea, over which the following ladies presided: —Miss Sobey, Miss Collin, Miss Mellor, Miss Lilley, Miss Richardson, and Miss Rowley. The conversazione was opened by Mr. A. Mackie, and amongst those present were: —Messrs. J. B. Isaacs (superintendent of the school), Thos. Prince, Wm. Nicholson, Henry Barber, John Waring, Wm. Clark, Proud (Frodsham), R. W. Collin, E. B. Bowser, F. Dixon, J. Dobsw, J. M. Muir, John Gaudy, and Weaver. Mr. MACKIE, who was received with applause, said it was at least 25 years since he was invited to their annual tea meeting at Buttermarket schoolroom, and he asked what had the Wesleyans done during that long period? They had erected Wesley Hall and provided for a good portion of their fair share of the increase of the town. They rejoiced at the means and the success. But, had as much been done, after all, as ought considering the growth of the town? Butter- market school had been a doomed building for a quarter of a century, but it had been tinkered instead of rebuilt, or re- placed by a first-class building near to Bold-street chapel. The locallity, and the members of the present school pleaded for its life, under altered conditions. But the permanent success of Weslyanism in Warrington demanded a new Sunday school, with every modern comfort, and with every consistent attraction. The old churches and chapels he War- rington had been "restored " or re-built during the past twenty years; but with one marked exception, the schools remained as they were. He believed the success of every church and chapel in Warrington,so far as keeping up a crop of zealous worshippers was concerned, was indissolubly con- nected with a good and attractive Sunday school room—a room that, first, secured privacy to the senior classes; second, easy inspection to the superintendent; third, an opportunity i of opening and closing the school n the presence of the teachers, and all the scholars; fourth,. a really handsome, well-fitted up and internally adorned building, in which every one connected with it might take legitimate pride, and speak of it as" our'school," and lastly, a room that would during the week be open, both in the day time and evening, to every- one having any claim upon it, fires, and suitable books and i newspapers being provided, free f possible. In the evenings he would precede, or follow, the pure religious meetings by those more secular, and make the Sunday school building a home, a club, or a resting place, for every member, teacher, and scholar. (Applause.) On the continent the grandest churches were open daily to the poorest waifs. He had seen shoeless children i in the grandest of all buildings, Milan Cathedral, at six n the morning, no doorkeeper forbidding them. We had not and could not Jaave such daily services In churches and chapels filled with pews. But might we not have resting places such as he had described in connection with all the Sunday schools, and these made public and popular? Lang ere this some faint-heart was saying— " But what about the money ?" Who had ever known War- rington slack in a good cause? He had not. No Wesleyan had. During the last 12 or 14 years they must have spent close on a thousand a year on buildings ancient and modern Might he expressl a hope that the time was fast approaching when they would once more arise and build? (Applause.) They should go in and win a first-class Sunday schoolroom, attractive within and without. Speaking to the teachers, he urged them to continue at the work. There were and had been some excellent examples in Warrington, such as Mr. Beamont, Mr. Parkinson, and the late bite. In conclusion he said their ministers were deserving in the very highest i degree of all the assistance they could give them n, connec- tion with a first-class Sunday school. He knew nothing more likely to feed, both Bold-street chapel and Wesley chapel than good Sunday schools, in which the young, when they bad once been admitted, might be nurtured and preserved. which was the more difficult of the two, and led into these two places of worship. (Applause.) He thought the ministers had claim upon them all for assistance in this work, for assistance in procuring a day school iii connection with these places of worship of a superior kind, or at least of a second school. If they found it in their hearts to do

(Applause.)—A pianoforte duet (overture) "IL Barbiere de Seviglia " (Rossini) was then given in a very creditable manner by Mr. J. M. Muir and Mr. G. S. Pendlebury. Mise Richardson sang in capital style "Cherry ripe ; " end the Rev. J. Agar Beet then delivered an address on "The Micro- scope." The microscopic views were very interesting, and considerable amusement was derived from the galvaniC batteries lent for the occasion. Mr. Gartland, late of the Royal Horse Artillery, exhibited a beautiful collection of Indian flies, the skin of a cobra capella, together with number of Indian saws shoes, and other curiosities. Mr. Mackie lent a number of books and maps; and Mr. Fletcher'S domestic heating acd cooking apparatus was also exhibited. The musical part of the grogramme was contributed to by Master Levi Richardson Miss H. Toft, Miss Sherlock, Miss Richardson, Mr. G. S. iendlebury, and Mr. J. M. Muir, the latter acting as accompanist. Mr. J. B. Isaac gave a reacting entitled "Leek-street chapel."—A vote of thanks to Mr. ; Mackie for his services was accorded at the conclusion Of the proceedings.

The Master reported that there were 547 inmates as against 493 in the corresponding week of last year. The number of vagrants relieved during the week was 128, 102 being men, 16 women, and 10 children,

HALTou Pilsrz Cullum—This church was beauti- fully decorated for the season of the year; the chancel by Lady Brooke, and the nave by various members of the con- gregation and choir. There were good congregations both morning and evening, when, being Christmas Day, each ser- vice began and ended with a processional hymn. THE WARRINGTON TRAGEDY : DEATH OF SCHOL'TZE. —At Liverpool, on Saturday last, before, Mr. Clarke Aspinall, the city coroner, an enquiry was held in relation to the death of Edward Scholtze, aged 48, a glass engraver, who lived in Hoyle-street, Warrington. In October last the deceased was committed to the city prison to await trial for wounding his wife with intent to murder, but owing to a self-inflicted wound of his throat, he was not in a condition to be tried. On the evening of the 22nd inst. he died, according to medical evidence, of dropsy and bronchitis, in conjunction with the injury to the throat. The verdict was , one of "Death from natural causes, accelerated by the , wound in the throat."

AN EARNEST APPEAL is made on behalf of JOHN HARRISON, formerly boatman at Runcorn Fetry. now permanently disabled by bodily inftrmlty at the advanced age of 66. During his 45 years' public service as ferryman, he gained the respect of all who knew him by his civility, kind- ness, and steady attention to duty in all weathers, as shown by the fact that not a single accident occurred during his time.
